summary: Study ~185 reference repos individually, distill their innovations by category, and design the nest master plan (most compact sovereign AI database)
logs: 3 architecture plans in; merging into master

categories.name: compression-general
categories.focus: general-purpose byte compression and entropy coding

repos.one_liner: A general-purpose LZ77-family compressor that pairs a fast match-finder with two entropy back-ends (Huff0 Huffman for literals, FSE/tANS table-based ANS for sequence symbols), plus trained dictionaries, long-distance matching, and a repeat-offset cache, all wrapped in a self-describing frame/block format.
repos.core_innovation: Trained dictionaries: zstd's ZDICT trainer (COVER/fastCover greedy segment selection) builds a small shared "prior" -- a synthetic past window plus pre-baked entropy tables (Huffman tree + FSE tables for literals/match-lengths/offsets + 3 seed repeat-offsets) -- prepended to the decode window so each tiny, independently-decodable payload compresses against shared cross-record statistics instead of starting cold. This is exactly nest's regime: many small structurally-similar records (chunk_ids, spans, provenance JSON, BM25 postings) compressed in isolation, where per-payload entropy tables and LZ history are pure overhead today.
key_techniques: Two-stage entropy: Huff0 (canonical Huffman, max 11-bit codes, weight-encoded tree) for literals; FSE = table-driven tANS for literal-length/match-length/offset symbols, with an Accuracy_Log power-of-2 normalized distribution and per-symbol (Symbol, Num_Bits, Baseline) decode rows
4 independent Huffman bitstreams decoded in parallel for ILP vs 1 stream; bitstreams read backward from the last byte
Repeat-offset cache: 3 most-recent offsets (rep1/rep2/rep3) with single-stepped wrapping rotation, so periodic data spends ~1 offset code instead of a full offset
Per-block FSE table modes: Predefined / RLE / FSE_Compressed / Repeat (reuse previous block's table) to amortize table cost
ZDICT dictionary trainer (COVER / fastCover): greedy frequent-segment selection building a shared prior + pre-baked entropy tables + seed repeat offsets
Long-distance matching (LDM): a coarse hash-chain over a large window (up to 2GB) catching far-apart duplicates before the normal match-finder
Self-describing frame: 4-byte magic + 2-14B header, 3-byte block headers, optional xxHash-64 checksum, plus 16 skippable-frame magics (0x184D2A5x) for additive metadata old decoders skip
Configurable speed/ratio via levels incl. negative --fast levels; decode speed roughly constant across levels
repos.nest_application: Three concrete moves, all in nest-format/src/encoding/zstd_codec.rs and the writer. (1) DICTIONARY: add zstd_encode_with_dict/zstd_decode_with_dict using zstd's dictionary API. Train ONE deterministic dictionary at build time over the small repetitive sections (chunk_ids, chunks_original_spans, provenance, search_contract, BM25 postings/terms in 0x08) and store it as a new additive section (reserved id 0x09) or in the manifest. Determinism holds because ZDICT is a pure function of sorted samples (feed them in canonical/alphabetical order). (2) KNOBS: replace hardcoded encode_all(bytes, 19) with a ZstdParams struct (level + enable_long_distance_matching + window_log) set per preset (tiny -> level 22 + LDM for the whole-database/repo payloads in the north star). (3) SKIPPABLE-FRAME PATTERN as a format lesson for nest-format/src/layout: zstd's 0x184D2A5x magics are the canonical way an additive format lets old readers skip unknown extensions -- mirror this for nest's reserved section ids 0x09+. Constraints respected: zstd never touches embeddings (hot SIMD path), section checksums still hash physical bytes, content_hash still hashes decoded bytes so a dict-compressed section yields the same content_hash as raw.
repos.compression_relevance: Central to "compress more than everyone." nest already vendors zstd but uses its weakest config: level-19, no dictionary, no LDM, each small section compressed cold. Trained dictionaries are the single highest-leverage zstd feature for nest's many-small-similar-records workload and can sharply cut the non-embedding footprint at tiny corpus sizes; LDM extends the same engine to whole-repo/whole-database payloads. FSE/tANS and the repeat-offset trick are reference designs for any future nest-native entropy coder over postings or quantized residuals.
repos.license: Dual-licensed BSD-3-Clause OR GPL-2.0 (permissive BSD path -> safe to vendor/link; the Rust zstd crate nest already depends on wraps this).
repos.perf_notes: Reference C: ~510 MB/s compress, ~1550 MB/s decompress at level -1; decode speed is roughly level-independent (entropy-bound, not match-bound). The 4-stream Huffman split exists purely to exploit superscalar ILP. FSE/tANS decode is a tight table-lookup loop (1 lookup + bit-refill per symbol), branch-light and cache-friendly with a power-of-2 table. Dictionary decode adds a one-time window prefill, no steady-state cost. None runs on nest's hot path (embeddings never zstd-compressed), so all zstd cost is amortized one-time at build/cold-section decode.

repos.one_liner: A general-purpose lossless byte compressor combining a modern LZ77 with a 16 MiB sliding window, a 121-transform static dictionary, per-category Huffman prefix codes selected by 2nd-order context modeling, and block-type switching, standardized in RFC 7932.
repos.core_innovation: The static dictionary + word-transform layer: ~13,504 base words (4-24 bytes) expanded by 121 reversible word transforms (prefix/suffix add, FermentFirst/FermentAll case-shifts, OmitFirstN/OmitLastN cuts) into ~1.6M effective entries, addressed as ordinary LZ77 back-references whose distance overflows the sliding-window range. A tiny shipped dictionary acts as a giant priming corpus so the very first occurrence of a domain string compresses to one short reference, killing cold-start redundancy that pure window-based LZ cannot touch.
key_techniques: 121 word transforms over 13,504 base words: Identity, FermentFirst (uppercase first), FermentAll (uppercase all), OmitFirst1-9, OmitLast1-9, plus optional literal prefix/suffix bytes (RFC 7932 Appendix B); reconstruction is word_id=distance-(maxdist+1), index=word_id%NWORDS[len], transform_id=word_id>>NDBITS[len]

Static dictionary addressed through the SAME LZ77 <length,distance> mechanism: distance < maxdist+1 means window back-reference, distance >= maxdist+1 means dictionary lookup; one unified copy path, no separate opcode

2nd-order context modeling: per-literal Huffman tree chosen via CMODE[blocktype] + context-id from last two output bytes, indexing a 64-entry-per-blocktype context map CMAPL; distances use a 4-entry context map keyed on copy length

Block-type switching: independent block-length counters for Literals/InsertCopy/Distances; when a counter hits zero a new block type and run-length are read, swapping the active Huffman trees mid-stream (adaptive without re-sending tables)
Combined insert-and-copy command codes that fuse literal-run length with copy length into one symbol, cutting command overhead
Variable sliding window from 1 KiB-16 to 16 MiB-16, negotiated per stream
RFC 9841 Shared Brotli: custom/context-dependent dictionaries and custom transform lists that override Appendix B, enabling domain-trained shared dictionaries
repos.nest_application: Two distinct steals, both in nest-format encoding/sections. (1) Domain shared-dictionary for text sections: nest already vendors zstd for non-embedding sections; zstd natively supports trained dictionaries (zstd --train / ZDICT). Train one deterministic dictionary over chunks_canonical at build time in nest-python, store it as a new additive section (reserved id 0x09+, encoding id stays a zstd variant in the 4-255 reserved range), and have nest-runtime mmap+prime the zstd decoder with it. For nest's corpora (PT-BR fake-news, repeated boilerplate, JSON/YAML keys) this is exactly brotli's cold-start win and should materially shrink the 'tiny' preset's text bytes below the current 0.283 ratio while keeping content_hash stable (dict affects only physical encoding, not decoded canonical bytes). (2) The transform idea itself adapts to a nest-native lightweight text codec: a small frozen word-list + reversible transforms (case/prefix/suffix/cut) is a deterministic, dependency-free way to squeeze repetitive structured text (JSON/YAML field names, URL prefixes, dataset schemas) without pulling brotli's C core into the small rust core. Either way it lives entirely on the non-embedding text path, never touching the float embedding hot path that must stay raw-scored from mmap.
repos.license: MIT (brotli reference implementation); RFC 7932/9841 formats are open standards
repos.compression_relevance: Directly on the north-star 'compress more than everyone' axis. The shared-dictionary trick is the single highest-leverage gain for nest's text/JSON/YAML sections: it attacks inter-chunk and cold-start redundancy that per-chunk zstd misses, and is the standard way trained dictionaries beat generic compressors on many small similar records. Window/context/Huffman details are reference-grade but lower priority since nest delegates byte entropy coding to vendored zstd.
repos.perf_notes: Brotli decompresses at deflate-class speed (browser-grade) and compresses 17-25% denser than gzip on web text; levels 10-11 do near-exhaustive dictionary+transform search and are slow, levels 1-9 are fast. The transform table is data-only (no SIMD); dictionary lookup is O(1) array indexing. For nest the relevant cost is build-time only (dictionary training in python) plus a one-time decoder prime in rust; runtime decode stays cheap and the embedding hot path is untouched, so zero impact on SIMD dot-product latency.

repos.one_liner: A speed-first LZ77 byte compressor that emits a stream of tag-byte-prefixed elements (literals + back-reference "copies") with no entropy coding, hitting ~250 MB/s compress / ~500 MB/s decompress at ~1.5-4x ratio, plus a chunked framing format with per-chunk masked CRC-32C for streaming.
repos.core_innovation: The transferable idea is the tag-byte element stream: every element begins with one byte whose low 2 bits select element type (00 literal, 01/10/11 copy with 1/2/4-byte offset) and whose high 6 bits pack the small-case length/offset inline, so the common case costs exactly one control byte with zero entropy-coding state. This makes the format branch-cheap, alignment-tolerant (LE unaligned loads), and table-free to decode — the opposite of zstd/FSE which need decode state. Paired with it: a base-128 varint preamble (7 data bits + continuation bit) for total length, and an independent chunked framing layer (4-byte header = 1 type byte + 3-byte LE length) where each chunk carries a masked CRC-32C of its UNCOMPRESSED bytes so streams are splittable, concatenable, and verifiable per-chunk.
key_techniques: tag-byte element encoding: low 2 bits = type {literal, copy1B, copy2B, copy4B}, high 6 bits = inline length/offset for the common small case

three copy classes by offset width: 1-byte offset (0-2047, len 4-11, 3 high offset bits in tag), 2-byte offset (0-65535, len 1-64), 4-byte offset (full 32-bit), trading control-byte size against reach
literal length escape: high-6-bits 0-59 = (len-1) inline; 60-63 = read 1-4 following LE bytes as the length, keeping long literals cheap
LE base-128 varint preamble for total uncompressed length (7 payload bits + MSB continuation)
single-probe hash table of 4-byte fragments for match finding (no lazy match, no entropy coder) - source of the speed/ratio tradeoff
framing: back-to-back chunks, 4-byte header (1 type byte + 3-byte LE length), ids partitioned into reserved-skippable (0x80-0xfd) vs reserved-unskippable (0x02-0x7f) for forward-compatible extension
masked CRC-32C per chunk over UNCOMPRESSED data, mask = ((x>>15)|(x<<17)) + 0xa282ead8 to avoid CRC-of-CRC weakness
format assumes cheap unaligned LE 32/64-bit loads, enabling overlapping copies and word-at-a-time literal moves
repos.nest_application: Two adaptations, both in nest-format. (1) Adopt Snappy's reserved-id partitioning for nest's section/encoding id space: Snappy splits skippable vs unskippable extension ranges so old decoders behave predictably on unknown chunks. nest v1 is additive-only with section ids 0x09+ and encoding ids 4-255 RESERVED; formalize a "skippable optional vs unskippable required" bit on section entries in crates/nest-format/src/layout and reader so a future v1 file with an unknown OPTIONAL section (e.g. a new graph index) still validates and serves on an older runtime, while unknown REQUIRED sections error cleanly via NestError - extending the additive guarantee without a v2 bump. (2) Use Snappy's tag-byte stream as the blueprint for a pure-Rust, panic-free, deterministic LZ77 fallback codec in crates/nest-format/src/encoding (new module behind a reserved SECTION_ENCODING id, never applied to embeddings) for when nest must drop the zstd C dependency to stay fully sovereign/offline in one binary. Import only the stream layout (varint preamble + 1/2/4-byte copy classes), not Snappy's CRC, since nest's four SHA-256 surfaces already cover integrity. The same varint+tag scheme is directly reusable to shrink small metadata sections (chunk_ids, chunks_original_spans) where deltas are tiny and zstd's container overhead dominates.
repos.compression_relevance: Indirect, not on the hot ratio path. nest already uses zstd level 19, which compresses TEXT meaningfully better than Snappy (Snappy explicitly trades 20-100% larger output for ~10x speed and applies no entropy coding), so Snappy's codec must NOT replace zstd for the headline "compress more than everyone" goal. Its relevance is structural: (a) a sovereign zero-C-dependency fallback codec when nest vendors everything into one binary; (b) the tag-byte/varint scheme as low-overhead encoding for small metadata sections where zstd container overhead dominates; (c) the skippable/unskippable extension discipline that protects the additive-format guarantee as the format grows toward repos/audio/video.
repos.license: BSD-3-Clause (permissive; safe to vendor or reimplement the documented, unpatented format)
repos.perf_notes: ~250 MB/s compress, ~500 MB/s decompress single-core 64-bit x86; ratios ~1.5-1.7x plain text, 2-4x HTML, ~1.0x already-compressed (jpeg/png). Speed comes from word-at-a-time unaligned LE loads, overlapping copy loops, and single-probe hash-table match finding (no lazy matching, no entropy coder). Format assumes cheap unaligned 32/64-bit LE loads - already true on nest's x86_64+aarch64 targets and aligned with nest's repr(C) little-endian-unsigned convention. Decompression is allocation-light and streamable, matching nest's mmap model.

repos.one_liner: A byte-aligned LZ77 compressor with no entropy coder, whose block format is a stream of [token | literal-length-extension | literals | 2-byte LE offset | match-length-extension] sequences decodable at multiple GB/s per core via branch-light wildcopy.
repos.core_innovation: A deliberately entropy-coder-free, byte-aligned block format whose decoder is so simple (no bit-unpacking, no Huffman/FSE tables, just memcpy-style literal and match copies) that decompression runs at RAM-bandwidth speed -- trading a few points of ratio for the ability to decode in a latency-critical hot path.
key_techniques: token byte split into two nibbles: high 4 bits = literal length, low 4 bits = match length (both 0-15)
LSIC (Linear Small-Integer Code) varint extension: when a nibble is 15, read add-255 continuation bytes until a non-255 byte, summing them onto the length
minmatch=4: match-length nibble of 0 already means a 4-byte copy, so the encoded value is matchlen-4, saving the unrepresentable short matches
2-byte little-endian back-reference offset, max 65535 (64KB sliding window); offset 0 is reserved as a corruption sentinel
hash table over 4-byte sequences mapping prefix->latest position for O(1) greedy match finding; LZ4_HC adds chain tables / lazy+optimal parsing for higher ratio at lower speed
wildcopy: copy literals and matches in fixed 8-byte machine-word chunks past the exact length (requires output over-allocation slack) to eliminate per-byte branching
frozen end-of-block invariants (last 5 bytes always literals, last match >=12 bytes before end) that let speed-oriented decoders skip bounds checks
frame layer (magic 0x184D2204, FLG/BD descriptor) with selectable 64KB/256KB/1MB/4MB block sizes, optional block-linking within the 64KB window, and xxHash-32 block/content checksums
repos.nest_application: Add an lz4 block codec to nest-format/src/encoding/ as a new wire-encoding id (reserve one of the free 4-255 slots, additive within v1, registered in layout alongside SECTION_ENCODING_ZSTD and wired into decode_payload in encoding/mod.rs). Its purpose is NOT to beat zstd on cold sections (zstd already wins on ratio) but to be the first compressor nest can legally apply to hot-path-decoded surfaces that zstd is currently banned from. Two concrete targets: (1) chunks_canonical/text when nest-runtime materialize() reads it per query -- GB/s lz4 decode makes 'always-compressed text' viable without per-citation latency; (2) a future lz4-framed transparent layer over int8 embeddings where the runtime decodes a 64KB block into a small scratch buffer just-in-time before the SIMD dot product, since the branch-light wildcopy is cheap enough to amortize against the AVX2/NEON kernel cost -- the only realistic path to compressing embeddings (today raw/f16/int8 only) without breaking 'scored directly from mmap.' Also steal the LSIC add-255 varint and the frozen end-of-block invariants pattern for nest's own section-length and manifest varints (byte-granular, zero bit-shift, deterministic). Respect constraints: each codec file <=300 lines, typed thiserror errors, no panics; the format's repr-stable, little-endian, byte-aligned nature matches nest's repr(C) + LE rule exactly.
repos.compression_relevance: Indirect but strategic. lz4 LOSES to zstd on raw ratio, so it does not advance the 'compress more than everyone' headline on cold sections. Its relevance is unlocking compression on surfaces nest currently leaves uncompressed because the decode budget is too tight: embeddings (hot SIMD path) and per-citation text materialization. A GB/s-class, mmap-friendly, allocation-free codec is the prerequisite for ever compressing those, widening the set of compressible bytes even if each byte compresses less than under zstd.
repos.license: BSD 2-Clause for the library (lib/), GPLv2 for the programs/ CLI. The C library nest would bind or reimplement is BSD-2, permissive and Rust-reimplementation-friendly.
repos.perf_notes: Default ~780 MB/s compress at ~2.1x ratio; LZ4_HC ~41 MB/s compress at ~2.72x ratio; decompression multiple GB/s per core (often 4-5 GB/s), frequently RAM-bandwidth-bound. Decode has no entropy stage, is allocation-free and branch-light; wildcopy needs output-buffer over-allocation slack (copies in 8-byte chunks). xxHash-32 in the frame layer is a fast non-cryptographic checksum (not a substitute for nest's four SHA-256 surfaces, but a useful cheap per-block guard if nest ever streams sub-section blocks).

repos.one_liner: The canonical C reference implementation of DEFLATE (RFC 1951) and its zlib/gzip wrappers: LZ77 sliding-window matching via hash chains plus per-block dynamic Huffman entropy coding, with a table-driven multi-level inflate decoder.
repos.core_innovation: The two-stage table-driven Huffman decoder optimizing the common (short-code) case.
key_techniques: LZ77 sliding window (32KB) with backward (length,distance) references
hash-chain match finder: head[HASH_SIZE] + prev[w_size] linked chains, capped by max_chain_length
lazy matching (Wams): defer a literal to check if a longer match starts at the next position (levels >=4)
tunable heuristics good_match/nice_match/max_lazy_match/max_insert_length to trade ratio vs speed per level
canonical Huffman: per-block dynamic trees (dyn_ltree, dyn_dtree) built from symbol frequencies via a heap, code lengths transmitted compactly via bl_tree
block-type selection: stored vs fixed-Huffman vs dynamic-Huffman, picking the cheapest per block
multi-level inflate decode tables: root table covers root_bits, sub-tables handle overflow codes (1-15 bits)
deflateSetDictionary: prime the window with a known dictionary so the first bytes can back-reference it (great for many small similar payloads)
repos.nest_application: Two concrete steals. (1) The preset-dictionary idea (deflateSetDictionary) maps directly onto nest-format's encoding layer (crates/nest-format/src/encoding + sections): nest already zstd-compresses non-embedding sections, and chunks_canonical/provenance across a corpus share huge vocabulary overlap. Train one shared zstd dictionary (zstd has native zstd_compress_usingDict / trained dictionaries) over the corpus, store it once as a small additive sub-blob keyed under the existing zstd encoding id, and compress every text/json chunk against it. This is the single biggest win for nest's "compress more than everyone" north star on many-small-chunk corpora, and stays additive (no NEST_FORMAT_VERSION bump, deterministic if the dictionary is built deterministically). (2) The two-stage canonical-Huffman decode table is the reference design for any future bespoke entropy codec nest adds for a section type (e.g. a custom int8/residual codec): implement it in nest-runtime as a small repr-aligned decode table read straight from the mmap, keeping the no-panic, little-endian, <=300-loc-per-file constraints. The LZ77 hash-chain + lazy-match design is reference-level only (zstd already supersedes it for nest's actual codec).
repos.compression_relevance: High for text/json sections: shared preset dictionaries are the proven lever for compressing many small, vocabulary-overlapping payloads (exactly nest's chunks_canonical + provenance), directly serving the "compress data more than everyone" goal. Irrelevant to embeddings, which nest deliberately never entropy-codes because they are SIMD-scored off mmap on the hot path. The table-driven decode is relevant only if nest builds its own entropy codec rather than leaning on zstd.
repos.perf_notes: Decode hot loop is a bit-buffer + single table lookup for common codes, one extra indirection for rare long codes; root_bits sized "one bit above average code length" to minimize duplicate-entry fill cost. Encode speed is dominated by hash-chain walk length (max_chain_length) and lazy-match second searches; levels 1-3 skip lazy matching and limit hash insertions for speed. zlib-ng is the modern SIMD/perf fork (SIMD hash, faster CRC, slide) if kernel-level speed matters. CRC32 has a well-known slice-by-8/PCLMULQDQ vectorization but base zlib is largely scalar table-driven.
repos.license: zlib license (permissive, BSD-like, commercial-friendly, no attribution-in-binary requirement) -- vendor-safe for nest.

repos.one_liner: A modernized, SIMD-accelerated fork of zlib implementing DEFLATE (RFC 1951), zlib (RFC 1950) and gzip (RFC 1952) with runtime CPU dispatch over per-hot-path optimized kernels (CRC32, adler32, longest_match, slide_hash, compare256, inflate_fast).
repos.core_innovation: A central runtime "functable": a struct of function pointers (one per hot operation) resolved exactly once at startup from CPU feature detection, so every hot-loop call is a single indirect jump to the best kernel (scalar/SSE2/AVX2/AVX512/VPCLMULQDQ/NEON/PMULL+EOR3/RVV) with zero per-call CPUID branching. This cleanly decouples algorithm from microarchitecture across ~10 ISAs behind one stable dispatch surface.
key_techniques: functable: one-time-resolved struct of fn pointers per hot op, indirect call per hot loop, no per-call feature check
CRC32 via carryless multiply folding (PCLMULQDQ/VPCLMULQDQ on x86, ARMv8.2 PMULL+EOR3) instead of byte-at-a-time table
CRC32-C hardware intrinsic reused AS the hash function for the hash-chain match finder
Intel-derived deflate 'quick' and 'medium' match-finding strategies as fast tiers distinct from greedy/lazy slow tiers
longest_match / compare256 SIMD match extension (Cloudflare + fast_zlib lineage) comparing 256 bytes per SIMD step
slide_hash SIMD to bulk-decrement hash-chain heads on window slide
inflate_fast chunked copy (chunkmemset): overlapping vector loads/stores for LZ back-references instead of byte loops
ZLIB_COMPAT vs zlib-ng-native dual ABI: one engine, two header surfaces
repos.nest_application: Two concrete steals plus a reference boundary. (1) HASHING fast-path: nest's four SHA-256 surfaces in nest-format/src/hashing are the integrity contract and must stay cryptographic, but non-crypto work (dedup keys, section identity probes, future bm25 term hashing in nest-runtime) should use CRC32-C via carryless-multiply / ARMv8 CRC behind nest's existing OnceLock dispatcher in nest-runtime/src/simd/mod.rs, reusing the exact 'resolve once, indirect-call forever' pattern nest already uses for dot products. (2) DISPATCH PATTERN: generalize nest's SimdBackend OnceLock into a small functable-style struct of fn pointers so new kernels (f16 convert, i8 widen, a future bitpacked decoder) register one entry each instead of growing match arms inside every dot_* fn, keeping each simd/*.rs file under the 300-line cap as kernels multiply. (3) REFERENCE only for codecs: nest must NOT add a DEFLATE codec -- zstd-19 already beats DEFLATE on nest's text sections; the value is the engineering scaffolding, not the entropy coder.
repos.compression_relevance: Low-to-moderate for ratio: DEFLATE's Huffman+LZ77 is strictly weaker than the zstd FSE/Huffman+large-window nest already uses, so adopting zlib-ng's codec yields NO ratio win. Transferable compression-adjacent value: the SIMD inflate chunking pattern (overlapping vector copies for back-references) is the right template if nest ever ships a lightweight bitpacked/varint section decoder, and CRC-as-hash speeds dedup/identity work that precedes compression. Serves the 'compress more than everyone' north star only indirectly.
repos.perf_notes: Kernels resolved once at startup; hot loops pay one indirect call. VPCLMULQDQ+AVX512 CRC32 folds ~64 bytes/iter; ARMv8.2 PMULL+EOR3 is the aarch64 analog (directly relevant to nest's NEON target). inflate_fast replaces byte-wise LZ expansion with overlapping 16/32/64-byte vector moves; compare256 extends matches a full vector register per step. Tight inner loops, minimal extra memory.
repos.license: zlib license (permissive, BSD-like, no binary-attribution requirement). Vendor-friendly for nest's single-file ethos, but nest should reimplement the patterns in Rust rather than vendor C.

repos.one_liner: A heavily optimized MIT-licensed C library for DEFLATE/zlib/gzip that beats stock zlib ~2x on both compress and decompress by combining a minimum-cost-path ("near-optimal") parser at high levels with a two-level Huffman decode table and a 64-bit branchless bit-buffer refill on the decode side.
repos.core_innovation: Entropy-cost-driven optimal parsing: model the LZ choice as a shortest-path DAG over byte positions where each literal/match edge is weighted by its actual Huffman codeword length in fractional bits, then iterate (parse -> rebuild Huffman -> recompute costs -> reparse) until the bit cost converges. The encoder optimizes for the real post-entropy size, not a greedy length heuristic. The single transferable idea: pick encodings by measured bits-out, iterated to a fixpoint, rather than by a static rule.
key_techniques: Near-optimal parser: min-cost-path over a DAG of literal/match edges, cost = Huffman codeword length scaled by BIT_COST=16 for fractional-bit accounting

Iterative cost refinement: parse->count freqs->rebuild Huffman->recompute symbol costs->reparse, stop when improvement < threshold; unused symbols default to LITERAL/LENGTH_NOSTAT_BITS=13, OFFSET_NOSTAT_BITS=10
Two-level Huffman decode table: main table indexed by N bits (LITLEN_TABLEBITS=11, OFFSET=8, PRECODE=7), long codewords escape to on-demand subtables via a HUFFDEC_SUBTABLE_POINTER entry
Packed decode-table entry: one u32 holds literal value / length-base / offset-base plus 'remaining codeword length + extra bits' in low bits, so decode is one table read + shift, branch-free
64-bit branchless bit-buffer refill: bitbuf |= get_unaligned_leword(in) << (bitsleft&7), advance pointer/bitcount by arithmetic with no per-symbol branch
Block-type selection by measured cost: emit each block as cheapest of dynamic-Huffman / static-Huffman / stored, comparing final bit costs incl precode overhead
Entropy-divergence block splitting: accumulate 10-category symbol observations every 512 positions, cut a block when running stats diverge (SOFT_MAX_BLOCK_LENGTH=300000)
bt_matchfinder (binary trees, one candidate per length) for the optimal parser vs hc_matchfinder (hash chains) for greedy/lazy levels
repos.nest_application: Two concrete steals into crates/nest-format/src/encoding and writer/encoding_choice.rs. (1) Make encoding_choice.rs cost-driven instead of preset-driven: for each non-embedding section (chunks_canonical text, provenance/search_contract JSON), trial-encode under candidate codecs and pick the smallest measured output (a one-pass analog of libdeflate block-type-by-cost selection). Fits the additive format: no new section ids, the chosen encoding id is just recorded per-section in the manifest. (2) Add a new entropy codec under a reserved encoding id 4+ (additive within v1) for the text section: a deterministic canonical-Huffman/DEFLATE-style coder whose static decode table uses the two-level layout and packed-u32 entries above, giving a tiny dependency-free Rust decoder for the runtime mmap path. The iterative measured-bits idea also seeds a future token-codebook builder for chunks_canonical (choose codebook by measured bits to a fixpoint) where extreme text gains live. Keep embeddings off this path: they stay raw/f16/int8 scored from mmap as today.
repos.license: MIT (maintainer states no relevant patents)
repos.perf_notes: ~2x zlib on x86_64/ARM at default level 6 both directions. Decode speed from a 64-bit bitbuffer refilled rarely via branchless unaligned word loads, single-read packed table entries, and a BMI2-compiled decode variant selected at runtime. Compression cost scales hard at top levels: experimental level 13 saves only ~0.134% over level 12 on Silesia but runs ~56x slower -> 'compress once, serve many', perfect for nest's deterministic offline build step, not real-time edits. Runtime CPU feature detection, no compile flags. No streaming: tuned for chunks < ~1MB, matching nest's per-section/per-chunk granularity.
repos.compression_relevance: Directly on the north star (compress more than everyone). The iterate-on-measured-bits parser is the principled route to squeezing text/json sections harder than single-shot zstd. The two-level decode table + packed entries + branchless refill is a blueprint for a small, fast, deterministic in-house entropy decoder running off mmap with no C dependency, preserving offline/single-file/no-hot-path-alloc guarantees.

repos.one_liner: A pure-Go suite of optimized compression codecs (zstd, S2/Snappy, flate/deflate) built on separable entropy primitives — huff0 (Huffman) and fse (Finite State Entropy / tANS) — with dictionary training, four match-finder tiers, and assembly-accelerated decode.
repos.core_innovation: Entropy coding and dictionary training are factored into reusable primitives independent of the LZ layer: fse (table-based asymmetric numeral systems) and huff0 (Huffman) are standalone packages, and a trained dictionary ships a precomputed shared entropy table plus a common-substring content prefix so a corpus of many tiny similar payloads stops re-transmitting its own statistics and re-discovering shared strings on every blob — exactly the regime of nest's thousands of short canonical chunks.
key_techniques: FSE / tANS finite-state entropy coding (table-driven ANS) as a standalone codec for near-arithmetic-coding density at table-lookup speed
huff0 Huffman entropy coder with 1X and 4X interleaved-stream variants for parallel/SIMD decode
zstd dictionary training (ZDICT): mine common substrings across many small samples + precompute a shared FSE/Huffman entropy table, embed both as a reusable dictionary prefix
four-tier match finder (fast/default/better/best ~ levels 1/3/7/11) trading encode time for ratio via hash-chain variants
S2 seekable streams: a sparse index of frame offsets enabling random access / decompress-from-offset without inflating the whole stream
RLE detection and predefined/static FSE tables to skip header cost on tiny or low-entropy blocks
assembly matchLen and a 4-stage decoder pipeline (input / literal / sequence / output) for decode throughput
repos.nest_application: Add a trained-dictionary codec to crates/nest-format/src/encoding/ alongside zstd_codec.rs. At build time (nest-python build_fn -> writer/encoding_choice.rs) train ONE zstd dictionary from the file's own canonical chunks, store it as a new additive section (reserved id 0x09+, NOT a v2 bump) plus a new SECTION_ENCODING id in the reserved 4-255 range, then compress chunks_canonical (and spans/provenance) against it. For nest's many short PT-BR chunks this removes the per-section entropy-table and shared-substring overhead that zstd level-19-without-dict pays today, advancing the 'compress more than everyone' north star while staying single-file (dict lives inside the container), deterministic (training is seedable + sorted input), and additive. Second steal: S2's seekable sparse-offset index is the blueprint for a future chunk-granular random-access codec so a single chunk decodes without inflating the whole section. Decode stays on the existing zstd crate (it reads dict-prefixed frames natively) so no new decode dependency; embeddings remain untouched on the mmap SIMD hot path per nest's hard rule.
repos.compression_relevance: Directly central. Dictionary training is the single biggest unrealized ratio win for nest's actual payload shape (thousands of short, mutually-similar text chunks) where whole-section zstd-19 wastes bytes re-encoding shared statistics per blob; fse/huff0 as separable primitives are the longer-term path to a custom nest entropy stage.

repos.perf_notes: zstd decode has x86-64 + ARM64 assembly (~2x); decoder runs a 4-stage concurrent pipeline, encoder uses light 2-goroutine concurrency. huff0 4X variant interleaves 4 bitstreams for parallel decode; static decode buffer ~30% faster. matchLen and FSE decode are hand-written asm on amd64. For nest these are build-side one-time costs; decode and dict-prefix reads are cheap and stay off the SIMD scoring hot path since embeddings are never entropy-coded.

repos.one_liner: A meta-compressor that does not invent an entropy coder but front-loads a SIMD-vectorized, pipelinable byte-transform stage (shuffle / bitshuffle / delta / bytedelta / trunc_prec) ahead of stock LZ codecs (BloscLZ, LZ4, Zstd), restructuring numerical byte streams so the downstream coder sees long runs and small residuals, all wrapped in a documented blocked chunk/superchunk/frame container.
repos.core_innovation: Decouple "byte rearrangement / decorrelation" from "entropy coding" and make the transform stage a tiny, composable, SIMD-accelerated filter pipeline applied per fixed-size block. The shuffle filter groups the Nth byte of every typesize-N element together (a strided transpose), so the high-order bytes of a numerical array (mostly constant) form long zero/constant runs and the low-order bytes cluster, turning data Zstd can barely touch into data it crushes. bytedelta then deltas within each per-byte stream for gradually-varying series. The codec is unchanged; the win comes entirely from presenting it better-conditioned bytes. This routinely lifts float32 array ratios from ~3.9x to ~5.9x at near-memcpy speed.
key_techniques: Byte shuffle: strided transpose grouping byte-position k of all elements of typesize T into contiguous planes (SoA-of-bytes), exposing constant high-order bytes as runs
Bitshuffle: same idea at bit granularity, transposing bit-planes within a block for more redundancy on low-entropy floats
bytedelta filter: SIMD delta within each shuffled byte-plane; forward uses simd_sub+simd_concat over 16-byte lanes, inverse uses a Kogge-Stone parallel prefix-sum scan to un-delta
trunc_prec: zero the low mantissa bits of f32/f64 before shuffle to manufacture trailing-zero runs (lossy, controllable precision)
Composable 6-slot block-level filter pipeline (shuffle->bytedelta, trunc_prec->bitshuffle) keeping temp buffers L1/L2-resident
Blocked chunk format with int32 bstarts offset table + csize sentinels (csize==0 = all-zeros block stored as nothing, csize<0 = RLE/special token)
Shared Zstd dictionary trained once and stored in the superchunk header, reused across all chunks to lift ratio on small blocks
Container hierarchy chunk->superchunk->frame (contiguous cframe header+chunks+index+trailer, or sparse sframe one-file-per-chunk) with MessagePack metadata + metalayers
repos.nest_application: Add a pre-codec filter stage in nest-format/src/encoding/ (new shuffle.rs + bytedelta.rs, each <300 loc, pure deterministic functions, no panic). Wire it as a new SECTION_ENCODING id (the reserved 4-255 space is additive-safe within v1) that is shuffle+zstd: before zstd_encode, transpose section bytes by a typesize stored in the manifest, optionally bytedelta the planes, then zstd; reverse it in decode_payload. Highest-value targets are the COLD numerical sections that already accept zstd: chunks_original_spans (arrays of u32/u64 offsets whose high bytes are near-constant, so shuffle yields huge runs) and the int8 scales array in encoding/int8.rs (n contiguous f32 LE scales, the classic shuffle case). CRITICAL constraint: do NOT apply it to the embeddings body bytes scored from mmap on the hot path (shuffle destroys the row-contiguous layout the SIMD dot-product reads), so gate it strictly to non-hot-path sections via writer/encoding_choice.rs. trunc_prec is a separate future lever for a lossy archival embeddings variant. The SIMD prefix-sum un-delta maps onto nest-runtime's existing AVX2/NEON/scalar dispatcher if decode ever becomes hot.
repos.compression_relevance: Directly central. This is the cheapest known multiplier on top of an existing entropy coder for numerical/binary sections: nest already ships zstd but applies it to raw bytes; inserting a deterministic byte-shuffle (and optional bytedelta) transform in front of zstd is a pure ratio win on the offsets/spans and scale arrays with zero new dependency and no format break (just a new additive encoding id). Blosc's own ERA5 numbers (3.86x -> 5.86x) quantify the headroom. It is the textbook technique behind 'compress data more than everyone' for structured numeric payloads.
repos.perf_notes: Shuffle/bitshuffle and bytedelta are SIMD-vectorized (SSE2/AVX2 on x86_64, NEON on aarch64, scalar fallback) over 16-byte lanes, so transform overhead is near memcpy and bandwidth-bound. Block-level application keeps working sets in L1/L2. Tradeoffs measured by Blosc: with shuffle+bytedelta, Zstd compression time can roughly double at high levels and decompression can slow ~20% for most codecs (Zstd less affected) - acceptable since nest's targets are build-time (python writer) and cold sections, not the mmap scoring path. The all-zeros/RLE csize sentinels make sparse numeric data near-free.
repos.license: BSD-3-Clause (permissive; safe to cleanly reimplement shuffle/bytedelta in Rust, and the format spec is open and documented in under 4000 words)

repos.one_liner: Reference C implementation of Finite State Entropy (tANS, table-based Asymmetric Numeral Systems) plus Huff0, the entropy-coder backends that power zstd, providing near-arithmetic compression accuracy at hundreds of MB/s via a single state-transition table lookup per symbol.
repos.core_innovation: tANS replaces per-symbol arithmetic with a precomputed state-transition table making decode a single LUT lookup plus a bit read; the accuracy depends entirely on quasi-regular symbol spreading across the state table.
key_techniques: tANS decode table {symbol, nbBits, newStateBaseline} with 4-line decode hot loop
Symbol spread stride step=(tableSize>>1)+(tableSize>>3)+3 mod tableSize
FSE_normalizeCount to sum=2^tableLog with rtbTable rounding thresholds and minTableLog rejection
FSE_optimalTableLog auto-selecting smallest cache-friendly tableLog (~14)
nbBits/baseline assignment via next-power-of-2 shares, low states cost +1 bit
Normalized-count table bit-packed into the compressed header; RLE special case
Huff0 canonical Huffman with 4 interleaved bitstreams for OoO ALU throughput
FSEU16 16-bit-symbol variant for large alphabets
repos.nest_application: Vendor a pure-Rust FSE+Huff0 entropy codec into crates/nest-format/src/encoding/, registered as new additive encoding ids in the reserved 4-255 range, applied only to non-embedding sections (text, provenance, search_contract, and especially bm25_index 0x08 postings and hnsw_index 0x07 neighbor lists) where skewed integer/token residuals after delta-coding beat zstd's generic stage at lower complexity. Table build is a pure function of the histogram so output is byte-identical/deterministic, preserving content_hash and reproducible builds; FSEU16 suits 16-bit tokenized term streams. Keep under 300 lines by sharing the spread/table-build core between encode and decode, typed thiserror errors, no panics.
repos.compression_relevance: Core to compress-more-than-everyone: tANS hits within a fraction of a percent of Shannon entropy on skewed symbol streams (BM25 postings, HNSW adjacency, term dicts) where Huffman loses up to ~1 bit/symbol, at hundreds of MB/s, giving nest a sovereign in-house entropy floor below generic zstd.
repos.license: BSD-2-Clause
repos.perf_notes: FSE ~325/440 MB/s, Huff0 ~600/1350 MB/s on i7-5600U with 32KB blocks; tableLog<=14 to fit L1; Huff0 uses 4 interleaved streams for ALU parallelism. Pure scalar, branch-light LUT decode portable to x86_64/aarch64.

repos.one_liner: A C library (BSD/GPL, ~96% C, posix-threads) that adds multithreaded streaming compression/decompression on top of seven codecs (Zstandard, LZ4, LZ5, Lizard, Brotli, Snappy-c, LZFSE) by chunking input and wrapping each independently-compressed chunk in a self-describing skippable-frame header.
repos.core_innovation: A codec-agnostic, backward-compatible "skippable frame" chunk container: each parallel-compressed chunk is prefixed with a 12-byte header built on zstd's reserved skippable-frame magic 0x184D2A50 (a magic-range whose high nibble flags "skip me" to any compliant decompressor), so a multithreaded/chunked stream is still decodable by a stock single-threaded decompressor that simply skips the metadata frames, while a parallel decompressor uses the embedded compressed-size and uncompressed-size hint as random-access seek points and single-pass allocation sizes.
key_techniques: Skippable-frame chunk header: 4-byte magic 0x184D2A50 + 4-byte framesize(4) + 4-byte compressed-size = 12 bytes per chunk for zstd/lz4/lz5/lizard

Extended 16-byte header for codecs lacking native framing (brotli 'BR', snappy 'SP', lzfse 'LF'): adds 2-byte codec magic + 2-byte uncompressed-size hint as a 64KiB multiplier for one-shot output allocation

Decentralized self-scheduling worker pool: no dispatcher thread; each worker loops {acquire read-mutex -> read one input chunk -> release -> compress independently -> acquire write-mutex -> emit framed chunk} until EOF
Two-mutex (read/write) coordination instead of a producer-consumer queue, preserving output order by chunk while keeping per-thread compression fully parallel
User-tunable input chunk size (-b N MiB, auto default) trading parallelism granularity vs ratio, and thread count (-T N, defaults to core count)
Three interchangeable backends (single-stream st, pthread create/join mt, thread-pool tp) over one shared frame format
Uniform multi-codec abstraction: one streaming API and one container format reused across 7 entropy/LZ backends
repos.nest_application: nest-format/src/encoding can adopt the skippable-frame chunking convention for its zstd-compressed non-embedding sections (chunks_canonical text, provenance, bm25_index, future json/pdf/parquet payloads): instead of one monolithic zstd frame per section, store a section as a sequence of independently-compressed chunks each prefixed with a 12-byte self-describing header. This is purely additive (a new internal layout inside an existing encoding id, no NEST_FORMAT_VERSION bump, no new section id), and unlocks (1) parallel decompression of large text sections at materialize time in nest-runtime via the simd/rayon-style dispatcher, (2) random-access decode of a single chunk for nest://content_hash/chunk_id citation reopen without inflating the whole section, and (3) the 64KiB uncompressed-size hint enables exact output buffer pre-allocation so materialize never reallocates. Determinism is preserved by fixing chunk size and codec params; per-section physical-bytes SHA-256 stays stable because the framed byte layout is deterministic. Embeddings stay raw/f16/int8 as today (never touched, still scored from mmap). The two-mutex worker pattern itself is the wrong concurrency model for Rust (use rayon/crossbeam), but the on-disk frame format is the steal.
repos.compression_relevance: Indirect to raw ratio (multithreading and chunking slightly HURT ratio versus one big frame because each chunk resets the codec window/dictionary), but high relevance to nest's broader 'compress AND serve' north star: it is the canonical pattern for making compressed sections seekable and parallel-decodable without giving up single-file/offline/deterministic guarantees. To recover the ratio loss when nest grows to large corpora, pair it with a shared trained zstd dictionary (zstd ZDICT) referenced by all chunks, so small-chunk random access stops costing ratio. The uncompressed-size-hint trick is directly reusable for any nest codec lacking self-framing.
repos.perf_notes: posix-threads only (Windows via mingw CreateThread/WaitForMultipleObjects in later builds); self-scheduling worker pool was benchmarked faster than upstream zstd's job-based --nbWorkers and competitive with pzstd. Throughput scales near-linearly with cores up to memory bandwidth; chunk size -b trades parallelism vs ratio. Decompression historically single-threaded in zstd; the skippable-frame headers are exactly what make per-chunk parallel decode and seek possible. Per-chunk overhead is only 12-16 bytes, negligible for >=128KiB chunks.
repos.license: BSD-3-Clause / GPL-2.0 dual (follows upstream facebook/zstd licensing convention; library code under permissive BSD, suitable for vendoring the format idea, though nest would reimplement in Rust rather than link the C)

repos.one_liner: An autoencoder-style neural prompt compressor that uses a frozen LLaMA-3-8B (with ~0.3% trainable LoRA params) as the encoder to squeeze up to ~500 natural-language tokens into the per-layer KV-cache values of a single learned special token, which the same frozen LLM then decodes for text regeneration or QA.
repos.core_innovation: Carry compressed information as the full per-layer key/value (KV) tensors of a handful of learned "gist" tokens rather than as a single final-layer embedding vector. KV-at-every-layer has far higher information capacity than one embedding, which is what unlocks the 6x-480x ratios; the decoder is the identical frozen LLM, so the compressor adds no decode-side parameters and "stores" nothing in weights (no data leakage).
key_techniques: Autoencoder framing: encoder = frozen LLM + LoRA, decoder = same frozen LLM, only LoRA (~0.3%) trained
Soft/gist tokens: append N learnable special tokens; their attention-aggregated state becomes the compressed payload
KV-value carrier instead of last-layer embedding (the ICAE improvement) -- store K and V per transformer layer for each gist token
Two-phase training: (1) pretrain on text regeneration with teacher forcing + cross-entropy, (2) fine-tune on extractive QA
Non-selective compression: compresses ALL prompt tokens into the latent, vs hard methods (LLMLingua) that drop tokens
Lossy reconstruction measured by F1/EM, retaining ~62-84% of uncompressed-prompt task ability
repos.nest_application: Mostly a REFERENCE, not a steal. This is lossy neural compression needing an 8B LLM forward pass at both compress AND decompress time -- it cannot live on nest's mmap+SIMD hot path, breaks determinism (float GPU kernels), breaks offline/single-file/small-rust-core constraints, and cannot losslessly reconstruct bytes, so it is unusable for chunks_canonical, provenance, or any required section. The ONLY transferable seed: the KV-as-carrier insight reinforces nest's existing embedding-quantization direction in nest-format encoding (the int8/float16 codecs) -- it argues a richer per-layer latent preserves more than a flattened vector, useful as academic background for any future learned/product-quantization codec but nothing nest can ship now. nest should cite 500xCompressor as the canonical reason neural/semantic text compression costs an LLM at read time and therefore stays OUT of the frozen v1 format and off the offline runtime. No code, section, or codec adopted.
repos.compression_relevance: Low for nest's mission. Headline "500x" is lossy latent compression of prompts for LLM consumption, not lossless byte compression of stored data, and the decompressor is an 8B GPU model -- the opposite of nest's offline/single-file/deterministic/mmap-SIMD design. It compresses for an LLM to read, not for a byte-exact citation to reopen, so it cannot back content_hash stability or nest://content_hash/chunk_id span reopen. Useful only as the reference point for why neural/semantic text compression is incompatible with nest's frozen container and offline runtime.
repos.license: Code repo public on GitHub (paper ACL 2025, arXiv 2408.03094); datasets/weights on HuggingFace marked not open to the public. No explicit OSI license confirmed in README -- treat as all-rights-reserved/research-use until a LICENSE file is verified before any code reuse.
repos.perf_notes: Reported at 500x: ~27-90% reduction in attention FLOPs and ~55-83% KV-memory savings when generating 100-400 tokens, retaining ~70-74% F1 / ~77-84% EM vs uncompressed prompts. Base model LLaMA-3-8B-Instruct; LoRA adds ~0.3% params. All numbers assume GPU LLM inference at both ends -- irrelevant to nest's CPU mmap/SIMD throughput model and not a fixed-cost codec.

synthesis.summary: nest already vendors zstd but runs its weakest config: every non-embedding section is compressed cold at a hardcoded level 19 (crates/nest-format/src/encoding/zstd_codec.rs DEFAULT_ZSTD_LEVEL=19, zstd::encode_all with no dictionary, no LDM, no params struct), and the encoding choice is preset-driven not measured (writer/payload.rs::maybe_zstd is a binary raw-vs-zstd switch). The collective state of the art across these 12 repos points to three concrete, high-leverage, fully-sovereign-compatible moves for nest's actual payload shape (thousands of short, mutually-similar PT-BR chunks plus small structured metadata): (1) TRAINED SHARED DICTIONARIES (zstd ZDICT/COVER, echoed by brotli's static dictionary, zlib deflateSetDictionary, klauspost, c-blosc2 superchunk dict) -- the single biggest unrealized ratio win, attacking the per-section entropy-table + cold-start redundancy that level-19-no-dict pays on every blob; deterministic because ZDICT is a pure function of sorted samples and content_hash is over DECODED bytes so it stays stable. (2) BYTE-SHUFFLE/BYTEDELTA PRE-CODEC (c-blosc2) -- a near-memcpy SIMD transpose in front of zstd that turns the near-constant high bytes of nest's u64 span offsets (sections/spans.rs) and the contiguous f32 int8-scale array (encoding/int8.rs) into long runs, a pure ratio multiplier (Blosc shows 3.9x->5.9x on float arrays) with zero new dependency and no format break. (3) COST-DRIVEN ENCODING SELECTION (libdeflate's measure-bits-out, klauspost block-type-by-cost) -- trial-encode each section and keep the smallest, replacing nest's preset-only choice. The entropy-coder family (FSE/tANS, Huff0 from FiniteStateEntropy, klauspost separable primitives, libdeflate two-level Huffman table) is the longer-horizon path to a sovereign in-house entropy floor below generic zstd, especially over delta-coded BM25 postings (0x08) and HNSW adjacency (0x07). snappy/lz4/zstdmt contribute FORMAT discipline rather than ratio: skippable/unskippable extension bits and self-describing skippable-frame chunk headers that make nest's reserved 0x09+ sections forward-compatible and large sections seekable/parallel-decodable for citation reopen. 500xCompressor is a pure reference (lossy neural, 8B-LLM at decode time) and the canonical reason semantic compression stays OUT of the frozen offline v1. Every recommendation respects the hard rules: embeddings stay raw/f16/int8 scored from mmap (shuffle and dict NEVER touch the hot float path), encoding ids 4-255 and section ids 0x09+ are additive within v1, no NEST_FORMAT_VERSION bump, no panics (typed thiserror), repr(C)/LE, <=300 loc per file.
top_innovations: Trained shared zstd dictionary (ZDICT/COVER greedy frequent-segment selection + pre-baked FSE/Huffman tables + seed repeat-offsets): build ONE deterministic dictionary at build time over nest's many short similar chunks so each tiny blob compresses against shared cross-record statistics instead of re-transmitting its own entropy tables and re-discovering shared strings cold. Highest-leverage zstd feature for nest's exact workload; confirmed by brotli static dict, zlib deflateSetDictionary, klauspost, c-blosc2.

Byte-shuffle + bytedelta pre-codec (c-blosc2): SIMD strided transpose grouping byte-position k of every fixed-size element into contiguous planes so near-constant high-order bytes of numeric arrays form long runs zstd crushes, optionally deltaed per plane. Cheapest known ratio multiplier on top of an existing entropy coder (3.86x->5.86x on Blosc's float32/ERA5), near-memcpy speed, build-time only.

Cost-driven encoding selection (libdeflate iterate-on-measured-bits; klauspost/zlib block-type-by-cost): pick the section encoding by actual measured output size, not a static preset rule. One-pass analog: trial-encode each non-embedding section under candidate codecs/params and keep the smallest; the chosen encoding id is just recorded per-section in the manifest, fully additive.

FSE/tANS table-based ANS entropy coder (Cyan4973/FiniteStateEntropy, klauspost fse, zstd back-end): single state-transition LUT lookup per symbol hitting within a fraction of a percent of Shannon entropy on skewed streams where Huffman loses up to ~1 bit/symbol. The sovereign in-house entropy floor for delta-coded BM25 postings, HNSW neighbor lists, and term dictionaries, dependency-free and deterministic (table build is a pure function of the histogram).

Huff0 + libdeflate two-level Huffman decode table with packed-u32 entries and branchless 64-bit bit-buffer refill: a tiny, fast, deterministic, no-C-dependency entropy decoder that runs straight off mmap (one table read + shift per symbol, 4 interleaved bitstreams for ILP). The reference design for any future nest-native entropy section decoder under the no-panic / LE / mmap constraints.

LZ77 repeat-offset cache + LDM (zstd): 3-most-recent-offset cache so periodic/structured data spends ~1 offset code, and long-distance matching over a large window (up to 2GB) catching far-apart duplicates -- the engine extension that scales nest toward the north-star whole-repo / whole-database / parquet payloads where cross-file duplication dominates.

Skippable/unskippable extension discipline + self-describing skippable-frame chunk header (snappy reserved-id partitioning, zstd 0x184D2A5x magics, zstdmt 12-16 byte per-chunk header with compressed+uncompressed size hints): the canonical way an additive format lets old readers skip unknown OPTIONAL extensions while erroring cleanly on unknown REQUIRED ones, and the blueprint for seekable per-chunk random-access decode (citation reopen) + exact output-buffer pre-allocation without inflating a whole section.

Pure-Rust byte-aligned LZ77 fallback codec (snappy tag-byte stream / lz4 token+LSIC varint): an entropy-coder-free, allocation-light, GB/s-class block format whose decoder is table-free and branch-light. Two uses for nest: a zero-C-dependency sovereign fallback when everything is vendored into one binary, and the only realistic path to compressing surfaces zstd is banned from (per-citation text materialize, a future just-in-time lz4 block over int8 embeddings decoded into scratch before the SIMD kernel).

Functable dispatch pattern (zlib-ng resolve-once struct of fn pointers; CRC32-C via carryless multiply): generalize nest's existing SimdBackend OnceLock in nest-runtime/src/simd/mod.rs into a small functable so new kernels (f16 convert, i8 widen, shuffle/un-delta, future bitpacked decoder) register one entry each instead of growing match arms, keeping each simd/*.rs under the 300-line cap; CRC32-C as a fast non-crypto hash for dedup/identity probes that precede compression.
