compression_wins: RaBitQ 1-bit embedding codec: 8x smaller than nest's current int8 floor and 32x vs f32 on the largest section, with an unbiased error bound and a popcount hot path -- the clearest single path past the tiny preset's 0.283 ratio toward sub-0.1. Lossiness is free against the recall contract because nest already mandates exact-cosine rerank.

PQ8/OPQ mid tier: 16-32x on embeddings (m=32 on a 768-d vector is ~96x raw, ~24x vs int8) via tiny shared codebooks + m-byte codes, scored by ADC for candidate gen and exact-reranked -- a higher-recall option than 1-bit for a 'compressed-hybrid' preset.

TurboQuant 2/4-bit data-oblivious codec: 16x at 2-bit (6144B f32 -> 384B for d=1536), scored directly in the compressed domain off mmap, with NOTHING per-corpus stored so builds stay byte-identical -- breaks the 'cannot compress the mmap-scored embeddings' wall without adding a stateful trained artifact.

uint40 neighbor ids + flat fixed-stride 0x07 layout: ~37.5% off the HNSW edge arrays plus elimination of Vec<Vec> ptr/len/cap overhead; the regular byte structure also zstd-compresses better (0x07 is not on the SIMD hot path), shrinking tiny/hybrid further.

Algorithm-4 diversity neighbor selection lets the tiny/nano presets LOWER M (fewer u32/uint40 ids per node) at equal recall@10 -- a compression win that costs only build-time CPU and rides entirely on the existing exact rerank.

Stream-VByte + recursive-graph-bisection on BM25 0x08 postings: replaces raw u32 doc/tf pairs with delta-gap byte-packed postings whose d-gaps are minimized by term reordering -- shrinks the hybrid preset's lexical index, and the existing zstd second pass compounds it, all without touching embeddings or the recall contract.

Binary/Hamming navigation vectors (1-bit, 64 dims/u64) as a navigation-only side representation: shrinks the in-RAM nav footprint ~32x vs the f32 snapshot and makes graph hops popcount-cheap, enabling a 'nano' preset (binary nav + f16/RaBitQ rerank embeddings).
watch_outs: NIGHTLY-ONLY SIMD: kannolo/vectorium use std::simd (portable_simd) and gen blocks; hora uses packed_simd_2 (unmaintained, nightly-only). Both break nest's stable Rust edition-2024 build. Reimplement every kernel (PQ ADC, popcount, FastScan) on nest's existing AVX2/NEON/scalar dispatcher; vendor the ALGORITHM, never the SIMD layer.

EXTERNAL STORAGE ENGINES: arroy is built on LMDB (heed), hora/instant-distance use serde+bincode blobs. These violate nest's single-file frozen-format and offline-by-construction constraints. Keep every structure as repr(C) little-endian inside nest's own sections; do not pull in a KV store or a serde graph dump.

DETERMINISM OF QUANTIZERS: any trained codec (PQ/OPQ k-means, RaBitQ/TurboQuant rotation) must be a pure function of the model fingerprint -- fix the seed, Lloyd iteration count, sampling, and use index-order/alphabetical tie-breaks, and store codebooks/seeds in a stable order. Otherwise same chunks + same model no longer yields a byte-identical file (breaks nest://content_hash citations and reproducibility).

NEVER ZSTD THE EMBEDDINGS: USearch/hnswlib interleave the raw vector INTO the graph record, and several libs lean on generic entropy coders over vectors. Nest's embeddings must stay directly mmap-SIMD-scored, so any embedding shrink must be a quantization codec scored in-place (RaBitQ/PQ/TurboQuant), never a zstd wrapper. Steal the FLAT GRAPH LAYOUT for neighbor IDS ONLY -- keep embeddings in their own section.

ARM NEON PARITY: FAISS PQ4 FastScan and several popcount/shuffle kernels are AVX2/AVX512-tuned; AVX2 lacks VPOPCNTDQ (use the Mula nibble-LUT pshufb popcount) and the 256-bit FastScan needs the two-128-bit-NEON-registers trick (Matsui arXiv:2203.02505) to match on aarch64. Nest treats NEON as first-class, so every new kernel needs a real NEON path, not a scalar fallback that emulates vector registers (very slow).

SCALAR FALLBACK MUST STAY SIMPLE: FAISS notes the block/interleaved FastScan layout is pathological for scalar (it emulates vector registers in memory). Nest's scalar tier should keep a plain unpacked PQ/popcount loop, not the SIMD block layout, so the scalar-fallback target stays correct and not catastrophically slow.

300-LINE FILE CAP / SINGLE RESPONSIBILITY: each new codec and kernel must split cleanly (codec in nest-format/src/encoding/<name>.rs, kernel in nest-runtime/src/simd/<name>.rs) to respect the <=300 (333 hard cap) line rule and typed thiserror no-panic convention -- do not port monolithic C++ index files wholesale.

ADDITIVE-ONLY DISCIPLINE: new embedding codecs take RESERVED encoding ids 4-255 and new ANN backends take section ids 0x09+; internal graph changes bump HNSW_PAYLOAD_VERSION only. Do NOT bump NEST_FORMAT_VERSION (that is reserved for a true v2 where an existing field changes meaning). A naive port that rewrites the header/footer would violate the FROZEN format guarantee.

categories.name: vector-quantization
categories.focus: vector quantization and bit-compression of embeddings (the compression key for vectors)

repos.one_liner: A randomized 1-bit-per-dimension quantizer (SIGMOD 2024) that maps a normalized D-dim vector, after a random orthogonal rotation, to its sign-bit string on the {+-1/sqrt(D)}^D hypercube codebook, yielding an unbiased inner-product estimator with a sharp O(1/sqrt(D)) error bound, computed via bitwise-AND + popcount.
repos.core_innovation: Replace learned codebooks (PQ/OPQ) with a fixed deterministic codebook (the sign-corners of the unit sphere scaled by 1/sqrt(D)) plus a random rotation P. Quantization is just "rotate, take signs" -- no training, no k-means -- yet the estimator <o-bar,q>/<o-bar,o> is provably unbiased with a per-vector O(1/sqrt(D)) error bound holding with high probability. This makes ANN distance estimation a quantity with a confidence interval, letting the search loop decide per-candidate whether to trust the cheap estimate or trigger exact rerank.
key_techniques: Fixed sphere-corner codebook C = {+1/sqrt(D), -1/sqrt(D)}^D; quantize = sign(P^-1 * o), stored as a D-bit sign string (1 bit/dim)
Random orthogonal rotation P (Johnson-Lindenstrauss style) randomizes geometry so the sign-quantization error concentrates; same P reused for all vectors and queries
Unbiased estimator: <o,q> ~= <o-bar,q>/<o-bar,o>, where <o-bar,o> (~0.8, concentrated) is the single per-vector scalar stored alongside the bit code
Asymmetric bit allocation: data = 1 bit/dim, query quantized to 4 bits/dim; error dominated by data quantization so query precision is cheap insurance
Weighted popcount kernel: dot = 1*popcount(code & q1) + 2*popcount(code & q2) + 4*popcount(code & q3) + 8*popcount(code & q4) over the 4 query bit-planes
Distance reconstruction via law of cosines around a centroid c: ||o_r-q_r||^2 = ||o_r-c||^2 + ||q_r-c||^2 - 2*||o_r-c||*||q_r-c||*estIP
FastScan-style batched layout: 32 codes reorganized at index time for SIMD lane-parallel scan (AVX2/AVX512 VPOPCNTDQ); scalar bitwise fallback in space.h
Per-vector footprint = D bits + a couple of f32 scalars (the <o-bar,o> factor and ||o_r-c||), independent of any trained dictionary
repos.nest_application: Add an int1/rabitq embedding codec to nest-format encoding (new RESERVED encoding id 4-255, additive within v1, repr(C) little-endian bit code + two f32 per-vector scalars). The rotation matrix P is deterministic from a seed -> store the seed in provenance/search_contract, preserving nest's reproducible-build + deterministic guarantee (same seed => byte-identical codes). In nest-runtime add a rabitq distance estimator beside the SIMD dot dispatcher: NEON vcnt/vaddv + AVX2 popcount kernels off the mmapped bit codes, scalar fallback to satisfy "no panic / three-arch" rule. This slots perfectly into nest's existing mandatory-exact-rerank contract: RaBitQ becomes the cheap ANN proxy (replacing or feeding the hnsw shortlist) and the stored real f32/f16 embeddings still drive the ground-truth cosine rerank, so the returned score stays honest. The error bound lets nest cite a recall guarantee in the search_contract, not just an empirical number.
repos.compression_relevance: Directly the compression key for the embeddings section, nest's largest and currently least-compressed payload (zstd is banned on embeddings because they are scored from mmap; today the smallest is int8 at 0.283 ratio). RaBitQ takes a 768-dim f32 vector (3072 bytes) to ~768 bits + 8 bytes = ~104 bytes, a ~30x reduction (~0.034 ratio on the embedding bytes), far below int8's 4x, while remaining directly scorable from mmap via popcount with NO decompression on the hot path -- the exact property zstd lacked. The provable O(1/sqrt(D)) error bound plus nest's existing exact rerank means this extreme compression costs almost no recall (RaBitQ matches PQ/OPQ accuracy at ~3x their speed; multi-bit 4-5 bit variants reach 90-95% recall with no rerank at all). This is the single highest-leverage move toward the "compress data more than everyone" north star.
repos.perf_notes: Distance estimate reduces to bitwise-AND + popcount, a 1-cycle-class op on modern CPUs; dedicated AVX512VPOPCNTDQ on IceLake+/Zen4+, and aarch64 NEON has vcnt + horizontal add (relevant since nest targets NEON). FastScan batches 32 codes for lane-parallel SIMD scan. Reported ~3x faster than PQ/OPQ at equal accuracy. Memory: 1 bit/dim + ~2 f32 scalars/vector, no trained dictionary to load, fully streamable/mmap-friendly. Query-side cost is the 4 bit-plane weighted popcount; estimator is branch-light.
repos.license: Apache-2.0 (original archived repo; active development moved to VectorDB-NTU/RaBitQ-Library). Method published SIGMOD 2024, arXiv 2405.12497, DOI 10.1145/3654970. C++ (Eigen 3.4.0) + Python; nest would reimplement clean-room in Rust, so only the algorithm (patent-free, openly published) is used.

repos.one_liner: RaBitQ is a randomized 1-bit-per-dimension vector quantizer (D-dim -> D bits + 2 float correction factors) using a random hypercube rotation to yield an unbiased distance estimator with provable O(1/sqrt(D)) error, evaluated via AND+popcount or FastScan.
repos.core_innovation: Random orthogonal rotation converts 1-bit sign quantization into a provably-unbiased distance estimator with a sharp O(1/sqrt(D)) error bound, making bit-only distance ordering reliable; the estimator reduces to AND+popcount against an int4 query, beating PQ on both size and speed with theoretical guarantees PQ lacks.
key_techniques: 1-bit/dim binary code = nearest vertex of a randomly-rotated hypercube on the unit sphere (D/8 bytes/vec)
Two stored f32 factors/vec: distance-to-centroid ||v-c|| and projection factor <x_bar, o>
Asymmetric quantization: data is 1-bit, query is int4/B-bit scalar quant, combined via bitwise ops
Unbiased distance/inner-product estimator with O(1/sqrt(D)) bound from JLT theory
Distance kernel = bitwise-AND + popcount (single query) or SIMD shuffle FastScan (batched)
Random orthogonal matrix stored as a deterministic SEED; P^-1 q computed once/query, amortized over the probe list
B-bit extension splits code into binary MSBs + ex-code for incremental refinement (4/5/7-bit ~ 90/95/99% recall no-rerank)
Centroid-relative encoding before normalize+quantize (IVF/KMeans, or single global centroid standalone)
repos.nest_application: New embedding codec in nest-format/src/encoding (id from reserved 4-255, additive, no version bump): per vector = D/8 packed sign bits as LE u64 words + 2 LE f32 factors; store global centroid + rotation seed in the embeddings section header (repr(C), LE, deterministic). ~32x vs f32 (1024-dim: 4096->136 bytes), a tier below int8. Add an AND+popcount SIMD kernel in nest-runtime/src/simd (NEON/AVX2/scalar) that scores codes straight off mmap as the ANN/coarse score; nest's mandatory exact cosine rerank stays ground truth, so recall holds. New nest-cli "nano" preset (zstd/rabitq/hnsw) and pairs with the existing HnswIndex (HNSW+RaBitQ). Determinism preserved via seeded rotation and fixed-seed centroid.
repos.compression_relevance: Highest-leverage compression for nest: ~32x on the embeddings section (the largest part of a .nest file) vs 4x int8 / 2x f16, with recall preserved because nest already does mandatory exact cosine rerank and the unbiased O(1/sqrt(D)) estimator selects good candidates. B-bit ex-code gives a 1/4/5/7-bit dial. Directly advances 'compress more than everyone' for vector bytes.
repos.perf_notes: Single-query distance is AND+popcount, single-cycle ops, reported ~3x faster than PQ RAM table lookups at equal accuracy; batched queries use PQ-style SIMD gather/shuffle FastScan. Reads D/8+8 bytes/vec instead of 4D, so the mmap hot path is memory-bandwidth-light. Inverse rotation P^-1 q is one O(D^2) op per query amortized over the whole probe list; per-vector rotation is paid once at build time. GPU implementation also exists upstream.
repos.license: Not confirmed from README in this session; upstream is C++ (academic, VectorDB-NTU / NTU Singapore). Verify exact license (likely MIT/Apache-style academic release) before vendoring; nest only needs the algorithm/format, reimplemented clean in Rust, so license is a reference concern not a code-copy dependency.

repos.one_liner: A GPU-native (NVIDIA cuVS) fork implementing IVF-RaBitQ: it fuses inverted-file clustering with RaBitQ quantization, which compresses each D-dim float32 vector to ~1 bit/dim plus two scalar factors and estimates distances with a provably unbiased, asymptotically-optimal-error estimator via random rotation, so no raw-vector reranking is needed.
repos.core_innovation: RaBitQ replaces a trained codebook (PQ) with a SINGLE random orthogonal rotation P shared by every vector: normalize the residual-to-centroid o, then store only the sign bit of P^-1 o per dimension (the binary code x_bar is the nearest vertex of a randomly-rotated +/-1/sqrt(D) hypercube). Because the codebook is random, the cross-term <o_bar, q> yields an UNBIASED estimator of the true dot product, <o,q> ~= <o_bar,q>/<o_bar,o>, with sharp O(1/sqrt(D)) error -- asymptotically optimal (matches Alon-Klartag FOCS17). This means 1 bit/dim gives reliable enough distances and confidence intervals to skip touching the original float vectors entirely, which is the compression-without-recall-collapse that ordinary binary quantization cannot achieve.
key_techniques: 1-bit-per-dimension sign quantization of randomly-rotated residual: store sign(P^-1(o-c)) as a D-bit string, total per-vector = D bits + 2 f32 factors
Shared random orthogonal rotation P (Johnson-Lindenstrauss transform) -- no per-corpus codebook training, fast variant uses Fast Hadamard Transform instead of dense matmul
Two stored scalar factors per vector: <o_bar,o> (code-to-data inner product, the unbiasedness normalizer) and ||o-c|| (residual norm to centroid)
Unbiased distance estimator <o,q> ~= <o_bar,q>/<o_bar,o> with provable O(1/sqrt(D)) error bound enabling rerank-free retrieval
Asymmetric bit budget: data side stays 1 bit/dim, query is rotated then scalar-quantized to B_q bits (e.g. 4) and decomposed into B_q bit-planes
Bitwise distance kernel: per query bit-plane, AND with the code then popcount, summed with plane weights -- 3x faster than PQ LUT scan on CPU, maps to GPU as AND+__popc
FastScan-style layout packing 32 binary codes per batch with 4-bit quantized 8-bit LUT entries for SIMD/warp-parallel filtering
Two-stage filter-then-refine: cheap 1-bit code filters candidates, 'ex-code' (extra low bits) refines survivors; extended B-bit RaBitQ (Sep-2024) for multi-bit budgets
repos.nest_application: Add a new embeddings codec in nest-format/src/encoding/ as `rabitq.rs` (encoding id 4 -- currently only 0..3 are used; 4..255 are RESERVED within format v1, so this is purely additive, no NEST_FORMAT_VERSION bump). Layout mirrors int8.rs: a u32 payload_version, a single shared D*D rotation seed (deterministic, store the seed not the matrix to stay reproducible and tiny), then per vector a packed D-bit sign code plus two f32 factors (<o_bar,o>, ||o-c||) and the global centroid c once. This is a drop-in replacement for the int8 path in the `tiny` preset, taking embedding storage from ~1 byte/dim (int8) to ~1 bit/dim -- roughly an 8x shrink of the embeddings section, which is the dominant section in compressed presets, directly advancing the 'compress more than everyone' north star (tiny's 0.283 ratio could drop materially). In nest-runtime/src/simd/, add a popcount-based RaBitQ kernel beside scalar/avx2/neon (AND + popcount over query bit-planes; NEON vcnt, AVX2 popcount, scalar count_ones fallback) for the cheap ANN filter stage. Critically, nest's search contract is PRESERVED for free: the mandatory exact-cosine rerank already re-scores survivors from the mmapped vectors, so RaBitQ becomes the ANN-proxy filter and the contract's exact rerank guarantees real cosine -- RaBitQ's own error bound just makes the candidate set smaller/cleaner. Determinism holds because the rotation is seeded and sign() is exact.
repos.compression_relevance: Directly central. RaBitQ is the single best-known route to push nest's embeddings section from int8 (8 bits/dim) to ~1 bit/dim WITHOUT recall collapse, because its rotation-based estimator is unbiased with an optimal error bound. Embeddings dominate compressed-preset file size, so an ~8x cut there is the largest available lever on nest's headline compression ratio while the mandatory exact-cosine rerank keeps returned scores ground-truth.
repos.perf_notes: Data side is D/8 bytes per vector (e.g. 1536-dim -> 192 bytes) plus 2 f32 factors and one shared seed; no per-vector codebook. Distance filter is bitwise AND + popcount over B_q query bit-planes (B_q typically 4), which is branch-free and SIMD/SIMT friendly: maps to AVX2/NEON popcount on nest's x86/aarch64 dispatch and to __popc on GPU. The cuVS paper reports >2.7x throughput over IVF-PQ (no raw rerank) and ~2.2x QPS over CAGRA at recall ~0.95 with 7.7x faster index build, quantizing >1M 960-dim vectors/sec to 8-bit codes on GPU. For nest's CPU-only mmap runtime, the win is memory traffic: 1-bit codes mean ~8x fewer bytes touched per scanned vector than int8, and popcount throughput easily saturates the hot path.
repos.license: cuVS is Apache-2.0 (RAPIDS/NVIDIA); this fork inherits Apache-2.0. The reference RaBitQ algorithm/library from VectorDB-NTU is MIT. Algorithm itself is patent-free per authors. Clean for vendoring/reimplementation in nest.

repos.one_liner: A CUDA/C++/PyTorch library for k-bit weight quantization whose transferable core is NF4 (a fixed 16-entry quantile codebook information-theoretically optimal for normally distributed data), blockwise absmax scaling, double/nested quantization of the scales, and a dynamic-tree 8-bit data type with per-value exponent/fraction allocation.
repos.core_innovation: Codebook quantization driven by the data's own distribution: instead of uniform int8 (which wastes code points on empty bins), NF4 places its 2^k reconstruction levels at the quantiles of a standard normal so each level is used equally often (minimum-entropy / Lloyd-Max optimal). Stored values are just k-bit indices into a tiny fixed lookup table; reconstruction is index -> codebook[index] * blockwise_absmax. This is strictly better than nest's current uniform int8 for L2-normalized embeddings, whose per-dimension components are approximately zero-mean Gaussian.
key_techniques: NF4 NormalFloat: hardcoded 16-level codebook at quantiles of N(0,1) (-1.0, -0.6962, -0.5251, ... 0.0 ... 0.7230, 1.0), store 4-bit index per value
Blockwise absmax scaling: split vector into blocks (default 64), normalize each block by its max-abs into [-1,1], store one scale per block to bound error and absorb outliers
Double/nested quantization: quantize the fp32 block scales themselves (groups of 256) to 8-bit, reclaiming ~0.4 bits/parameter of scale overhead
Dynamic tree 8-bit: per-value variable exponent/fraction split via sign bit + run-of-zeros exponent + indicator '1' bit + linear fraction, low relative error across magnitudes
Quantile quantization (estimate_quantiles): build a data-adaptive codebook from the empirical CDF so each code point holds equal mass (equal-frequency binning)
Separation of storage dtype (4-bit index) from compute dtype (fp16/fp32): dequantize on the hot path only, keep the dot product in float
k-bit generalization: same codebook+absmax machinery parameterized to 8/4/lower bits, one codec family spanning tiny->exact presets
repos.nest_application: Add codebook-based vector codecs to nest-format's encoding layer (crates/nest-format/src/encoding) as new encoding ids in the additive v1 RESERVED space (ids 4-255 free): e.g. id 4 = nf4-blockwise, id 5 = quantile-codebook-int8. The embeddings section keeps its mmap-friendly fixed-stride layout but each vector becomes [block_scales | packed k-bit indices], with a single shared 16- or 256-entry f32 codebook stored once in the section header. Determinism holds: the codebook is either the fixed NF4 constants or computed by a seeded/sorted quantile estimate over the corpus, so same chunks => byte-identical file. nest-runtime's simd dispatcher (crates/nest-runtime simd module) gains a dequantize-and-dot kernel: AVX2 vpermps / NEON vqtbl gather from the LUT into f32 lanes, multiply by block absmax, then the existing SIMD dot, preserving the mandatory exact-cosine rerank (ANN proxy never returned). Double-quantizing the block scales shrinks per-vector scale overhead further. Unlocks a new preset below 'tiny': nf4 embeddings at ~0.5 bytes/dim vs int8's 1 byte/dim, roughly halving the dominant embeddings section while staying offline, single-file, deterministic, exact-on-rerank.
repos.compression_relevance: Directly central. Embeddings are the largest section and the one nest deliberately leaves uncompressed (zstd banned on the hot path). NF4/quantile codebooks attack exactly that: ~4 bits/dim instead of int8's 8 or f32's 32, near-lossless recall because the codebook matches the Gaussian shape of normalized embedding components. Blockwise absmax + double quantization push bytes/dim lower while bounding error, and the LUT dequant is cheap enough to run inline before the SIMD dot, serving straight from mmap. Most credible path to beating int8/'tiny' on the 'compress more than everyone' north star for the vector payload.
repos.license: MIT
repos.perf_notes: Reference kernels are CUDA; nest must reimplement in pure Rust SIMD. Dequant is a 16-entry LUT gather (fits in registers/L1) plus one fp32 multiply by block scale before the dot. AVX2: shuffle/permute-based 16-entry LUT (_mm256_permutevar8x32_ps / vpermps for 8 f32 lanes); NEON: vqtbl byte-table lookup of indices then convert. Packing 4-bit indices is 2 values/byte, halving hot-path memory bandwidth vs int8, which often makes dequant effectively free relative to bandwidth saved. Block size 64 keeps scales in cache; double-quant of scales is a second tiny LUT.

repos.one_liner: A multi-backend (PyTorch/ONNX/TF) post-training quantization toolkit whose LLM core implements weight-only quantization (RTN, GPTQ, AWQ, AutoRound/SignRound) and microscaling block-float formats (MXFP4/NVFP4, NF4/FP4) at 1-8 bits with group-wise scales and zero-points.
repos.core_innovation: Block/group-wise affine quantization with a shared per-group scale (and optional zero-point) where the scale maps the group amax to the format max, combined with learned rounding direction (AutoRound SignSGD) and microscaling block-float element formats (MXFP4 E2M1+E8M0, NVFP4 E2M1+E4M3+FP32) to hit near-lossless 4-bit.
key_techniques: RTN group-wise affine quant: per-group scale=amax/qmax, sym (signed, no zero-point) vs asym (unsigned + zero-point) schemes, group_size from 32/128 down to per-channel(-1)
AutoRound/SignRound: SignSGD optimization of per-weight rounding offset v in [-0.5,0.5] plus learned clip scales alpha/beta over ~200 steps, block-wise output reconstruction, no inference overhead
GPTQ: Hessian-based (inverse activation covariance) error-compensated quantization, column-by-column with percdamp dampening and actorder reordering
AWQ: protect ~1% salient channels (chosen by activation magnitude) via per-channel scaling before quant
MXFP4 microscaling: E2M1 4-bit element (values +/-{0,.5,1,1.5,2,3,4,6}) + shared E8M0 8-bit power-of-two scale per 32-element block (decode = pure exponent add, no multiply)
NVFP4 two-level scaling: E4M3 FP8 scale per 16 elements + per-tensor FP32, finer granularity, amax encoded near-FP8 precision
NF4 non-uniform codebook: information-theoretically optimal 4-bit levels for normally-distributed weights (QLoRA), plus FP4
Double quantization: quantize the scales themselves (fp16->fp8->int4) to amortize per-group scale overhead; layer-wise quant to stay within memory
repos.nest_application: Adapt block/group-wise quantization to nest's embeddings section codec in nest-format (crates/nest-format/src/encoding.rs + sections.rs). Today nest has only flat int8 and float16 for embeddings. Add a new additive encoding id (4-255 reserved) for grouped/microscaled vectors: split each embedding vector into fixed groups of 16 or 32 dims sharing one scale (mirroring MXFP4/NVFP4), giving int4-equivalent footprint at far better recall than per-vector int8 because the scale adapts to local dynamic range. Two concrete codecs worth adding: (1) group-int8 with per-group fp16 scale (asym), and (2) an MXFP4-style block-float (E2M1 nibble-packed, one E8M0 byte scale per 32 dims) for a ~4x size cut over f32. Critically, the E8M0 power-of-two scale means decode is an exponent-add not a multiply, so the nest-runtime SIMD dot-product hot path (crates/nest-runtime simd dispatcher, AVX2/NEON) can dequant-on-the-fly cheaply during the mandatory exact-cosine rerank without breaking the score-straight-off-mmap design. AutoRound's learned rounding is a build-time (python, nest builder) one-shot pass that picks better int4/fp4 rounding per dimension to recover recall lost at 4 bits; it adds zero runtime cost and keeps determinism (seeded, fixed 200 steps). Store per-group scales contiguously after the packed codes so layout stays repr(C), little-endian, and reproducible.
repos.compression_relevance: Directly central to nest's north star of compressing embeddings harder than anyone. Group/block-wise scaling is the proven path from int8 (0.5x) to int4-equivalent (~0.25x) without the recall collapse of naive flat int4, because each group of 16-32 dims gets its own scale matching local amax. MXFP4-style E8M0 power-of-two scales keep dequant cheap enough to survive nest's mmap-and-score hot path, and AutoRound recovers near-lossless accuracy at 4 bits as a free build-time step, advancing nest past its current tiny preset (0.283 ratio, recall 0.992) toward a sub-0.2 ratio preset while preserving the exact-cosine rerank guarantee.
repos.perf_notes: Group sizes 32/128 are the sweet spot in INC; -1 is per-channel. MXFP4 block=32 single power-of-two scale (decode via exponent add, shift-friendly, no FMA); NVFP4 block=16 two-level (needs real multiplies but tighter error). Int4 codes are nibble-packed two-per-byte. AutoRound quantizes a 72B model in ~37min on one A100 (build-time only, zero inference overhead). INC validated 20+ LLMs at 4-bit WOQ reaching ~99% of FP32 accuracy. For nest, the hot-path cost is one extra scale fetch + exponent-add per group of dims inside the existing SIMD dot kernel; nibble-unpack is a shift+mask, vectorizable on AVX2/NEON.
repos.license: Apache-2.0

repos.one_liner: A post-training quantization toolkit that compresses LLM weights to int4/int8/fp8 and microscale fp4 using calibration-driven, Hessian-aware algorithms (GPTQ, AWQ, SmoothQuant), serializing the result in `compressed-tensors`, a safetensors extension that bit-packs sub-byte values with per-group scales/zero-points.
repos.core_innovation: GPTQ-style error-compensated quantization: instead of rounding each vector dimension independently (nest's current naive int8), quantize columns left-to-right and redistribute each value's rounding error onto the not-yet-quantized dimensions, weighted by the inverse Hessian (H^-1 = (X^T X + lambda*I)^-1) of the per-dimension covariance computed once over a calibration set of embeddings. Because all rows share the same Hessian, the inverse is precomputed once via a Cholesky factorization and reused, with lazy block updates for cache locality. This recovers far more accuracy at a given bit-width than round-to-nearest, letting you push embeddings to ~4 bits while keeping cosine recall high.
key_techniques: GPTQ: OBS/OBQ-derived inverse-Hessian error compensation, fixed column order, one-time Cholesky factorization of (X^T X + 0.01*diag damping), lazy block updates (blocksize ~128)
ActOrder: reorder dimensions by sensitivity (largest Hessian diagonal first) so high-impact dims are quantized while more dims remain to absorb error
Group-wise scales: one scale/zero-point per contiguous group of 128 values, ~0.125 bits/value overhead but captures local distribution -> big win vs per-tensor
pack-quantized codec: logical int4 stored as int8 then packed 8-per-int32, with separate weight_scale (bf16) and weight_shape side tensors
NVFP4 microscale: 4-bit E2M1 elements, shared E4M3 fp8 scale per 16-value block, plus one fp32 per-tensor scale (two-level scaling)
MXFP4 microscale: 4-bit E2M1 elements with shared UE8M0 power-of-two scale per 32-value block (cheaper, lower quality than NVFP4)
SmoothQuant: migrate per-channel activation outliers into weights via a diagonal scaling transform so both quantize cleanly
safetensors-extension layout: quantized payload plus sibling scale/zeropoint/shape tensors named by convention, self-describing per-layer config
repos.nest_application: Three concrete steals. (1) nest-format/encoding: add two additive encoding ids in the reserved 4-255 range -- a `pack_int4` codec (8 logical int4 per int32, deterministic LE packing) and a `microfp4` codec (E2M1 elements + per-16 fp8 block scale + per-shard fp32 scale, NVFP4-style two-level), each storing scales in a side blob so the embeddings section stays a flat mmap-friendly array; nest-runtime SIMD dispatcher gets an unpack+dequant-to-f32 step before the AVX2/NEON dot product (or dequant-on-the-fly into the accumulator). This unlocks ~4x and ~8x smaller embedding sections vs f32, beating the current `tiny` int8 preset. (2) nest-python builder: add an offline GPTQ/group-wise calibration pass over corpus embeddings (compute X^T X once, Cholesky inverse, error-compensated round) producing quantized bytes; pure build-time, keeps the rust runtime offline and deterministic, and is where the real compression-ratio gains live. (3) Group-wise scales (group=128) become a tiny side-section feeding the rerank: since nest ALWAYS does an exact-cosine rerank, an approximate fp4/int4 ANN-stage score is acceptable because the mandatory rerank restores true cosine -- so aggressive quantization is risk-free for final scores. Determinism holds: seeded calibration, fixed column order, alphabetical/index group order; format stays additive (new encoding ids only, no NEST_FORMAT_VERSION bump).
repos.compression_relevance: Directly central to nest's 'compress more than everyone' north star: GPTQ error compensation + group scales let embeddings drop from int8 (nest's current floor) to ~4 bits at comparable recall, roughly halving the largest section again, and NVFP4/MXFP4 give a principled sub-byte float path. The mandatory exact-cosine rerank in nest's search contract is the perfect safety net that makes aggressive lossy embedding quantization safe for final-score fidelity.
repos.perf_notes: Quantization cost is all build-time (Cholesky is O(d^3) in embedding dim d once, e.g. d=384/768/1024 is trivial; per-vector pass is O(d^2) within a block). Runtime cost is the unpack/dequant before SIMD: int4-into-int32 unpack is a few shifts+mask vectorizable under AVX2/NEON; NVFP4 needs a small E2M1 LUT + fp8 scale multiply. Memory: int4 group=128 adds ~0.125 bits/value; NVFP4 adds ~0.5 bits/value (fp8 scale per 16) plus negligible per-tensor fp32. Smaller embeddings also mean less mmap page traffic on the hot dot-product path, partly offsetting dequant overhead.
repos.license: Apache-2.0 (both llm-compressor and compressed-tensors) -- permissive, safe to vendor/learn algorithms from

synthesis.summary: The whole category converges on one move that is nearly tailor-made for nest: RaBitQ (SIGMOD 2024, NTU) replaces trained PQ/OPQ codebooks with a fixed, deterministic codebook (sign-corners of the unit sphere) plus a single shared random orthogonal rotation P, giving 1 bit/dim plus ~2 f32 correction scalars per vector (~32x vs f32, ~8x vs nest's current int8 floor) AND a distance estimator that is provably unbiased with a sharp O(1/sqrt(D)) error bound, computed as bitwise-AND + popcount straight off mmap with no decompression. It is patent-free, openly published, and reimplementable clean-room in Rust. The bitsandbytes/INC/llm-compressor cluster supplies the complementary mid-tier: codebook (NF4 quantile-optimal for Gaussian-shaped normalized embeddings), block/group-wise absmax scaling, microscale block-float (MXFP4 E2M1 + power-of-two E8M0 scale that decodes by exponent-add, no multiply), and build-time accuracy recovery (GPTQ inverse-Hessian error compensation, AutoRound learned rounding). These are the 4-bit tier that sits between int8 and RaBitQ's 1-bit. nest is unusually well positioned to adopt all of this because (a) the format is additive-only with encoding ids 4-255 RESERVED in v1, so new codecs need no version bump, (b) the runtime already mandates a rerank stage, and (c) rotation/codebook determinism maps cleanly onto seeded reproducible builds. CRITICAL FINDING confirmed by reading the code: nest's current rerank in crates/nest-runtime/src/search.rs::score_subset reranks against the SAME lossy dtype stored on disk (int8/f16), NOT against full-precision f32. The search_contract docstring claims 'real cosine, never an ann proxy', but for quantized presets the returned score already carries quantization error. Aggressive 1-bit/4-bit quantization makes this latent gap material: to keep the contract honest, nest must either keep a full-precision (or f16) shadow copy of survivors for rerank, or accept that 'exact cosine' means 'exact at the stored precision'. This decision gates the entire category and must be made before shipping a rabitq/nf4 preset.
synthesis.state_of_the_art: As of 2024-2025 the frontier for vector-byte compression splits into two regimes. (1) Sub-byte randomized quantization: RaBitQ and its B-bit extension are the state of the art for reaching ~1 bit/dim while preserving recall, because the random orthogonal rotation (Johnson-Lindenstrauss) turns naive sign quantization into an UNBIASED estimator with an O(1/sqrt(D)) error bound that matches the Alon-Klartag FOCS17 lower bound (asymptotically optimal). The estimator <o,q> ~= <o_bar,q>/<o_bar,o> reduces to AND+popcount against a 4-bit query, ~3x faster than PQ table lookups at equal accuracy, and the B-bit dial (1/4/5/7 bits via an 'ex-code' refinement) reaches ~90/95/99% recall with NO rerank. Library maturity is high (VectorDB-NTU CPU/GPU, cuVS IVF-RaBitQ fork reporting >2.7x throughput over IVF-PQ). (2) Codebook + block-scaling at 4 bits: from the LLM-weight world, NF4 (quantile-optimal 16-level codebook for N(0,1) data), blockwise absmax scaling (block=32/64, one scale per block absorbs outliers), double/nested quantization of the scales (~0.4 bits/param reclaimed), microscale block-float MXFP4 (E2M1 nibble + shared E8M0 power-of-two scale, decode = exponent add) and NVFP4 (two-level E4M3 fp8 scale per 16). Accuracy at 4 bits is recovered to ~99% of FP32 by build-time-only passes: GPTQ (inverse-Hessian error compensation, one Cholesky over the calibration covariance) and AutoRound/SignRound (SignSGD-learned per-weight rounding offset, fixed ~200 steps, zero inference overhead). The unifying principle across both regimes: separate storage dtype from compute dtype, keep the dot product in f32, and let the data's own distribution (Gaussian for L2-normalized embeddings) or geometry (random rotation) dictate where the few code points go. For an L2-normalized-embedding database with a rerank stage, RaBitQ is the clear headline lever and NF4/MXFP4 are the safe 4-bit intermediate.
top_innovations: RaBitQ 1-bit randomized quantizer: rotate by a shared seeded orthogonal P, store sign(P^-1 (o-c)) as D bits + 2 f32 scalars (<o_bar,o> and ||o-c||). ~32x vs f32, ~8x vs nest int8, distance = AND+popcount off mmap. THE headline compression lever for nest's embeddings section.

Unbiased estimator with provable O(1/sqrt(D)) error bound: turns ANN distance into a quantity with a confidence interval, so nest's search_contract can cite a recall GUARANTEE, not just an empirical number. This is what makes 1-bit safe where naive binary quantization collapses.

Asymmetric bit allocation: data side 1 bit/dim, query side 4 bits/dim (4 bit-planes). Error is dominated by data quantization, so query precision is cheap insurance; distance = sum_k 2^k * popcount(code & q_plane_k).

B-bit ex-code refinement dial (RaBitQ extended, Sep-2024): one codec spanning 1/4/5/7 bits (~90/95/99% recall no-rerank). Gives nest a single tunable knob from a 'nano' preset up to near-lossless, replacing the discrete float32/float16/int8 ladder.

NF4 quantile-optimal codebook: 16 reconstruction levels at the quantiles of N(0,1), strictly better than uniform int8 for L2-normalized embeddings whose per-dim components are ~zero-mean Gaussian. 4 bits/dim, near-lossless, dequant is a 16-entry LUT gather (AVX2 vpermps / NEON vqtbl).

Blockwise absmax + double quantization: per-block (32/64) scale bounds error and absorbs outliers; quantizing the scales themselves reclaims ~0.4 bits/dim. The reason int4 is viable where flat int4 collapses.

MXFP4 microscale block-float: E2M1 4-bit element + shared E8M0 power-of-two scale per 32 dims. Decode is an EXPONENT-ADD, not a multiply, which is the cheapest possible dequant on nest's SIMD hot path.

GPTQ inverse-Hessian error compensation (build-time only): quantize dims left-to-right, push each rounding error onto not-yet-quantized dims weighted by H^-1 of the embedding covariance. One Cholesky (O(d^3), trivial at d=384/768/1024). Recovers most of the recall lost at 4 bits, zero runtime cost.

AutoRound/SignRound learned rounding (build-time only): SignSGD over per-dim rounding offset in [-0.5,0.5], fixed seeded ~200 steps. Deterministic, zero inference overhead, free recall recovery at 4 bits.

FastScan batched layout: reorganize 32 codes at index time for SIMD lane-parallel popcount/shuffle scan (AVX2/AVX512 VPOPCNTDQ, NEON vcnt+vaddv). Makes the 1-bit scan memory-bandwidth-bound rather than compute-bound.

nest_recommendations.idea: Add a `rabitq.rs` codec under crates/nest-format/src/encoding/ as encoding id 4 (additive in the RESERVED 4-255 space, NO NEST_FORMAT_VERSION bump). Layout mirrors int8.rs: u32 payload_version, u32 variant/Bq, a single deterministic rotation SEED (store the seed, never the dense matrix), the global centroid c once, then per vector D/8 packed sign bits as LE u64 words + 2 LE f32 factors (<o_bar,o>, ||o-c||). Add EmbeddingDType::RaBitQ + 'rabitq' manifest_str in writer/encoding_choice.rs and expected_embeddings_size in encoding/mod.rs.
nest_recommendations.where_in_nest: crates/nest-format/src/encoding/rabitq.rs (new, keep <300 lines), encoding/mod.rs (pub use + expected size + decode_payload passthrough like int8), writer/encoding_choice.rs (new enum arm), layout/mod.rs (SECTION_ENCODING_RABITQ=4)
nest_recommendations.impact: Highest-leverage compression in nest: embeddings section (the dominant payload) drops from int8's ~1 byte/dim to ~1 bit/dim + 8 bytes/vec, ~8x over int8 and ~32x over f32. Directly the biggest single move on the 'compress more than everyone' north star for vector bytes.

nest_recommendations.idea: Add a RaBitQ AND+popcount distance kernel beside the existing dot dispatchers in the simd module. New rabitq.rs with NEON (vcnt + vaddv), AVX2 (popcount over 4 query bit-planes; VPOPCNTDQ when detected), and a scalar u64::count_ones fallback, wired through detect_backend() exactly like dot_f32_i8. Scores codes straight off mmap as the cheap ANN/coarse stage. Extend score_all/score_subset in search.rs with a DType::RaBitQ arm.
nest_recommendations.where_in_nest: crates/nest-runtime/src/simd/rabitq.rs (new) + simd/mod.rs dispatch arm, crates/nest-runtime/src/search.rs (DType::RaBitQ in score_all/score_subset), mmap_file.rs DType enum
nest_recommendations.impact: Makes the 1-bit codec actually scorable on the hot path with no decompression (the property zstd lacked), at ~3x PQ speed; 1-bit codes touch ~8x fewer bytes/vector than int8, so the mmap scan becomes bandwidth-light.

nest_recommendations.idea: Decouple rerank precision from storage precision: keep a full-precision (f32) or f16 SHADOW copy of embeddings available so score_subset reranks survivors against true precision, not the lossy stored dtype. Either (a) store both rabitq codes AND an f16 embeddings blob (still ~17x smaller total than f32, exact-on-rerank), or (b) explicitly redefine the search_contract to say 'exact cosine at stored precision' and surface dtype in SearchHit. This resolves the confirmed gap where score_subset currently reranks int8 against int8.
nest_recommendations.where_in_nest: crates/nest-runtime/src/search.rs (score_subset rerank source), crates/nest-format/src/sections/contract.rs + search_contract docs, decode.rs content_hash semantics
nest_recommendations.impact: Keeps nest's headline 'returned score is real cosine, never an ann proxy' guarantee honest under aggressive quantization. Without this, the 1-bit/4-bit presets quietly degrade the contract. This is the gating design decision for the whole category.

nest_recommendations.idea: Add an NF4/quantile codebook codec as encoding id 5: per vector [block_scales | packed 4-bit indices], block=32, with a single shared 16-entry f32 codebook (fixed NF4 constants OR a seeded/sorted quantile estimate over the corpus) stored once in the section header. Double-quantize the block scales (group=256 to int8) to shave scale overhead. Dequant kernel = 16-entry LUT gather (AVX2 vpermps / NEON vqtbl) * block absmax, then the existing SIMD dot.
nest_recommendations.where_in_nest: crates/nest-format/src/encoding/nf4.rs (new), encoding/mod.rs, writer/encoding_choice.rs, crates/nest-runtime/src/simd/nf4.rs (new dequant-and-dot kernel)
nest_recommendations.impact: 4-bit tier between int8 and rabitq: ~0.5 byte/dim, near-lossless because the codebook matches the Gaussian shape of normalized embedding components. A safer intermediate preset and a fallback if RaBitQ recall is unsatisfactory on the PT-BR corpus.

nest_recommendations.idea: Add a 'nano' preset (zstd text / rabitq embeddings / hnsw) and a 'micro' preset (zstd / nf4 / hnsw) to the preset resolver, below the existing 'tiny'. Expose the B-bit dial as a build kwarg (rabitq_bits=1|4|5|7). Pair rabitq codes with the existing HnswIndex so the popcount scan feeds/replaces the HNSW shortlist.
nest_recommendations.where_in_nest: crates/nest-python/src/build_fn.rs (preset match arms + new dtype/bits kwargs), crates/nest-cli build surface
nest_recommendations.impact: Turns the codec work into a user-facing one-flag win and pushes tiny's 0.283 ratio toward sub-0.1 on embedding-dominated corpora. The bits dial gives one tunable knob spanning nano->near-lossless.

nest_recommendations.idea: Add a build-time-only GPTQ/AutoRound accuracy-recovery pass in the python builder, run before quantizing to 4-bit codes: compute X^T X once over corpus embeddings, Cholesky inverse, error-compensated rounding (or SignSGD learned rounding, fixed seed + fixed step count). Produces better int4/nf4 codes; pure build-time, zero runtime cost, keeps the rust runtime offline and deterministic.
nest_recommendations.where_in_nest: crates/nest-python (builder quantization stage, before encode), feeding the nf4/int4 codec bytes; no rust runtime change
nest_recommendations.impact: Recovers most of the recall lost at 4 bits (INC reports ~99% of FP32), making the micro/nano presets viable without a precision shadow copy. Free quality at build time.

nest_recommendations.idea: Add an MXFP4-style block-float codec (E2M1 nibble + per-32 E8M0 power-of-two scale) as a third sub-byte option, chosen specifically because its decode is an exponent-add not a multiply, minimizing hot-path dequant cost during rerank. Nibble-unpack is a shift+mask, vectorizable on AVX2/NEON.
nest_recommendations.where_in_nest: crates/nest-format/src/encoding/mxfp4.rs (new), crates/nest-runtime/src/simd/mxfp4.rs dequant-and-dot
nest_recommendations.impact: ~4x over f32 with the cheapest possible dequant; a principled float sub-byte path alternative to integer NF4. Useful if NF4's LUT gather proves slower than exponent-add on aarch64.

nest_recommendations.idea: Implement the rotation P as a Fast Hadamard Transform (FHT) variant rather than a dense D*D matmul, so per-query inverse rotation P^-1 q is O(D log D) and per-vector build-time rotation is cheap. Store only the seed + sign-flip pattern. Keeps the codec file small and the build deterministic.
nest_recommendations.where_in_nest: crates/nest-format/src/encoding/rabitq.rs (rotation helper) shared with crates/nest-runtime query-side rotation in search.rs/simd
nest_recommendations.impact: Avoids an O(D^2) dense rotation per query and a D*D matrix in memory; matters at D=768/1024/1536. Keeps the codec mmap-light and the build fast on brenner's minimal hardware.

nest_recommendations.idea: Group-wise int8 (per-group fp16 scale, group=16/32) as the lowest-risk first step before committing to 1-bit/4-bit: a tiny upgrade to the existing int8.rs that swaps per-vector scale for per-group scale. Lands recall improvement and de-risks the layout/scale plumbing the harder codecs reuse.
nest_recommendations.where_in_nest: crates/nest-format/src/encoding/int8.rs (add scale_kind=1 per-group, additive within the existing int8 encoding), simd/mod.rs score_int8_section group-aware
nest_recommendations.impact: Immediate recall win at the same ~4x ratio, and proves out the contiguous per-group-scale layout that nf4/mxfp4/rabitq all depend on. Low blast radius.

compression_wins: RaBitQ 1-bit embeddings: 768-dim f32 vector 3072 bytes -> ~768 bits + 8 bytes = ~104 bytes, ~30x on embedding bytes (~0.034 ratio), vs int8's 4x. 1024-dim: 4096 -> ~136 bytes. The single largest available lever on nest's headline ratio since embeddings dominate compressed-preset file size.

~8x cut specifically over nest's current floor (int8 at 1 byte/dim -> ~1 bit/dim), pushing the 'tiny' 0.283 ratio toward sub-0.1 on embedding-heavy corpora, while staying directly scorable from mmap via popcount (no decompression on the hot path, the property that banned zstd on embeddings).

NF4 / quantile codebook at 4 bits/dim: ~0.5 byte/dim (half of int8), near-lossless on L2-normalized embeddings because the codebook sits at N(0,1) quantiles. A safe intermediate that beats int8 with one LUT gather of dequant cost.
MXFP4 block-float: ~4x over f32 (4 bits/dim + one E8M0 byte per 32 dims) with decode-by-exponent-add, the cheapest sub-byte dequant for the rerank path.

Double/nested quantization of block scales reclaims ~0.4 bits/dim of scale overhead, and storing the rotation as a SEED (not a D*D matrix) keeps the rabitq codec header to a few bytes regardless of dimension.

B-bit ex-code dial gives a continuous size/recall tradeoff (1/4/5/7 bits) from one codec, letting nest ship a 'nano' preset and a near-lossless preset from the same code path instead of discrete f32/f16/int8 tiers.

Combined stack potential: zstd on text sections + RaBitQ on embeddings + HNSW pruned by popcount can plausibly take a vector-dominated corpus well below the current 0.283 tiny ratio while the rerank (against a precision shadow) keeps returned scores honest.
watch_outs: CONTRACT INTEGRITY (highest): confirmed in code that search.rs::score_subset reranks against the SAME lossy stored dtype, not full-precision f32. The search_contract claims 'real cosine, never an ann proxy', but quantized presets already violate the spirit of that. Shipping 1-bit/4-bit without either a precision shadow copy or a redefined contract turns the headline guarantee into a half-truth. Decide this first.

CONTENT_HASH STABILITY: nest's content_hash is documented as STABLE across encodings, but for quantized embeddings it hashes the on-disk bytes (per decode.rs). A RaBitQ file and an f32 file of the same corpus will NOT share content_hash, so citations nest://content_hash/chunk_id are tied to a specific quantization. This is acceptable but must be documented; do not claim cross-precision citation stability.

DETERMINISM of the rotation: RaBitQ determinism hinges on a seeded orthogonal P AND identical floating-point ops across the three SIMD backends. If P^-1 q or the rotation matmul is computed with FMA on AVX2 but separate mul/add on scalar, sign() can flip near zero, breaking 'same chunks => byte-identical codes' and the reproducible-build guarantee. The codec generation (build-time) must be backend-independent; only the popcount scan may vary.

AutoRound/GPTQ determinism: SignSGD and Cholesky must use fixed seed, fixed iteration count, fixed column/group order (nest already mandates alphabetical/index order). Any nondeterministic BLAS threading in the python builder would break reproducibility. Pin it.

NO-PANIC RULE: every new codec parse path (rabitq/nf4/mxfp4) must return typed thiserror NestError on malformed payloads (bad payload_version, size mismatch, unknown variant), mirroring Int8EmbeddingsView::parse. No unwrap on untrusted mmap bytes. The unsafe i8/u8 bitcast pattern in int8.rs is fine but the bit-unpacking must bounds-check section length first.

FILE HYGIENE: <=300 lines/file (333 hard cap), single-responsibility. RaBitQ encode + B-bit ex-code + rotation will not fit one file; split codec (format), kernel (runtime simd), and rotation helper. Do not bloat encoding/mod.rs.

SMALL-CORE / DEPENDENCY CREEP: do NOT vendor Eigen/cuVS/bitsandbytes; all are CUDA/C++ and would violate the offline single-file Rust runtime. Reimplement only the (patent-free, published) algorithm in pure Rust. The python builder may use numpy for the build-time GPTQ/quantile pass, but the rust runtime must stay dependency-light and socket-free.

QUERY-SIDE ROTATION COST: P^-1 q is one O(D^2) op per query (or O(D log D) with FHT) amortized over the probe list. For nest's small/embedded corpora the probe list may be short, so the rotation could dominate per-query latency. Benchmark vs the int8 flat scan before declaring a speed win; the compression win is real regardless, the speed win is corpus-size-dependent.

LICENSE diligence: RaBitQ algorithm is patent-free and openly published (SIGMOD 2024, arXiv 2405.12497); upstream code is MIT/Apache but one extract could not confirm the library license from the README. nest only needs the algorithm (clean-room Rust), so this is a reference concern, but record the citation/DOI in provenance rather than copying code.

BM25/CJK gap is orthogonal but interacts: aggressive vector quantization makes the lexical path relatively more important for the PT-BR (and any CJK) corpora; don't let a 1-bit vector preset ship without bm25 in the hybrid path as a recall backstop.

categories.name: vector-db
categories.focus: vector databases and sqlite vector/columnar extensions

repos.one_liner: A Rust vector database whose differentiating engine is a stack of rescore-backed quantization codecs (scalar int8, binary 1/1.5/2-bit, product, and the new data-oblivious TurboQuant) under an HNSW graph, where compressed vectors live hot and full-precision originals stay on disk purely for a two-stage rescore.
repos.core_innovation: TurboQuant (Google Research, ICLR 2026, as extended by qdrant): a DATA-OBLIVIOUS quantizer needing NO trained codebook. Apply a fast randomized Hadamard rotation (seeded deterministic sign flips + Walsh-Hadamard transform, O(d log d)) to each vector, which provably redistributes energy uniformly so every coordinate becomes ~Beta-distributed regardless of the embedding model. Then quantize every coordinate with ONE global precomputed Max-Lloyd (1-D k-means) codebook baked in at compile time. A per-vector scalar length-renormalization factor (orig_length/reconstruction_length, borrowed from RaBitQ) corrects the systematic length-shrink bias. Scoring is asymmetric: stored vectors pack to 1-4 bits, the query stays full precision and is rotated the same way, so one SIMD pass over packed codes yields a real distance estimate.
key_techniques: Randomized Hadamard rotation: seeded sign-flip (LCG) + fast Walsh-Hadamard transform in O(d log d), making any embedding distribution coordinate-uniform so a single global codebook suffices (no training, deterministic)
Compile-time baked Max-Lloyd codebooks: precomputed optimal 1-D k-means quantizers for Beta-distributed coords at 1/1.5/2/4-bit; data-oblivious so reproducible
Per-vector length renormalization (RaBitQ trick): store one f32 scale = orig_len/quantized_len to cancel quantization's systematic length-shrink, applied at score time
Asymmetric quantization: compress stored vectors to k bits, keep query full precision -> higher recall at same storage; query rotated then encoded into a SIMD scoring form

Scalar int8 with algebraic dot decomposition: expand (alpha*i8+offset)*(alpha*i8'+offset) so offset/min cross-terms precompute per-vector, leaving ONLY raw int8.int8 dot at query time -> AVX-512 VNNI vpdpbusd / NEON sdot
Binary quantization via sign bit + XOR/popcount Hamming; 1.5-bit and 2-bit variants explicitly encode near-zero values to fix binary's weakest case

Two-stage retrieve-then-rescore: oversample 2x-4x candidates on cheap quantized distance, then rescore the small set against full-precision originals via async IO (all ids known, no random-access penalty) -> recall 0.98-1.0
Quantile-calibrated bounds (e.g. 0.99) to clip outliers before linear int8 mapping
repos.nest_application: Add a TurboQuant codec to nest-format/src/encoding alongside int8/float16, applied ONLY to the embeddings section (new encoding id from the reserved 4-255 range, additive, no NEST_FORMAT_VERSION bump). Build pipeline (python side, nest-python): per vector -> normalize for metric -> pad to power of 2 -> seeded sign-flip + Walsh-Hadamard rotation -> assign coords against a codebook baked as a rust const -> pack to 1/2/4-bit -> store one f32 renorm scale per vector. Compile-time const codebook keeps builds byte-identical/deterministic (nest's hard constraint) and needs NO corpus stats. nest-runtime gets a new asymmetric SIMD scorer in the simd dispatcher: rotate the f32 query once, dot against packed codes (AVX2/NEON/scalar fallback already exist). This PRESERVES nest's mandatory exact-cosine rerank: TurboQuant is the cheap oversample stage, and the search-contract rerank reads the original f32 embeddings (kept raw/mmap, never zstd) so the returned score stays true cosine. Unlocks a preset below the int8 'tiny' floor: TurboQuant-4bit ~halves embedding bytes vs int8 at comparable recall; 1-bit/1.5-bit go smaller than binary while beating it on recall -- directly advancing 'compress more than everyone'. The Hadamard rotation is a self-contained, seeded, reversible ~one-file util respecting <=300-line and never-panic rules.
repos.compression_relevance: Directly central. TurboQuant is the single best lever for nest's 'compress more than everyone' goal on the embeddings section -- the largest, least-compressible part (zstd is forbidden there since vectors are scored from mmap). 4-bit gives ~2x over the current int8 'tiny' preset at similar recall; 1-bit/1.5-bit beat binary quantization on recall at smaller size. Being data-oblivious with compile-time codebooks, it is the ONLY high-end quantizer that keeps nest's deterministic/reproducible-build and no-training guarantees, and asymmetric full-precision query scoring plus the existing exact-cosine rerank make the compression lossless for the FINAL returned score.
repos.perf_notes: Hadamard rotation O(d log d) per vector (one-time at build for stored vectors; once per query at search). int8 path: only raw int8.int8 dot at query time -> AVX-512 VNNI vpdpbusd (x86) / NEON sdot (aarch64), ~4x lane density vs f32, ~75% RAM cut, <0.3% recall loss, 28-60% latency win on qdrant benchmarks. Binary: XOR+popcount Hamming, up to 40x speedup. TurboQuant 4-bit: scalar-quality recall at 2x compression; SIMD-accelerated for cosine/dot/L2 (L1 needs full reconstruction, slow). Rescore needs no random access -- all candidate ids known, originals streamed from disk, so cheap mmap/network disks suffice. nest already has AVX2/NEON/scalar dispatch, so the asymmetric scorer slots into existing infra.
repos.license: Apache-2.0 (qdrant core). TurboQuant algorithm is from a Google Research paper (arXiv:2504.19874) -- reimplement from the paper to stay clean; do not copy qdrant's exact source.

repos.repo: https://github.com/milvus-io/milvus (core vector engine: zilliztech/knowhere; storage: milvus-io/milvus-storage)
repos.one_liner: Distributed vector database whose single most transferable kernel is Knowhere/ScaNN's FastScan: 4-bit product quantization scored by SIMD in-register lookup tables, combined with anisotropic quantization and a mandatory full-precision refine stage.
repos.core_innovation: FastScan = 4-bit product quantization where each sub-vector maps to one of 16 centroids (4 bits/subspace), and the per-query distance lookup table is held entirely in SIMD registers so distance computation becomes register byte-shuffles (in-register ADC) instead of memory-bound table loads. Paired with anisotropic quantization, which trains the PQ codebook to penalize the residual component PARALLEL to each vector more than the orthogonal component, preserving inner-product/cosine ranking accuracy instead of minimizing raw reconstruction error. Both are made safe by over-fetching candidates and re-ranking the top reorder_k with exact full-precision distance.
key_techniques: FastScan 4-bit PQ: 16 centroids per subspace packed at 4 bits, distance LUT kept in SIMD registers (in-register ADC) eliminating the memory-load bottleneck of classic PQ table lookups
Anisotropic vector quantization (Guo et al 2020 MLR): score-aware loss weighting parallel residual error higher than orthogonal, optimizing for MIPS/cosine ranking not L2 reconstruction
Runtime SIMD dispatch via Google Highway generating AVX2/AVX512 from one source; AVX2 pshufb / AVX512 vpermb / NEON vqtbl1q for the 16-entry table gather
Mandatory exact refine stage (reorder_k / with_raw_data / FP32 refiner): over-fetch from lossy index then recompute true distance on raw vectors -- identical to nest's mandatory exact cosine rerank
SQ8 scalar quantization: per-dimension f32->uint8 affine map storing min/scale (~4x), with IVF clustering as a coarse quantizer

JSON shredding: classify keys into typed columns (frequent+consistent type), dynamic columns (frequent+mixed type, path-named like /user/name), and a shared binary-JSON column with an inverted index for sparse keys
Per-field columnar binlog: each column is its own file with a magic-number header + typed event stream and an ExtraBytes slot for additive format evolution without breaking compatibility

Storage Format V2 adaptive layout: 'narrow column merging + wide column independence' co-locates small scalar columns, keeps large vector columns independent, enabling random point lookups without Parquet I/O amplification
repos.nest_application: Add a PQ codec to nest-format as a new encoding id (reserved 4-255 space, additive within v1) applied ONLY to the embeddings section -- the one place nest currently refuses to compress because it scores from mmap. FastScan flips that: the 4-bit PQ codes ARE the mmap'd hot-path data and the per-query LUT is built once into registers, so you keep zero-copy scoring while reaching 8-32x compression vs raw f32 (beyond today's int8 4x and zstd's no-op on embeddings). Concretely: (1) nest-format gains a pq codec module -- write side runs deterministic seeded k-means per subspace, stores tiny codebooks in a sub-section plus 4-bit codes. (2) nest-runtime simd adds a FastScan kernel building the 16-entry-per-subspace LUT per query, then AVX2 pshufb / AVX512 vpermb / NEON vqtbl1q in-register gather to accumulate distances -- mirrors the existing AVX2/NEON/scalar dispatch shape, stays <=300 lines, typed errors. (3) Search path needs ZERO contract change because nest ALREADY mandates an exact cosine rerank: PQ becomes another approximate first stage, over-fetch then rerank against existing raw/f16 vectors so returned scores stay real cosine. (4) New preset 'micro' (zstd/pq/hnsw) targeting <0.1 size ratio below 'tiny'. Anisotropic codebook training is a pure build-time python change to the k-means loss (deterministic, no format change, better recall at same bytes). Separately, JSON shredding maps onto nest's roadmap to compress json/yaml/datasets: a future shredding codec for a structured-data section turns repetitive nested docs into typed columns that zstd compresses far better than raw text.
repos.compression_relevance: Directly central to 'compress more than everyone'. Embeddings are nest's largest, currently-incompressible section (zstd skips them, int8 reaches only 4x). FastScan 4-bit PQ reaches 8-32x on exactly that section while staying mmap-scored on the hot path, and anisotropic training recovers the recall PQ would otherwise lose -- the single biggest available win on nest's dominant byte cost. The exact-rerank safety net nest already enforces is precisely what makes aggressive lossy quantization acceptable.
repos.perf_notes: In-register LUT turns PQ scoring from memory-bound to compute-bound; ScaNN reported ~5x QPS over IVF_FLAT on Cohere-1M. 4-bit codes pack 2 subspaces/byte: a 768-d vector with 96 subspaces = 48 bytes vs 3072 bytes f32 (~64x raw, before tiny codebook overhead). AVX2 pshufb is a 16-byte shuffle (exact fit for 16 centroids); AVX512 vpermb; aarch64 NEON vqtbl1q. Refine cost scales with reorder_k only, not corpus size, so the exact-rerank tax stays bounded.
repos.license: All components Apache-2.0 (milvus core, knowhere, milvus-storage, google-research/scann). Clean to study and reimplement the algorithms in nest's Rust core; do not vendor C++ -- reimplement the FastScan kernel and anisotropic loss from the public MLR 2020 paper and PQ literature.

repos.one_liner: Chroma is a log-structured, Rust-core embedded/distributed vector DB whose index crate has converged on rotation-based binary/low-bit quantization (RaBitQ 1-bit/4-bit and TurboQuant 3-bit) over a SPANN inverted index, with an Arrow-RecordBatch blockfile storage layer and HNSW centroid routing.
repos.core_innovation: RaBitQ-family quantization: a random orthogonal rotation decorrelates coordinates so each dimension can be stored in 1 bit (sign of the rotated, centroid-residual, normalized vector), and distance is recovered via a provably UNBIASED inner-product estimator (error O(1/sqrt(D))) computed as bitwise AND + popcount plus two precomputed corrective scalars (centroid distance, and inner product between the quantized and normalized vector). This gives ~28x compression over f32 (vs nest's current 8x int8) with no codebook training, no iterative optimization, and a binary-only hot loop; an exact rerank then fixes residual error. TurboQuant extends this to a tunable 3-bit point (PolarQuant Lloyd-Max 2-bit per coordinate + QJL 1-bit sign-of-residual correction scaled by Sigma|e[i]|/dim) for a higher-recall operating point.
key_techniques: RaBitQ 1-bit quantization: random rotation + store sign per dim -> nearest hypercube vertex (144B/1024-dim, 28.4x vs f32)
Unbiased inner-product/distance estimator from binary codes with two corrective scalars per vector (centroid dist + <quantized,normalized> dot)
Bitwise asymmetric distance kernel: AND + popcount (~111ns/code) instead of float dot products on the hot path
Random orthogonal rotation as decorrelation preprocessing so per-coordinate scalar quantization becomes near-MSE-optimal
TurboQuant 3-bit = PolarQuant (Lloyd-Max MSE-optimal 2-bit scalar quantizer per coord) + QJL (1-bit sign of PolarQuant residual, scaled by Sigma|e[i]|/dim)
24-byte per-code header of precomputed factors (norm, radial, correction, qjl_scale) for fast decode/estimate
SPANN inverted index: in-memory HNSW over centroids routes to on-disk posting lists (nprobe), residuals quantized -> tiny disk footprint
Two-stage search: cheap quantized estimate for candidate generation, then exact full-precision rerank for true scores

Determinism is preserved by SEEDING the random rotation and storing the seed in the header so build stays byte-identical/reproducible (same chunks + model fingerprint => same file), satisfying nest's hard constraint. nest-runtime/src/simd dispatches a new AND+popcount kernel (trivial AVX2/NEON/scalar, popcnt is one instruction) to produce the unbiased estimate straight off mmap, feeding candidates into the EXISTING mandatory exact-cosine rerank in nest-runtime search; that is the perfect home because nest already guarantees the returned score is real cosine, so the quantizer only needs to be a good RANKER not a good scorer. repos.compression_relevance: Directly central to 'compress more than everyone': embeddings are the largest binary section nest cannot zstd (scored from mmap on the hot path), so they are the single biggest lever. RaBitQ takes embeddings from 8x (current int8) to ~28x compression while nest's mandatory exact rerank absorbs the accuracy loss; highest-leverage compression win available, attacking the one section currently uncompressable.
repos.perf_notes: Binary kernel ~111ns/code (AND+popcount) vs ~3.94us scalar path -> ~35x faster candidate scoring; popcount is a single CPU instruction so AVX2/NEON/scalar dispatch is trivial for nest's existing simd module. RaBitQ needs NO training/codebook (rotation + sign only), so build stays deterministic and cheap (~1us/vector encode at 1-bit). 1-bit codes keep far more vectors resident in page-cache, improving mmap locality. TurboQuant 3-bit is the higher-recall knob (cosine P95 error 0.96% vs RaBitQ 1-bit 3.56%) at 10x compression for presets needing better pre-rerank recall, but encode is ~12x slower (13.7us vs 1.1us).
