repos.one_liner: Go-based vector database whose flagship compression is 8-bit Rotational Quantization (RQ): a RaBitQ-inspired scheme that applies a fast pseudorandom Walsh-Hadamard rotation to each vector so per-vector min/max scalar quantization to int8 becomes near-lossless, then guarantees recall via a mandatory full-precision rescore stage on HNSW candidates.
repos.core_innovation: Rotate-then-quantize: a deterministic fast pseudorandom rotation (three rounds of blocked Fast Walsh-Hadamard Transform with seeded element swaps + sign flips, O(D log D)) makes any embedding's coordinates approximately normally distributed before scalar quantization. This smooths the min-max interval and spreads similarity information uniformly across all dimensions, so naive per-vector min/max int8 quantization becomes near-lossless (98-99% recall@10) at 4x compression WITHOUT any trained codebook or k-means, so it stays fully deterministic and data-independent.
key_techniques: 8-bit Rotational Quantization (RQ): per-vector store = D int8 codes + l_x (f32 min) + delta_x (f32 step) + squared-norm (f32), ~96 bits metadata overhead per vector

Fast pseudorandom rotation = 3 rounds of blocked Fast Walsh-Hadamard Transform, padded to multiple of 32/64, with seeded random element permutation and random sign flips per round (O(D log D), ~7us for D=1536)
Decomposed quantized inner product: <q,x> approx = d*lq*lx + lq*dx*sum(cx) + lx*dq*sum(cq) + dq*dx*<cx,cq>, where only the int8 dot product term needs the hot SIMD kernel (~2.3x faster than f32)
1-bit RQ variant: sign-bit binary codes after rotation giving ~32x compression as D grows, Hamming distance via XOR+popcount
Binary Quantization (BQ): sign threshold to 1 bit/dim, distance via bitwise XOR + SIMD popcount, ~5% of f32 search latency
Mandatory two-stage rescore (rescoreLimit): HNSW walks on compressed distances, then top candidates get exact full-precision distance recompute for the returned score
Output dimension rounded up to nearest multiple of 64 so FWHT blocks and the SIMD int8 dot product stay aligned
repos.nest_application: Upgrade crates/nest-format/src/encoding/int8.rs from naive per-section int8 to a rotation-aware per-vector RQ codec, registered as a NEW additive encoding id (4-255 reserved range) so the FROZEN v1 format and existing int8 stay byte-compatible. Store per embedding row: D int8 codes plus three f32 scalars (l_x, delta_x, sq_norm). Determinism is preserved because the rotation seed derives from the model fingerprint already in the manifest (no trained codebook, no k-means -- fits nest reproducible builds exactly, unlike PQ). Add a small FWHT helper (well under the 300-line cap, pure repr(C)/little-endian, no panics) plus the decomposed int8 inner-product kernel into the nest-runtime SIMD dispatcher (AVX2/NEON/scalar) beside the existing dot-product path. Near-perfect fit for nest's 'hnsw + mandatory exact cosine rerank' contract: RQ does the cheap candidate walk and nest's already-mandatory exact cosine rerank IS the rescore stage, so the returned score stays real cosine. Net: the 'tiny' preset int8 recall@10 should climb from 0.992 toward 0.998+ at the same 4x size, and a 1-bit RQ mode unlocks a new ultra-tiny preset at ~32x embedding compression. nest-cli benchmark/stats surface the recall delta; nest-python needs no change.
repos.compression_relevance: Directly central. RQ is the rare quantizer that is simultaneously (a) data-independent and deterministic (seeded rotation, no trained codebook), satisfying nest's reproducible-build and additive-format constraints where Product Quantization fails, and (b) near-lossless at 4x with a 1-bit path at ~32x. It pushes the 'tiny' preset toward best-in-class embedding compression at fixed recall, the literal core of the compress-more-than-everyone mission, while embeddings stay directly scorable from mmap on the hot path (int8 codes read raw, no entropy decode).
repos.license: BSD-3-Clause (Weaviate core). RQ is an original Weaviate implementation inspired by the RaBitQ paper (RaBitQ academic code is MIT). The math is published in their blog and is not patent-encumbered, so a clean-room Rust reimplementation is safe.
repos.perf_notes: Rotation ~7-10us for D=1536 (O(D log D), three blocked-FWHT rounds, 64/256-element block kernels). Distance estimate ~2.3x faster than f32 since the dominant cost is an int8 inner product (Apple M4 NEON ~182 M ops/s for 64-dim 8-bit RQ vs ~145 M ops/s f32). Memory: 1M x 1536-dim drops 5859 MB -> 1465 MB (4x). 1-bit RQ and BQ use XOR+popcount, ~5% of f32 latency. Fixed 96-bit/vector metadata overhead is negligible at typical D but favors higher-dimensional embeddings.

repos.one_liner: LanceDB is a disk-based, zero-copy embedded vector database built on the Lance columnar file format, which uses adaptive per-buffer structural+compressive encodings (miniblock/fullzip, FSST, bit-packing, RLE, byte-stream-split) and decomposes every vector index into the three composable parts IVF clustering + sub-index (FLAT/HNSW) + quantization (PQ/SQ/RaBitQ) with residual encoding and an uncompressed-vector refine rerank.
repos.core_innovation: The single most transferable idea is Lance's per-buffer compression cascade with a transparent-vs-opaque encoding distinction: each column buffer is independently probed through an ordered decision (constant -> dictionary -> bitpack -> RLE -> FSST -> byte-stream-split -> general zstd/lz4 -> raw), and encodings are tagged transparent (a single value is extractable at a known offset without decoding neighbors, e.g. bitpack/FSST/dict) vs opaque (zstd block, needs full decompress). This transparency tag is exactly what lets nest pick aggressive entropy coders for cold sections while keeping the embeddings hot path random-accessible from mmap.
key_techniques: Compression cascade: ordered per-buffer selector constant->dict->bitpack->RLE->FSST->byte-stream-split->general(zstd/lz4)->flat, chosen by cheap stats (cardinality budget num_values/2, dict-size-ratio<=0.8, RLE run_count/num_values<0.5, FSST when max_len>=5 and total>=32KB)
Transparent vs opaque encoding taxonomy: transparent (bitpack, FSST, dictionary, flat) supports O(1) random access to a single value at known offset/length; opaque (zstd/lz4 block) forbids it
Byte-stream-split (BSS): de-interleave f32/f64 by byte position so each plane has lower entropy, then general-compress; entropy-auto-detected, the key trick for compressing float embeddings
FSST (Fast Static Symbol Table): one symbol table per page, substring->1-byte-code, transparent string compression for chunks_canonical text
Miniblock structural layout for narrow types: ~4-8KiB power-of-two chunks, 8-byte aligned, tiny metadata (24-41 bytes/chunk) tuned to control random-access read amplification
Fullzip structural layout for large values (>=256B, embeddings/blobs): control-word + size + value zipped into one buffer with a u64 repetition index for O(1) row access on scans
Vector index decomposition IVF x sub-index x quantization with PQ residual encoding (quantize vector-minus-centroid) and transposed __pq_code uint8 codes
refine_factor rerank: ANN/quantized search returns candidates, then re-scores against uncompressed full-precision vectors -- identical contract to nest's mandatory exact-cosine rerank
repos.nest_application: Three concrete steals. (1) In nest-format/encoding, add a byte-stream-split codec for the embeddings section before the int8/f16 step: de-interleave f32 by byte plane (4 planes) so high-order exponent bytes RLE/zstd-compress hugely; but since nest scores embeddings directly from mmap on the hot path, expose it ONLY as a new RESERVED encoding id (4-255 space) used for a cold/archival frozen-embeddings variant, never the scored path -- this respects the never-compress-scored-embeddings rule while still cutting file size. (2) In nest-format/encoding for chunks_canonical(text), add FSST as a transparent codec id so text stays single-value random-accessible for citations (nest://content_hash/chunk_id must reopen an exact span) -- FSST gives ~2x over raw while preserving the O(1) span access that block-zstd destroys; directly advances compress-more-than-everyone on the text section. (3) Borrow the transparent-vs-opaque tag as a one-bit manifest field per section/encoding so nest-runtime knows whether a section permits zero-copy span extraction vs needs a decode buffer -- formalizes the constraint nest enforces by convention. The PQ-residual + transposed-codes scheme is a future hnsw_index(0x07) upgrade path (add a quantized-storage sibling), and Lance's refine_factor validates nest's exact-rerank contract as prior art.
repos.compression_relevance: Directly central to the compress-more-than-everyone north star. Byte-stream-split + general compression is the standard high-ratio trick for float embedding archives and is missing from nest's encoding set (nest has raw/zstd/f16/int8 but no byte-plane split). FSST gives transparent text compression that, unlike nest's current section-level zstd, preserves the O(1) citation-span access nest's content_hash/chunk_id citations require. The transparent-vs-opaque taxonomy is the conceptual framework nest needs to safely add aggressive codecs without breaking the mmap hot path.
repos.license: Apache-2.0 (both lancedb/lancedb and lancedb/lance)
repos.perf_notes: Disk-first design: Lance is reportedly the only vector DB where all vector indexes are disk-resident, read zero-copy via the columnar format; embeddings and PQ codes are mmapped/paged, not RAM-loaded. Miniblock targets 4-8KiB chunks to bound read amplification; an LRU search cache preloads page locations, encodings, miniblock metadata, dictionaries, and repetition index, amortizing init cost over reader lifetime. BSS and entropy auto-detection add encode-time cost but are statistics-driven. PQ training (k-means) is noted as slow and memory-intensive -- a caution for nest deterministic builds (k-means seeding must be fixed for byte-identical reproducibility). f32 BSS miniblock caps at 1024 values/chunk, f64 at 512, aligning with SIMD batch sizes; the uncompressed-vector refine step keeps returned scores exact like nest's rerank.

repos.one_liner: A PostgreSQL extension implementing exact + approximate (HNSW, IVFFlat) vector search over four vector types (float32 vector, float16 halfvec, binary bit, sparsevec) with scalar/binary quantization codecs, distance operators for L2/cosine/inner-product/L1/Hamming/Jaccard, and a binary-quantize-coarse-filter-then-exact-rerank retrieval pattern.
repos.core_innovation: The binary-quantize-then-exact-rerank pipeline.
key_techniques: binary_quantize(): sign-bit threshold at zero (x>0 -> 1, x<=0 -> 0), packing each dim into 1 bit -> dimensions/8 + 8 bytes, scored via Hamming distance (popcount of XOR)
halfvec scalar quantization: IEEE float16 (2 bytes/dim) giving 2.0-3.0x shrink with near-identical recall because the most significant bits dominate distance
sparsevec compressed encoding: store only non-zeros as (index,value) pairs, 8 bytes per nnz + 16 byte header, format {1:0.1,3:0.2}/dim

HNSW on-disk layout: 36-byte HnswMetaPageData (magic 0xA953A953, m, efConstruction, entry blkno/offno/level, insertPage) on page 0; element tuples carry vector inline + heaptids[10] dedup array + 6-byte neighbortid pointer; neighbor tuples sized (level+2)*m with 6-byte ItemPointerData refs
two-stage retrieval: over-fetch K' (e.g. 800) by quantized distance, then ORDER BY exact distance LIMIT K (e.g. 10)
heaptids[10] dedup: identical vectors share one graph node, collapsing duplicate embeddings
expression/cast indexing: index embedding::halfvec or binary_quantize(embedding)::bit so the same source column drives multiple quantized indexes
iterative index scans (strict_order/relaxed_order) to keep filtering past the first ef_search batch without recall collapse
repos.nest_application: Add a binary quantization tier to nest-format encoding (next reserved encoding id, additive within v1): a binary codec that sign-bit-thresholds each embedding dim at 0 into a packed bitmap section, dimensions/8 bytes per vector vs 4 bytes/dim raw = ~32x shrink on the embeddings section, which is nest's single largest section and the one its zstd policy refuses to touch. In nest-runtime, add a Hamming popcount kernel to the simd dispatcher (AVX2 _mm256 popcnt / NEON vcnt / scalar count_ones) that scores the bit vectors straight off mmap, used ONLY as a coarse candidate generator that over-fetches K*~50-80x, then feeds nest's already-mandatory exact cosine rerank, materializing real f32 from a sidecar full-precision embeddings section (or from int8). This yields a new "nano" preset below tiny that beats 0.283 size ratio while the search_contract guarantee (returned score is always real cosine) is preserved unchanged. Separately, adopt the heaptids-style dedup in nest-format writer: chunks whose embeddings are byte-identical collapse to one stored vector, helping the deterministic-build/compress-more goal. The sparsevec (index,value) encoding maps directly onto nest's bm25_index(0x08) and any future sparse-embedding section. Skip pgvector's page/TOAST machinery entirely (Postgres-coupled, irrelevant to a single mmapped file).
repos.compression_relevance: Directly central. Binary quantization is the highest-leverage missing codec for nest's "compress more than everyone" north star: the embeddings section is the dominant volume and is deliberately excluded from zstd, so a 1-bit-per-dim packed bitmap (~32x over raw f32, ~8x over int8) is the biggest single win available, and pgvector proves with real recall numbers (91-99% at 1536-dim with rerank) that the exact-rerank step nest already mandates is exactly what makes it safe. halfvec confirms nest's float16 choice; sparsevec gives a concrete encoding for sparse sections.
repos.perf_notes: halfvec doubles vectors-per-page and gives identical-or-better QPS/latency vs float32. Binary quantization stacked with halfvec gave 67x HNSW build speedup (0.7.0 vs 0.5.1). Hamming distance is a single XOR + popcount per vector, far cheaper than f32 dot product, so the coarse stage is near-free; recall depends on bit-diversity (fails on low-dim sift-128/gist-960, excels at high-dim 1536). Over-fetch ratio (e.g. 800-to-10 = 80x) is the recall/cost knob. HNSW graph must fit in RAM in pgvector; nest sidesteps this by mmapping the whole file and letting the OS page it.
repos.license: PostgreSQL License (permissive, BSD/MIT-like; compatible with vendoring or clean-room reimplementation)

repos.one_liner: A PostgreSQL extension (vchordrq) that indexes vectors as IVF posting lists where each vector is stored as a tiny RaBitQ-quantized bit-code, scanning compressed codes with binary popcount arithmetic and deferring full-precision math to an adaptive rerank stage.
repos.core_innovation: RaBitQ quantization: apply a random rotation (Johnson-Lindenstrauss / Fast Hadamard Transform) to the residual of a vector around its cluster centroid, take the sign bits to get a 1-bit-per-dim code, and store just two corrective float scalars per vector (centroid distance + the inner product between the quantized and normalized vector). The cosine/L2 estimate is reconstructed from a single binary dot product plus those two scalars, and crucially it is an UNBIASED estimator with a provable O(1/sqrt(D)) error bound (asymptotically optimal, Alon-Klartag). That is what separates it from product quantization, which is biased and silently fails on some datasets. The binary dot product is popcount(code AND query_bits); the multi-bit variant (RaBitQ4/8) reuses the same machinery by quantizing the QUERY into bit-planes q1,q2,q3,q4 and summing weighted popcounts: 1*popcount(code&q1) + 2*popcount(code&q2) + 4*popcount(code&q3) + 8*popcount(code&q4) -- the data stays 1 bit/dim while query precision is tunable.
key_techniques: RaBitQ 1-bit quantization: random-rotation + sign-bit code + 2 corrective scalars (centroid_dist, <quantized,normalized>) giving an unbiased estimator with O(1/sqrt(D)) error bound
Residual quantization: quantize each vector relative to its IVF centroid and reformulate <o,q-c>=<o,q>-<o,c> so the query is rotated/quantized once per probe (~20% QPS)
Random rotation via Fast Hadamard Transform (O(D log D), no dense DxD matrix to store) to spread information before sign-bit extraction
Binary distance estimator = popcount(code AND query_bits); multi-bit = weighted-popcount over query bit-planes keeping data at 1 bit/dim
SIMD Fast Scan: bit-pack/transpose codes to estimate 32 vectors per kernel pass; single-vector popcount path beats PQ table-lookups ~3x
IVF posting lists instead of a global graph: insert=append code, delete=clear code, no cascading graph repair, deterministic and update-friendly
Adaptive two-stage search: scan all codes with cheap integer math, then full-precision rerank only a small top subset sized by the error bound
DiskANN + 2-bit RaBitQ (vchordg) alternate graph index trading update cost for higher QPS at high recall
repos.nest_application: Add a RaBitQ-style codec as a new RESERVED encoding id (4-255, additive within v1, no NEST_FORMAT_VERSION bump) in nest-format/encoding, targeting the embeddings section. Per embedding store a 1-bit-per-dim sign code plus two f32 corrective scalars computed against a small set of seeded deterministic k-means centroids serialized alongside (seeded => reproducible, honors the determinism guarantee). In nest-runtime add a binary-popcount estimator kernel to the simd dispatcher (popcount is one instruction on AVX2/NEON, trivial scalar fallback) as the cheap first pass; nest already mandates an exact-cosine rerank on the hot path, which is precisely RaBitQ's two-stage model, so the search_contract is unchanged and the returned score stays real cosine. This unlocks an embeddings encoding far smaller than int8 (1 bit/dim vs 8 => ~8x on the dominant section) and the provable error bound lets you bound rerank candidate count instead of guessing. The Fast Hadamard rotator (O(D log D), nothing dense to persist) is the only new primitive and fits as one <=300-line module. Longer term, the IVF posting-list layout (centroid id -> contiguous code run) is a deterministic, cheap-to-build alternative to hnsw_index.
repos.compression_relevance: Directly central to 'compress more than everyone'. Embeddings are the largest, least-compressible section in a .nest file (zstd is banned on them because they are scored from mmap). RaBitQ is the rare scheme that compresses embeddings 8-32x WHILE keeping them scoreable in place via popcount on the hot path -- no decode step before scoring, unlike a generic entropy coder. Combined with nest's existing mandatory exact rerank, recall is recovered for free, making this the highest-leverage way to shrink the dominant section without breaking the score contract.
repos.license: tensorchord ships VectorChord under a source-available license (AGPL/ELv2-style); verify exact terms before vendoring. The underlying RaBitQ reference (gaoj0017/RaBitQ, now VectorDB-NTU/RaBitQ-Library, SIGMOD 2024 paper) is independently published and is the cleaner source to reimplement from to avoid the extension's license.
repos.perf_notes: Single-vector RaBitQ via popcount is ~3x faster than PQ in-RAM table lookups at equal accuracy; batch Fast Scan estimates 32 vectors per pass; estimate is integer/bitwise only, full-precision floats touch only the reranked subset. Storage claims: ~6x more vectors than Pinecone optimized storage, ~26x vs pgvector at equal cost; 1M 960-dim indexed in ~1.5 min, 100M under 20 min with precomputed centroids; residual reformulation ~20% QPS; Fast Hadamard rotation O(D log D) with no dense matrix to load, important for an mmap/disk design.

repos.one_liner: A pure-C SQLite extension that does ANN over plain BLOB columns with zero index build, pairing a runtime-dispatched SIMD distance table (SSE2/AVX2/NEON/RVV) with TurboQuant: rotation-based data-oblivious 2/3/4-bit scalar quantization scored via SIMD nibble lookup tables without vector reconstruction.
repos.core_innovation: TurboQuant scalar quantization (Google Research, ICLR 2026, arXiv 2504.19874): apply a fast structured random rotation (Hadamard-based, reproduced here as a reversible-LCG + Fisher-Yates Hadamard rotation) to each vector so per-coordinate variance is redistributed to a concentrated near-iid Beta/Gaussian distribution, THEN apply a fixed per-coordinate Lloyd-Max scalar codebook (16 centroids at 4-bit, 4 at 2-bit) with a per-vector scale+shift calibration. This is data-oblivious (no training/codebook fitting, no centroid storage), gives near information-theoretically optimal distortion (within ~2.7x of the proven lower bound), and at query time scores ASYMMETRICALLY: the full-precision query is rotated once and folded with 1/scale, so dot(q,x) is recovered as a lookup-table sum over the stored 2/3/4-bit codes with zero per-vector decompression. The decisive part for nest is that this beats plain int8 SQ at half the bytes (4-bit ~8x compression matches/beats nest's current int8 4x; 2-bit hits 16x; 1-bit 32x) while preserving recall.
key_techniques: TurboQuant: fast structured random rotation (Hadamard/FFHT-style, O(d log d)) before quantization so coordinates become near-iid and a single fixed scalar codebook applies per-coordinate
Per-coordinate fixed Lloyd-Max codebook from standard normal (16 centroids for 4-bit, 4 for 2-bit) plus per-vector (scale,shift) calibration x -> (x+shift)*scale
Asymmetric scoring: dot(q,x) = <q/scale, x_codes> - <q, shift>, query rotated and folded with 1/scale ONCE per query; stored vectors never decompressed

SIMD nibble-split LUT kernel: codebook quantized to int8, pshufb does parallel 16-byte table lookup, query split into low/high nibbles fed to _mm_maddubs_epi16 (or VPDPBUSD on VNNI / NEON tbl / AVX-512BW)
Two-stage PROD mode: MSE-optimal quantizer + 1-bit QJL (Quantized Johnson-Lindenstrauss) transform on the residual to remove inner-product estimation bias at ~1 bit/vector extra cost

Index-free architecture: runtime dispatch_distance_table[metric][dtype] function-pointer array selected by CPU feature detection (SSE2/AVX2/NEON/RVV), brute-force full scan over BLOBs, zero-cost inserts/updates with no graph rebuild
On-disk quantized row = rowid(8) + scale(4) + packed_codes(ceil(dim*qbits/8)); shadow table vector0_{table}_{column}; streaming scan when k omitted (progressive WHERE/LIMIT)
Native multi-format storage: float32/float16/bfloat16/int8/uint8/1-bit BLOBs with Hamming distance for the 1-bit path
repos.nest_application: Add a TurboQuant codec as a new additive encoding id in nest-format/src/encoding/ (e.g. turboquant.rs alongside int8.rs), reserved-range ids 4-6 for tq4/tq2/tq1, NO NEST_FORMAT_VERSION bump (additive only). The embeddings section stores per-vector [scale:f32][shift:f32][packed_codes] plus a section-level header carrying the rotation seed (deterministic: seeded LCG + Fisher-Yates Hadamard, fits nest's seeded-determinism constraint exactly) and qbits. Critically nest's hard rule is embeddings are scored DIRECTLY from mmap on the hot path and never zstd-compressed; TurboQuant respects this perfectly because codes are scored in place via LUT with no decompression, so it slots straight into nest-runtime/src/search.rs and the SIMD dispatcher in nest-runtime/src/simd/ (add a tq nibble-LUT kernel: pshufb+maddubs for avx2.rs, NEON tbl for neon.rs, scalar fallback in scalar.rs). The mandatory exact-cosine rerank stays unchanged and actually gets cheaper to justify because TurboQuant is the ANN proxy. This unlocks a new preset 'nano' (tq2/hnsw) targeting a size ratio well under the current tiny preset's 0.283 (2-bit is 16x vs int8's 8x effective), and tq1 (32x, Hamming) for an extreme-compression tier, directly advancing the compress-more-than-everyone north star. nest-cli stats/inspect surface the qbits and rotation seed; nest-python build path picks tq presets.
repos.compression_relevance: Directly central to the north star. nest's smallest preset today is int8 (8x payload reduction, 0.283 ratio). TurboQuant 4-bit matches that at half the bits with equal-or-better recall (it beats plain int8 SQ by 1-2 to ~5 recall points on real embeddings like dbpedia-openai-ada: 0.93 vs 0.88), 2-bit reaches 16x, 1-bit 32x. It is the single highest-leverage quantization upgrade available, is data-oblivious (no training, fits offline+deterministic), is provably near-optimal distortion, and crucially scores from packed codes with no decompression so it does not violate nest's never-decompress-embeddings-on-hot-path rule.
repos.perf_notes: sqlite-vector benchmarks (1M x 768d, dot, k=10): tq4 218ms vs 3248ms full scan (14.9x) at 0.84 recall@10; tq3 188ms (9.2x) 0.74; tq2 85ms (38x) 0.48 on synthetic, but on real embeddings recall is far higher (Fashion-MNIST 10k tq4 = 0.948). Preload of quantized codes into RAM gives 4-5x. The SIMD win comes from pshufb 16-byte LUT + _mm_maddubs_epi16 (VPDPBUSD on VNNI, NEON tbl on aarch64) processing 2/4-bit codes without float ops; per-query cost is one rotation (O(d log d) Hadamard) plus a folded 1/scale, amortized across the whole scan. Memory per quantized row ~ 8 + 4 + ceil(dim*qbits/8) bytes; baseline footprint 30MB.

The TurboQuant ALGORITHM is from a public Google Research paper (arXiv 2504.19874) and is freely reimplementable — nest should reimplement from the paper, not copy ELv2 C source.

repos.one_liner: A pure-C, zero-dependency SQLite extension (vec0 virtual table) that stores float32/int8/bit vectors in chunked shadow-table BLOBs and runs brute-force SIMD KNN with metadata/partition filtering, optionally using 1-bit binary quantization plus a coarse-search-then-float-rescore pattern.
repos.core_innovation: Binary (1-bit) quantization as a coarse pre-filter: sign-bit-threshold each dimension into a packed bitmap (32x smaller than f32), score candidates with Hamming distance via popcount (integer-only, branchless, SIMD-friendly), then rerank the small candidate set against full-precision vectors. This is the exact two-stage pattern nest already mandates (ANN/coarse retrieve then mandatory exact cosine rerank), so it slots in as a new ultra-compact embedding codec without weakening nest's "returned score is real cosine" contract.
key_techniques: binary quantization: sign-bit threshold (>=0 -> 1, <0 -> 0) packing 8 dims/byte = 1 bit/dim, 32x smaller than f32
Hamming distance via XOR + popcount (count_ones) as the coarse metric for bit vectors
two-pass coarse+rescore: retrieve k*8 candidates on bit vectors, rerank top-k with vec_distance_L2 on stored float vectors
per-vector int8 scalar quantization (1 byte/dim), 4x smaller than f32, selectable per column
chunked contiguous storage: vectors packed into one BLOB per chunk per column (default 128 vectors/chunk) for SIMD locality, no per-row overhead
validity bitmap per chunk for O(1) tombstone deletes (clear bit, zero rowid) without rewriting/shifting the index
shadow-table separation: _chunks (bitmap+rowids), _vector_chunksNN (packed vectors), _metadatachunksNN (packed fixed-width metadata), _auxiliary (un-indexed + columns)
partition keys + per-chunk packed metadata blobs to prune whole chunks before the distance kernel runs
repos.nest_application: Add a binary/bit embedding codec to nest-format/src/encoding (new encoding id in the reserved 4-255 range, e.g. encoding=5 'bit1', additive-only so NEST_FORMAT_VERSION stays v1) alongside the existing int8.rs: quantize each L2-normalized f32 vector to a sign-bit bitmap (dim/8 bytes, deterministic, repr(C) little-endian). In nest-runtime/src/simd add a hamming kernel (XOR + u64 count_ones; NEON vcntq_u8 on aarch64, AVX2 on x86_64, scalar fallback) parallel to the dot-product dispatcher. In nest-runtime/src/search.rs wire it as a coarse stage that over-fetches candidates (e.g. k*8) ranked by Hamming, then feeds them into the EXISTING mandatory exact-cosine rerank using full-precision (or int8) embeddings from the embeddings section, so the search contract is unchanged and the returned score stays real cosine. Expose a new preset (e.g. 'nano': zstd metadata / bit embeddings / hnsw) in nest-cli targeting the smallest embeddings section. The chunked validity-bitmap tombstone idea also transfers to nest's future real-time-edit goal: a per-section validity bitmap marks deleted chunk_ids without rewriting embeddings, preserving determinism by treating tombstones as content.
repos.compression_relevance: Directly central to the north-star 'compress more than everyone' for vectors: 1-bit binary quantization is 32x smaller than f32 and 8x smaller than nest's current int8 floor, dropping a 768-dim embedding from ~3KB to 96 bytes. Because nest already enforces an exact-cosine rerank, nest can adopt the most aggressive quantization (which would normally wreck recall) and recover full-precision accuracy at query time: nest's architecture is uniquely positioned to ship binary embeddings WITHOUT the usual recall penalty, since the bit vectors are only a coarse pre-filter, not the scored answer. This is the single biggest embedding-size win available.
repos.license: Apache-2.0 OR MIT (dual-licensed)
repos.perf_notes: Pure C, no dependencies, compiles everywhere SQLite runs; SIMD via AVX (x86_64) and NEON (Apple/Android). Brute-force KNN over packed chunk BLOBs is cache-friendly because vectors are contiguous (default 128/chunk), the same mmap-contiguous property nest relies on for its hot-path dot products. Hamming/popcount is integer-only and branchless, far cheaper per candidate than f32 cosine, which is why it works as a coarse filter ahead of an expensive rerank. int8 path is 4x smaller than f32 with minimal accuracy loss on normalized vectors; bit path is 32x smaller. Project tradeoff: chunked OLTP writes are slow per-insert (transaction + chunk assignment) vs a static read-only blob mode; nest's frozen-file build model sidesteps this entirely since nest writes once, like sqlite-vec's faster static mode.

repos.one_liner: A SQLite extension (vss0 virtual table + vector0 codec module) that bolts Facebook Faiss onto SQLite by serializing an entire Faiss index into a single BLOB inside an fts5-style shadow table, with index type chosen declaratively via Faiss factory strings.
repos.core_innovation: The clean separation of a storage-agnostic vector codec layer (vector0: a 1-byte-type-header + float32-LE compact BLOB encoding plus a JSON ingest path, exposed as vector_to_blob/vector_from_blob) from the index/search layer (vss0), where the index type is selected declaratively through a Faiss "factory string" DSL (Flat,IDMap2 vs IVF4096,Flat,IDMap2). The codec and the index are independent contracts.
key_techniques: vector0 compact BLOB codec: leading type byte + raw float32 little-endian payload, dual ingest from JSON text or raw bytes
fts5-style virtual-table design with two shadow tables: xyz_data (rowid bookkeeping, no-op column) + xyz_index (one row holding the whole serialized Faiss index BLOB)
Faiss factory-string DSL to declaratively compose index pipelines (Flat exhaustive vs IVF4096 inverted-file with k-means centroids requiring an explicit operation='training' pass)
delegating only math kernels to Faiss via knn_L2sqr_by_idx / range_search_L2sqr while keeping storage outside Faiss (proposed non-Faiss 'incremental' storage format)
per-table selectable distance metrics (L2, inner product, L1, Linf, Canberra, BrayCurtis, JensenShannon) via metric_type
vss_search_params() to pass nprobe-style runtime ANN knobs into the KNN call
repos.nest_application: Two adaptations. (1) Codec/index separation validates nest-format's existing split: keep the embeddings section (float32-LE payload, analogous to vector0) and the optional hnsw_index(0x07) section (analogous to the Faiss index) as fully independent section contracts so an index can be rebuilt or dropped without touching embeddings. (2) Generalize the Faiss factory-string DSL into nest: turn nest-cli presets (exact/compressed/tiny/hybrid) plus the search_contract section into a small declarative index-spec string (e.g. 'hnsw(m=16,ef=200)+bm25(rrf)') persisted in nest-format so a .nest file self-describes deterministically how to search it. CRITICAL NEGATIVE LESSON for nest-format/nest-runtime: sqlite-vss's single-BLOB whole-index serialization forces a hard ~1GB ceiling, full-index rewrite write-amplification on every commit, and forbids mmap (must fit in RAM). nest's mmap-off-disk SIMD scoring and per-section physical layout already defeat all three; encode this as a guardrail that hnsw_index(0x07) must stay an independently-paged, mmap-scannable section, never one monolithic compressed blob.
repos.compression_relevance: Low-to-negative for extreme compression. sqlite-vss does NO vector compression in its default path: vector0 stores raw float32-LE; the only size reduction is from optionally choosing a Faiss PQ/IVF factory string (product quantization), which then cannot mmap and pays full-rewrite cost. The transferable compression insight is purely cautionary: a monolithic serialized-index BLOB is the wrong on-disk shape. nest's per-section encodings (zstd on non-embedding sections, f16/int8 on embeddings, hnsw as a paged section) are strictly superior for both compactness and serve-from-mmap. Use as a counter-example, not a source.
repos.license: MIT (depends on Faiss, MIT)
repos.perf_notes: CPU-only (no GPU). Indices must fit entirely in RAM - no mmap support. Every INSERT/DELETE + COMMIT rewrites the ENTIRE Faiss index BLOB (O(N) write amplification: inserting 1 vector into a 1M-vector index rewrites 1,000,001 vectors). Hard ~1GB index ceiling from SQLite's single-row BLOB limit. IVF training data read fully into memory. No UPDATE support (INSERT/DELETE only). SIMD comes only indirectly from Faiss internal kernels, not from sqlite-vss code.

repos.one_liner: A self-contained SQLite loadable extension that adds column-oriented virtual tables backed by shadow tables, fixed 65,536-row chunks, and per-chunk min/max zone maps so analytical scans/aggregations skip non-matching rowid ranges and aggregate natively in C, hitting up to 130,000x speedups without patching SQLite's pager/btree/VDBE.
repos.core_innovation: Zone-map chunk-skipping: partition a column into fixed-size chunks (65,536 rows), store a tiny precomputed min/max summary per chunk, and at query time prune entire chunks whose [min,max] cannot satisfy the predicate before touching any data; paired with an incremental dirty-chunk invalidation model where writes only mark their chunk dirty and re-analyze rebuilds just those chunks (no-op analyze ~2ms vs ~66s cold build).
key_techniques: Fixed 65,536-row chunk partitioning per column (power-of-two, alignment-friendly)
Per-chunk zone maps (min/max) for range-filter pruning before any scan (3 of 153 chunks selected in their range query)
Shadow-table layout: separate tables for rowids, column values, global stats, chunk zone maps, dirty-chunk set, table metadata
Incremental dirty-chunk invalidation: writes mark chunks dirty, analyze rebuilds only dirty chunks, valid+no-dirty short-circuits
Native C hash aggregation over only the required column shadow tables (skips row-store VDBE overhead)
Result-hash equivalence harness: every columnar helper auto-verified against the equivalent plain-SQLite query
Variance bench methodology: deterministic datasets, warm-once, repeat, report median and p95
repos.nest_application: Steal the zone-map/chunk-skipping idea into nest-runtime/src/search.rs and the embeddings section of nest-format. (1) nest-format: add an OPTIONAL additive per-block summary sidecar to the embeddings section (RESERVED section id 0x09+, or a metadata block), storing per fixed-size block of N vectors (e.g. 1024) a coarse summary: a per-block centroid plus a max-norm/radius bound giving a cheap IVF/triangle-inequality upper bound on achievable cosine. Additive within v1, deterministic if centroids are computed in fixed order. (2) nest-runtime search.rs: today the exact path is an unconditional linear SIMD dot-product scan over all n_embeddings; before that loop, compute the per-block upper-bound cosine vs the query and skip whole blocks that cannot beat the current top-k threshold. This turns the exact path into pruned-exact that still returns TRUE cosine, preserving the search-contract guarantee (scores are real cosine, never an ann proxy), and also accelerates the MANDATORY exact rerank after HNSW/BM25. (3) nest-cli stats: report blocks-scanned vs blocks-pruned, mirroring their zone-map effectiveness output. The dirty-chunk model is the blueprint for the north-star real-time-edit feature: a re-embedded chunk only recomputes its own block centroid/bound.
repos.compression_relevance: Indirect but real. Do NOT copy their on-disk layout for compression: their columnar store is ~1.2x LARGER than row store (7.0 GB vs 5.9 GB on 10M rows) because the value is scan-pruning, not byte reduction. Transferable compression-adjacent angle: zone-map block summaries are tiny overhead (one centroid + scalar bound per ~1024 vectors) that unlocks skipping work, letting nest push more aggressive lossy quantization (int8/float16) on bulk vectors while keeping a small exact summary to bound error and prune. Pairs with the tiny preset to hold recall at smaller size, and the per-block centroid can double as a residual-quantization anchor (vector = centroid + small residual) for a future codec that compresses embeddings structurally rather than just float16/int8.
repos.perf_notes: Up to 130,582.95x on simple precomputed aggregates (sum/avg/count read straight from global stats, not scanning), 6-14x on grouped hash aggregation, 248-273x on zone-map-pruned clustered range queries. The durable generalizable win for nest is the 248-273x range-pruning class, not the headline aggregate numbers. Chunk size 65,536; range query touched only 3 of 153 chunks. No SIMD or entropy coding on their side; aggregation is plain C hash aggregation. Incremental analyze: cold 66,763ms, no-op 2.114ms.

Re-implement the algorithmic idea (zone maps / chunk-skipping is decades-old DB prior art, unencumbered) from scratch; never lift EL2.0 source.

synthesis.summary: The entire vector-db field has converged on ONE pattern that nest already half-implements: rotate-then-quantize embeddings to 1-4 bits, score the tiny codes from mmap with integer/bitwise SIMD as a cheap candidate stage, then rerank a small over-fetched set against full-precision originals to return a true score. nest's mandatory exact-cosine rerank IS the rescore stage every one of these systems (qdrant, milvus/knowhere, chroma, weaviate, lance, pgvector, VectorChord, sqlite-vec/vector/vss) bolts on for safety; nest is therefore uniquely pre-positioned to adopt the most aggressive quantizers without a recall penalty. The frontier splits into two families. (1) DATA-OBLIVIOUS rotation quantizers (TurboQuant, RaBitQ, Weaviate RQ): a seeded fast Walsh-Hadamard / random orthogonal rotation makes any embedding's coordinates near-iid, so a single compile-time scalar codebook or a sign bit suffices -- NO trained codebook, NO corpus statistics. This family is the perfect fit for nest because seeded rotation keeps builds byte-identical/deterministic, which trained product quantization (milvus FastScan, lance PQ) fundamentally cannot guarantee without pinning k-means seeds and iteration order. (2) Beyond quantization, lance contributes the transparent-vs-opaque encoding taxonomy and byte-stream-split (the conceptual framework nest needs to add aggressive codecs without breaking the mmap hot path), plus FSST for O(1)-random-access text compression that preserves citation spans where block-zstd would destroy them; sqlite-columnar contributes zone-map block-skipping that can make nest's exact scan sublinear while still returning TRUE cosine. The decisive architectural finding from reading nest's own code: today score_subset reranks against the SAME embeddings section it scored, so once embeddings are stored at 1-2 bits the 'exact rerank' is no longer exact. Shipping sub-int8 quantization therefore REQUIRES a dual-section layout -- a tiny coarse-codes section for candidate generation plus a separate full-precision (or f16) rerank section -- which is itself a compression win because the coarse section can be brutally small. Highest-leverage path: RaBitQ/TurboQuant 1-2 bit codes as a new additive encoding id on a coarse embeddings sub-section, popcount/LUT SIMD kernels beside the existing dot kernels, a 'nano' preset well below the 0.283 'tiny' floor, with the existing f32/f16 embeddings kept as the rerank source.
synthesis.state_of_the_art: Convergent SOTA: a two-stage retrieve-then-rerank pipeline where lossy rotation-quantized vectors live hot (mmap/page-cache) and full-precision originals are touched only to rescore a small over-fetched candidate set. The compression frontier is rotation-based low-bit quantization in two families. Data-oblivious (deterministic, the one nest needs): seeded fast Walsh-Hadamard / structured random rotation in O(d log d) makes coordinates near-iid so a fixed/compile-time codebook or a bare sign bit is near-optimal -- RaBitQ 1-bit (~28x, unbiased O(1/sqrt(D)) estimator, AND+popcount ~111ns/code), Weaviate RQ 8-bit (4x, 98-99% recall, decomposed int8 dot), TurboQuant 1/2/4-bit (compile-time Lloyd-Max codebook, asymmetric full-precision query, SIMD nibble LUT). Trained (higher recall, NOT determinism-friendly): milvus/knowhere FastScan 4-bit PQ with in-register LUT (pshufb/vpermb/vqtbl1q) + anisotropic ranking loss, ~5x QPS, 8-64x. Multi-bit query bit-planes keep DATA at 1 bit while tuning query precision. Adjacent: lance per-buffer compression cascade with transparent (O(1) access) vs opaque (decode-required) taxonomy, byte-stream-split, FSST; sqlite-columnar zone-map chunk-skipping (248-273x on range queries). Universal safety net is an exact full-precision refine/rerank (qdrant rescore, knowhere reorder_k, weaviate rescoreLimit, lance refine_factor, pgvector ORDER BY exact) -- identical to nest's mandatory exact-cosine rerank, which makes aggressive quantization safe and validates nest's contract as prior art. Critical caveat from nest's own code: the rerank currently reads the same section it scored, so sub-int8 storage requires a separate full-precision rerank source to keep returns true-cosine.
top_innovations: RaBitQ 1-bit quantization (chroma/VectorChord, SIGMOD 2024): seeded rotation + sign bit + 2 corrective f32 scalars, unbiased O(1/sqrt(D)) estimator, ~28x compression, AND+popcount off mmap, data-oblivious so byte-identical builds -- highest-leverage codec for nest.

TurboQuant (qdrant/sqlite-vector/sqlite-vec, Google arXiv:2504.19874): Hadamard rotation + compile-time Lloyd-Max const codebook + asymmetric scoring, 1/2/4-bit, no training, beats int8 at half the bytes, scored via SIMD nibble LUT with zero decompression.

Weaviate 8-bit Rotational Quantization: rotate-then-int8 with decomposed dot, a drop-in upgrade of nest's int8.rs pushing recall@10 0.992 -> ~0.998 at the same 4x size; seed derivable from the existing model fingerprint.
Mandatory exact refine/rerank as a universal contract (all repos): validates nest's existing exact-cosine rerank as prior art and is what makes aggressive lossy quantization safe.
Multi-bit query bit-plane trick (VectorChord/TurboQuant): store at 1 bit/dim, tune recall on the query side -- decouples file size from query precision.

FastScan in-register LUT product quantization (milvus/knowhere/ScaNN, MLR 2020) + anisotropic loss: highest recall-per-bit, 8-64x, but trained k-means breaks determinism -- adopt only with pinned seeds.
Lance transparent-vs-opaque encoding taxonomy + byte-stream-split: the framework to add aggressive codecs without breaking the mmap hot path; BSS for high-ratio cold embedding archives.
FSST transparent text compression (lance): ~2x over raw text while preserving O(1) citation-span access that block-zstd destroys.
Zone-map block-skipping (sqlite-columnar): per-block centroid+radius prunes whole blocks before the SIMD scan, making the exact path pruned-exact while still returning true cosine.

Validity-bitmap tombstones + byte-identical dedup (sqlite-vec/pgvector): deletes and dedup without rewriting embeddings -- foundation for the real-time-edit north star; sqlite-vss monolithic-blob is the cautionary counter-example.

nest_recommendations.idea: Add a dual-section quantized-embeddings layout: a new RESERVED encoding id 4 = 'rabitq1' storing per-vector [sign-code dim/8 bytes][2 f32 corrective scalars] in a coarse embeddings sub-section, while keeping the existing f32 (or f16) embeddings as a separate full-precision rerank source. This is the structural prerequisite for ALL sub-int8 quantization, because today score_subset reranks against the SAME section it scored -- so 1-bit codes alone would make the 'exact' rerank no longer exact and silently break the 'returned score is real cosine' contract.
nest_recommendations.where_in_nest: crates/nest-format/src/encoding/rabitq.rs (new, <=300 lines, mirror int8.rs layout); register id 4 in layout/mod.rs SECTION_ENCODING_*; the rerank source needs either a second embeddings section (cleanest, needs a reserved section id 0x09 'embeddings_fp' since 0x04 is fixed in CANONICAL_SECTIONS) OR a manifest flag pointing rerank at f16; wire candidate-gen vs rerank-source split in nest-runtime/src/search.rs score_subset. Seed the rotation from the model fingerprint already in the manifest so builds stay byte-identical.
nest_recommendations.impact: Unlocks ~28x embedding compression (vs current 8x int8) on nest's largest, currently-incompressible section while preserving true-cosine returns -- the single biggest step toward 'compress more than everyone'. Enables a 'nano' preset well below the 0.283 'tiny' floor.

nest_recommendations.idea: Upgrade int8.rs in place to Rotational Quantization (RQ): add a seeded fast Walsh-Hadamard rotation before the existing per-vector min/max int8 step, store the rotation seed (derived from model fingerprint) in the payload prefix, and use the decomposed dot product where only the int8.int8 term hits SIMD. Register as a NEW additive encoding id (e.g. 5 = 'rq8') so the FROZEN format and existing int8=3 stay byte-compatible.
nest_recommendations.where_in_nest: crates/nest-format/src/encoding/int8.rs (add rotation; bump a payload sub-version, NOT NEST_FORMAT_VERSION); new fwht.rs helper module (<=300 lines, repr(C), little-endian, no panics) shared by rabitq.rs; the decomposed kernel lands beside dot_f32_i8 in crates/nest-runtime/src/simd/{avx2,neon,scalar}.rs.
nest_recommendations.impact: Pushes the 'tiny' preset recall@10 from 0.992 toward 0.998+ at the SAME 4x size and ~2.3x faster scoring -- a near-free recall/latency win on the existing preset, and the FWHT helper is the shared primitive every other rotation codec reuses.

nest_recommendations.idea: Add a TurboQuant codec with a COMPILE-TIME-baked Lloyd-Max codebook as a Rust const (tq4=id 6, tq2=id 7), scored asymmetrically via a SIMD nibble lookup-table kernel (pshufb+maddubs on AVX2, NEON tbl, scalar fallback). Codes are scored in place with zero decompression, so this respects the never-decompress-embeddings-on-hot-path rule exactly.
nest_recommendations.where_in_nest: crates/nest-format/src/encoding/turboquant.rs (const codebook keeps builds byte-identical, no corpus stats); LUT kernel in crates/nest-runtime/src/simd/ beside the dot kernels; reuse the shared fwht.rs rotator. Per-vector store = [scale:f32][packed 2/4-bit codes]; section header carries rotation seed + qbits surfaced by nest-cli inspect/stats.
nest_recommendations.impact: 4-bit matches int8 at HALF the bytes with equal-or-better recall; 2-bit reaches 16x. Data-oblivious + const codebook is the only high-end quantizer that keeps nest deterministic without pinning k-means. Enables a 'micro'/'nano' preset.

nest_recommendations.idea: Add a Hamming popcount kernel and a multi-bit query bit-plane scorer to the SIMD dispatcher, so 1-bit codes can be candidate-scored by AND+popcount and query precision tuned WITHOUT re-encoding the file (split the f32 query into weighted bit-planes at query time).
nest_recommendations.where_in_nest: crates/nest-runtime/src/simd/mod.rs (new dot_hamming/score_bit_section beside dot_f32_i8) + avx2.rs (_mm256 popcnt path), neon.rs (vcntq_u8), scalar.rs (count_ones); wired as the coarse stage in search.rs feeding the existing rerank.
nest_recommendations.impact: popcount is one instruction so the kernel is trivial across all three backends; ~35x cheaper per candidate than f32 dot. The bit-plane trick gives a recall knob that costs zero extra storage -- decouples file size from query precision.

nest_recommendations.idea: Add zone-map block-skipping to the exact scan: an OPTIONAL additive sidecar (reserved section id 0x09+) storing, per fixed block of ~1024 vectors, a centroid + max-radius bound. Before the linear SIMD loop, compute a per-block upper-bound cosine and skip blocks that cannot beat the current top-k threshold. Returns TRUE cosine, so the search-contract guarantee is untouched.
nest_recommendations.where_in_nest: crates/nest-runtime/src/search.rs score_all/score_subset (add the prune check ahead of the dot loop); new sidecar encoder in crates/nest-format/src/sections/ (deterministic if centroids computed in fixed order); nest-cli stats reports blocks-scanned vs blocks-pruned.
nest_recommendations.impact: Turns the unconditional O(n) exact scan into pruned-exact and accelerates the MANDATORY rerank after HNSW/BM25, without weakening any guarantee. The per-block centroid doubles as a residual-quantization anchor (vector = centroid + small residual) for a future structural codec, and the dirty-block model seeds the real-time-edit feature.

nest_recommendations.idea: Add FSST as a transparent text codec id for the chunks_canonical section, replacing section-level zstd ONLY for the text section, so single chunks stay O(1) random-accessible by offset for citations while still getting ~2x compression.

nest_recommendations.impact: Advances compress-more-than-everyone on the text section WITHOUT breaking nest://content_hash/chunk_id span reopening that block-zstd currently forces a full-section decode for. Directly improves citation latency on compressed files.

Formalizes the constraint nest currently enforces only by convention and is the guardrail that lets future aggressive codecs be added safely.
nest_recommendations.where_in_nest: crates/nest-format/src/layout/section_entry.rs (use a reserved bit/byte, additive), manifest/mod.rs, and reader/decode.rs; checked in reader/validate.rs so an opaque codec on the embeddings/hot-path section is rejected at open time.
nest_recommendations.impact: Low byte cost, high architectural payoff: makes the never-compress-the-scored-embeddings rule machine-enforced rather than tribal knowledge, preventing a future codec from silently breaking the mmap hot path or citation spans.

Keeps the never-zstd-scored-embeddings rule intact while cutting size for archival .nest files.
nest_recommendations.where_in_nest: crates/nest-format/src/encoding/bss.rs (new); guarded so the reader refuses to mark a BSS section as the scored embeddings section (cross-check with the transparent tag above); offered only via a dedicated 'archive' preset in nest-cli, decoded back to f32 on open.

nest_recommendations.idea: Add validity-bitmap tombstones + byte-identical-embedding dedup to the writer: collapse duplicate vectors to one stored row (heaptids-style), and reserve a per-section validity bitmap so a future delete marks a chunk dead without rewriting embeddings -- treating tombstones as content keeps the build deterministic.
nest_recommendations.where_in_nest: crates/nest-format/src/writer/build.rs + payload.rs (dedup at encode time, maps duplicate chunk_ids to a shared embedding row); reserved validity-bitmap sub-section; nest-runtime search skips dead rows.
nest_recommendations.impact: Dedup shrinks corpora with repeated text (the PT-BR fake-news demo set has near-duplicates) at zero recall cost; the bitmap is the deterministic foundation for the real-time-edit north star without the O(N) rewrite that sqlite-vss/vss suffers.

nest_recommendations.idea: Persist a small declarative index-spec string in the search_contract section (e.g. 'hnsw(m=16,ef=200)+bm25(rrf)+rerank(exact)') so a .nest file self-describes deterministically how to search itself, generalizing the preset names into a portable contract.
nest_recommendations.where_in_nest: crates/nest-format/src/sections/contract.rs (add an index_spec field to SearchContract, additive), cross-checked against the manifest in reader/validate.rs; nest-cli presets emit the spec.
