compression_wins: RaBitQ 1-bit on embeddings: ~28x vs f32 / ~8x vs current int8 (768-dim 3KB -> ~96 bytes + scalars), recall recovered by nest's existing rerank -- biggest single win on the dominant section.
TurboQuant 4-bit matches the int8 'tiny' preset at half the bytes (~8-16x) at equal-or-better recall; 2-bit 16x, 1-bit 32x, compile-time codebook so no determinism loss.
Rotational Quantization upgrade to int8: same 4x size, recall@10 0.992 -> ~0.998 -- free quality dividend buying room for a more aggressive global preset.
Dual-section split is itself a win: coarse section 1-2 bit + rerank source at f16 (2x) instead of f32 -> nano preset far below the 0.283 'tiny' ratio while keeping true-cosine returns.
FSST on chunks_canonical: ~2x over raw text while preserving O(1) citation-span access that block-zstd destroys.
Byte-stream-split + zstd for cold/archival embeddings: high ratio on f32 byte-planes for an 'archive' preset, off the scored hot path.
Byte-identical embedding dedup: collapses duplicate vectors to one row at zero recall cost -- helps the near-duplicate-heavy PT-BR fake-news demo corpus.
Multi-bit query bit-planes: ship 1-bit storage (smallest file) and recover recall on the query side -- smallest file no longer forces worst recall.
Zone-map centroids double as residual-quantization anchors (vector = centroid + small residual) for a future structural codec beyond float16/int8.
watch_outs: DETERMINISM TRAP: trained PQ/IVF (milvus/knowhere, lance) needs k-means that is not byte-reproducible unless seed/init/iterations/tie-breaking are all pinned, and SIMD float non-associativity can still perturb centroids -- conflicts with nest's byte-identical-build constraint. Prefer the data-oblivious family; treat PQ as a later pinned-only option.

BROKEN-RERANK TRAP (in nest's own code): score_subset reranks against the SAME embeddings section it scored, so 1-2 bit storage silently makes the 'exact' rerank lossy and the returned score no longer real cosine. Any sub-int8 codec MUST ship a separate full-precision/f16 rerank source section.

FORMAT-FREEZE: every codec must be a new additive encoding id (reserved 4-255) and any new section a reserved id 0x09+, never bump NEST_FORMAT_VERSION; the rerank-source section must be a new OPTIONAL id kept OUT of content_hash so it cannot invalidate citations (embeddings is pinned at 0x04 in CANONICAL_SECTIONS).

HOT-PATH PURITY: RaBitQ/TurboQuant codes are scored in place (fine), but byte-stream-split and FSST are decode-required and must be restricted to cold/text sections, never the scored embeddings path -- enforce with the proposed transparent/opaque tag, not convention.

LICENSE: do NOT vendor VectorChord (AGPL/ELv2-style) or sqlite-vector/sqlite-columnar (Elastic License 2.0, source-available). Reimplement from the public papers; even permissive repos (qdrant/milvus/chroma/lance/pgvector) should be reimplemented, not copied.

SMALL-CORE: each codec/kernel <=300 lines (333 cap), repr(C), little-endian, typed errors, never panic; share ONE FWHT rotator across RQ/RaBitQ/TurboQuant; land incrementally (RQ first, then RaBitQ, then TurboQuant) to respect the ~3k/~4.9k loc budgets.
RECALL CLIFFS: 1-bit excels at high dim (1536+) but fails at low dim (sift-128, gist-960) -- validate recall per demo model before any 1-bit default; keep int8/RQ as safe default, 1-bit opt-in nano.
DON'T copy sqlite-vss/sqlite-columnar on-disk shapes (monolithic blob caps at 1GB + O(N) write-amplification + no mmap; columnar store is 1.2x LARGER) -- steal only the algorithmic ideas.
Per-vector corrective scalars (2-3 f32) erode the ratio at low dim -- account for them so the nano size-ratio claim is honest.

categories.name: graph-db
categories.focus: graph databases, engines, and traversal

repos.one_liner: A GPLv3 Java graph database whose storage engine stores nodes/relationships/properties as fixed-size records (legacy Record format) or hardware-page-aligned 128B/8KB co-located blocks (Block format), with a multi-root generational B+ tree (GBPTree) for dense overflow and a CSR in-memory graph (GDS) that compresses adjacency lists via sort + delta + variable-byte, or optionally block-based bit-packing ("integer packing").
repos.core_innovation: The adjacency-list compression pipeline for graph edges: sort target node IDs ascending, delta-encode consecutive IDs into small gaps, then bit-pack those gaps in fixed-size BLOCKS where each block uses only as many bits as its largest value needs ("integer packing") -- this decompresses faster than per-value varint (branchless, SIMD-friendly, cache-local) while compressing at least as well. The deeper principle: choosing bit width per-block by the local maximum beats both a global encoding and per-value continuation-bit varints on the speed/ratio Pareto front.
key_techniques: sort + delta-encode adjacency targets so neighbor IDs become small monotone gaps before any entropy step
variable-byte (varint) encoding: 7 data bits + 1 continuation bit per byte (the slow baseline)
integer packing: block-of-N values bit-packed to ceil(log2(max_in_block)) bits, branchless unpack for cache locality
GBPTree: multi-root generational copy-on-write B+ tree giving lock-free readers via generation pointers (one root per dense node)
Block format co-location: node + labels + ~6-7 properties + first ~5 relationships packed into one 128B/8KB block aligned to NVMe/OS page size to cut IOPS and cache misses
inline short-string/short-array storage to avoid out-of-line block-store pointer chasing
CSR layout: offsets (HugeLongArray) + degrees (HugeIntArray) + compressed-target byte arrays as a flat columnar adjacency representation
repos.nest_application: Add an optional section to nest-format (a reserved 0x09+ section id, additive within v1) named e.g. graph_adjacency, encoding a CSR: a u64 offsets array + per-node degree + a packed-targets blob where chunk-to-chunk edges (citation links, semantic-neighbor graph, hnsw neighbor lists) are stored sort+delta+block-bit-packed. nest-runtime gains a graph traversal path beside ann::HnswIndex (e.g. graph::CsrIndex) that mmaps offsets and unpacks blocks branchlessly, reusing the SIMD dispatcher pattern. Critically, the SAME block-bit-packing codec belongs in nest-format/encoding as a new integer-stream codec (encoding id in the reserved 4-255 space) to losslessly shrink the existing chunk_ids and chunks_original_spans sections (monotone u64 offsets/spans are ideal delta+pack candidates) and to compress neighbor-id lists inside hnsw_index(0x07) -- advancing the compress-more-than-everyone goal without touching embeddings on the hot path. Determinism holds: sort gives canonical order, block size is fixed, no entropy-coder dictionary state. Keep the codec file under 300 loc, repr(C), LE-unsigned, thiserror-typed.
repos.compression_relevance: Directly on-mission. Delta+block-bit-packing is the canonical lossless codec for monotone integer streams, which nest already has in abundance: chunk_ids, chunks_original_spans (byte offset/length pairs), and HNSW neighbor lists. These are currently raw or zstd'd; a dedicated sort/delta/packed integer codec beats zstd on structured monotone integers at far lower decode cost, and unlike zstd it can decode a single value by block off mmap without inflating the whole stream. It also enables compressed on-disk graph search (a stated north-star feature) via CSR rather than a heavyweight adjacency structure, advancing both compression and graph-search goals with one codec.
repos.license: GPLv3 (Community Edition); Enterprise features commercial. GPL is incompatible with nest's likely-permissive licensing, so learn-from-only: do not vendor neo4j source. The sort+delta+block-bit-packing technique is a public algorithm (also in Lucene PForDelta, Roaring, StreamVByte, FastPFOR) and can be cleanly reimplemented from spec.
repos.perf_notes: Block bit-packing (integer packing) decodes strictly faster than continuation-bit varint because it is branchless and cache-local (one block = one tight loop, no per-byte continuation test) at equal-or-better ratio; Neo4j reports it always wins on decode and usually on ratio. Block format reports ~40% faster traversal fully in-memory and ~70% when only 1/3 fits, via co-location plus 8KB NVMe/OS-page alignment cutting IOPS. Caution: Block format can use MORE disk than the tightly packed Record format due to padding/headers, so for size-first nest adopt the co-location/alignment idea selectively and take primarily the integer codec.

repos.one_liner: A JVM graph-analytics library whose core asset is an immutable, in-memory Compressed-Sparse-Row (CSR) graph store that compresses each node's adjacency list with sort -> delta -> variable-length (VarLong) byte encoding, plus an optional block-based integer bit-packing strategy ("PackedAdjacencyList") tuned for branch-light, cache-local decompression during traversal.
repos.core_innovation: Lossless small-integer column compression via sort -> delta -> VarLong, plus block bit-packing at per-block minimum bit-width, decoded branch-free with cache locality on the hot path.
key_techniques: sorted delta encoding
VarLong/LEB128 variable-length integers
CSR: offsets + degrees + paged compressed targets
block bit-packing at per-block minimum bit-width
tail strategies for partial blocks
HugeArray paging
repos.nest_application: crates/nest-format/src/encoding: add an integer-stream codec module (delta+VarLong, optional block bit-pack) with a RESERVED v1 encoding id (4-255), applied first to the chunk_ids and chunks_original_spans sections; later, crates/nest-runtime/ann gets an on-mmap CSR adjacency index using the same codec with a branch-free unpack kernel in crates/nest-runtime/src/simd. Reimplement clean-room from the algorithm (GDS is GPL-3.0); determinism holds since all steps are pure functions of the sorted input.
repos.compression_relevance: Directly on-mission. nest currently leans on zstd for non-embedding sections, but zstd is a general entropy coder that underperforms specialized integer codecs on dense monotonic ID/offset columns (chunk_ids, chunks_original_spans). Delta+VarLong+bitpacking is the standard way to push those columns toward 1-2 bytes/value losslessly and decode at memcpy speed, advancing the compress-more-than-everyone goal while staying deterministic and mmap-friendly (no allocation, no entropy-decoder state). It also future-proofs the graph-search roadmap with a proven compact adjacency format.
repos.perf_notes: Reported ~8.2 bytes/edge uncompressed vs ~1.4 bytes/edge after sort+delta+VarLong (~6x) on real graphs. Packed (bit-packed) variant: similar-or-better ratio than VarLong but strictly faster decompression due to branch-free unpack and better memory locality; ideal for traversal-heavy / tight inner loops. Block bit-packing is the same family as SIMD integer codecs (e.g. lnx-search/upack, FastPFor) so an AVX2/NEON unpack kernel in nest-runtime/simd is realistic. Decode requires zero allocation and no dictionary/window state, unlike zstd, so it is mmap-pure.
repos.license: GPL-3.0 (sources assemble into "OpenGDS"). LICENSE-INCOMPATIBLE with nest if nest is permissively licensed: do NOT copy code. The techniques (delta, VarLong/LEB128, block bit-packing, CSR) are decades-old public-domain algorithms, so reimplement from the algorithm, not from GDS source.

repos.repo: https://github.com/dgraph-io/dgraph (with companion repos dgraph-io/sroar and dgraph-io/badger)
repos.one_liner: A distributed GraphQL/DQL graph database storing each predicate as a sorted posting list of 64-bit node UIDs, encoded as serialized roaring bitmaps (sroar) whose in-memory byte layout equals the on-disk layout, persisted in a WiscKey-style LSM+value-log KV store (Badger).
repos.core_innovation: sroar: a serialized roaring bitmap whose in-memory representation equals its on-disk representation (single []uint16 buffer), so an integer-id set / graph adjacency list is mmapped and set-operated with zero marshal/unmarshal -- compressed storage that is also directly operable, matching nest's no-decode-on-hot-path rule.
key_techniques: Serialized roaring bitmap (sroar): single []uint16 buffer, zero-copy mmap, no marshal/unmarshal; keys section (header of node-size + key-count, then 48-bit-base-key -> container-offset pairs) followed by sequential containers

Two container types selected by density: array container (sorted uint16 list) below 4096 cardinality, bitmap container (1024 uint64 = 8KB dense bitset) above it; run containers deliberately omitted to keep impl simple yet faster
64-bit keyspace split: mask 0xFFFFFFFF0000 isolates the high 48 bits as the container base key, low 16 bits are the index within a container (uint16)

Per-container header words: [size, type, cardinality] then payload, so And/Or/AndNot iterate matching base keys and run containerAnd/containerOr directly on slices via pointer/reslice arithmetic (FastAnd/FastOr pre-size the destination from cardinality estimates)

Group-varint delta encoding (the predecessor scheme): split sorted id list into fixed 128-int blocks, store first value whole then deltas as varints (frame-of-reference); cheap but requires decode -> superseded by sroar
Posting list as graph primitive: predicate:entity -> sorted list of value-ids, so a graph join becomes a sorted-set intersection (bitmap AND) instead of an application-layer hash join

WiscKey key-value separation (Badger): small keys stay in the LSM tree, large values go to an append-only value log, cutting write amplification; SSTable blocks compressed with Snappy or Zstandard, bloom filters + block cache for reads
Mutations as WAL + in-memory overlay layers over an immutable base posting list (separate layers for replace vs add/delete) to avoid re-sorting the whole list on every write
repos.nest_application: Two concrete steals. (1) Add a serialized-roaring-bitmap codec to nest-format (new RESERVED encoding id, e.g. 0x04, or a helper in encoding/) for any section that is a SORTED SET OF u32/u64 ids: chunk_ids, hnsw neighbor adjacency lists, and bm25 postings (term -> doc-id list in 0x08). Mirror sroar's contract exactly: the encoded bytes ARE the in-memory layout, so nest-runtime mmaps and runs set intersections (AND) with no decode, matching nest's "no decode on hot path" rule. Store containers little-endian repr(C) per nest constraints; determinism is free because roaring container choice is a pure function of the id set (array<4096 cardinality else dense bitmap). This unlocks (a) a graph_index section (0x09+) where each node's adjacency = a roaring bitmap, giving the "graph search" north-star item with compressed, mmap-scored traversal; and (b) much smaller bm25 postings than raw varint id lists, improving the tiny/hybrid presets' size ratio. (2) Adopt the array-vs-bitmap density switch as a general nest codec primitive in nest-format/encoding for sorted-id sections, and reuse the group-varint frame-of-reference (first value + 128-block deltas) as the int8-tier analog for monotonic id columns like chunks_original_spans offsets, shrinking provenance/span sections in compressed/tiny presets. Skip Badger/LSM entirely: it is a mutable multi-file server store and violates nest's single-file/offline/append-only invariants -- only the sroar byte-layout discipline and the posting-list=set-intersection model transfer.
repos.compression_relevance: Directly on-mission. Roaring bitmaps are the state-of-the-art compressed representation for sorted integer-id sets, and sroar proves you can get that compression while keeping a zero-copy mmap layout (no decode tax), which is exactly nest's hot-path constraint. For nest this shrinks bm25 postings, enables a compact compressed graph adjacency section, and gives a reusable sorted-id codec -- advancing "compress data more than everyone" for the non-embedding sections without ever touching the directly-scored embedding bytes.
repos.perf_notes: sroar benchmarks: ~15x less memory, ~25x fewer allocations, ~7x faster than the reference Go roaring library, largely because there is no encode/decode step. Integrated into Dgraph v21.12 (Zion) with posting-list cache off, >40% of a heavy production workload's queries became >=20x faster and >50% became >=10x faster. Array containers cap at 4096 cardinality before switching to an 8KB dense bitmap (1024 uint64); set operations are sorted-key merges over containers, so AND/OR are linear in container count and SIMD-friendly on the dense-bitmap path. Badger uses Snappy/Zstandard block compression plus bloom filters and a block cache; WiscKey separation trades read locality for far lower write amplification (not relevant to nest's read-only file).
repos.license: Dgraph core historically Apache-2.0 with portions under the Dgraph Community License / later relicensed (BSL-style) under Hypermode; sroar and badger are Apache-2.0. Treat sroar/badger as Apache-2.0 (permissive, attribution) -- safe to reimplement the byte-layout idea in nest's own Rust. Verify the current sroar LICENSE.md before vendoring any code; prefer a clean-room Rust reimplementation given nest's small-core and edition-2024 constraints.

repos.one_liner: ArangoDB is a multi-model (document + graph + search) database whose on-disk currency is VelocyPack (VPack): a single-type-byte, self-describing binary format with trailing offset-index tables that allow zero-copy O(1)/O(log n) random access into sub-documents without parsing the whole value, layered on a RocksDB LSM store.
repos.core_innovation: The trailing-offset-table layout enabling zero-copy random access into compactly-encoded structured values, with per-value smallest-width offset selection and an optional integer-key dictionary.
key_techniques: Single-type-byte self-description: one leading byte encodes both type and size class (0x40-0xbe inline short strings up to 126 bytes, 0x30-0x39 single-byte small ints 0-9, 0x20-0x27 width-tagged signed ints) so type+length read off the first byte(s)
Trailing index/offset table for O(1) array / O(log n) sorted-object random access without full parse
Smallest-width offset selection: pick 1/2/4/8-byte offsets based on max offset (<256, <64K, <4G, else) -- pay only for the addressing range actually needed

Compact types 0x13 (array) / 0x14 (object): drop the index table entirely and use LEB128-style varints (high bit = continuation) for bytelength + count, with the item count written backwards from the end for sequential-only/dump use cases
Object-key dictionary compression: two-pass collect+count of attribute names, replace repeated long keys with small integers via an O(1) hash table (e.g. 153KB->49KB, 20.8KB->9.2KB in their benches)
Sorted-by-bytewise-key object storage enabling binary search and deterministic byte layout
Contiguous single-block memory layout (zero-copy) -- sub-value pointers are just base+offset
repos.nest_application: nest currently stores chunks_canonical(text) and a future json/yaml/parquet payload as opaque encoded blobs. Adapt VPack's trailing-offset-table layout as a new additive section codec in nest-format (sections.rs + encoding.rs) for structured payloads: a json/yaml document section laid out as [tag][smallest-width offsets][values] so nest-runtime can mmap it and resolve a sub-path (e.g. doc.field[3].name) with pure base+offset arithmetic and binary search, zero decode, matching the same hot-path discipline already used for SIMD dot products straight off mmap. Two pieces are immediately stealable under nest's constraints: (1) the smallest-width offset selection (1/2/4/8 LE bytes) is a clean, deterministic, repr(C)-friendly encoding that fits the additive encoding-id space (ids 4-255 reserved in v1) and gives compact structured storage; (2) the object-key dictionary -- collect+count keys, emit a per-file key dictionary, replace keys with varints -- maps directly onto nest's content_hash determinism (sort keys bytewise => byte-identical output for identical input) and would massively shrink repeated-schema corpora like the PT-BR datasets and any parquet/jsonl ingest. The compact 0x13/0x14 varint mode is the right default for sequential/citation materialize paths where random access is not needed, squeezing the size ratio further toward the 'compress more than everyone' north star. All of this is offline, single-file, deterministic, and additive -- no v2 bump required.
repos.compression_relevance: Directly central. VPack's key-dictionary + smallest-width offsets is a proven recipe for compressing structured/repeated-schema data (json, yaml, parquet rows, datasets) while STILL serving random sub-document access from raw mmap -- exactly nest's twin goals of extreme compression AND fast serve. It gives nest a principled structured codec that beats naive zstd-of-json on access cost (no decompress to read one field) and complements zstd: store the VPack-encoded structured payload, optionally zstd the non-hot parts. The standalone size wins are modest vs JSON (5-20%) but the key-dictionary path shows 2-3x reductions on repeated-schema data, and the zero-parse access is the real unlock for serving compressed datasets/whole-databases.
repos.perf_notes: VPack is designed for in-kernel sub-document access used by indexes: type+length read from the first byte(s), values in one contiguous block, O(1) hash-table key->int translation. No SIMD in the format itself (it is a layout, not a kernel) -- it pairs well with nest's existing SIMD by keeping decoded fields byte-aligned and addressable. Index-table reads are random memory jumps; the compact 0x13/0x14 modes trade that random access for sequential scan to save the table bytes. Size benches: JSON->VPack typically 5-20% smaller; with key compression 153KB->49KB (~3.1x) and 20.8KB->9.2KB (~2.3x). Caveat: object-key dictionary needs a second pass over input (acceptable in nest's python build stage, not the rust serve path).
repos.license: Apache-2.0 (both arangodb/velocypack and arangodb/arangodb core; note ArangoDB server moved to BSL 1.1 / community license in newer releases, but the velocypack format library and spec are Apache-2.0 and the on-disk format is documented/open)

repos.one_liner: A distributed graph database that maps an adjacency-list graph onto any BigTable-model store (Cassandra/HBase/Bigtable), serializing each incident edge as one sorted cell whose bytes are sort-key-ordered and shrunk with variable-length integer encoding plus delta-encoded neighbor ids.
repos.core_innovation: The edge-as-cell encoding: each edge is one byte string laid out so that lexicographic byte order equals the logical sort order (label id with direction bit stolen into the low bit, then sort-key property bytes, then neighbor id, then edge id), and the neighbor vertex id is stored as a signed DELTA against the row-owner vertex id rather than its absolute 64-bit value. Combined with locality-aware id assignment (co-accessed vertices get numerically close ids), the deltas stay small and the whole edge collapses to a few varint bytes. Compression AND traversal-order indexing fall out of the SAME byte layout, with no separate index structure.
key_techniques: Adjacency-list-as-row: vertex = row keyed by 64-bit id, each edge/property = one sorted cell, enabling range-scan retrieval of edge subsets
Variable-length integer (varint) encoding of label ids, sort keys, neighbor ids, edge ids so small numbers cost 1-2 bytes
Delta encoding of the adjacent vertex id relative to the owning row's vertex id (store difference, not absolute)
Direction bit packed into the low bit of the label id (bit-stealing) instead of a separate byte
Order-preserving serialization: column bytes arranged so lexicographic order == edge-label sort order, making the sort the index (vertex-centric indices are column-range scans)
Locality-aware id allocation: ids assigned so co-accessed entities have small absolute id difference, partitioning data and minimizing deltas
Column/value split: structural+sort bytes in the sorted column, signature property values get compressed serialization in the value, ad-hoc properties uncompressed in the value
repos.nest_application: Two targeted lifts, both in nest-format (crates/nest-format/src/sections + encoding). (1) Add a graph-search section (reserved id 0x09+, additive within v1) when nest grows graph search: encode each node's adjacency list as a sorted run of (varint label, delta-to-owner neighbor index, varint edge-id) triples with the direction bit stolen into the label low bit. chunk_ids are already a dense 0..N index space, so delta-to-owner makes neighbor refs 1-2 bytes; a new codec, not a format break. (2) Useful even without graph search: apply varint+delta to the existing chunks_original_spans section (offset/length pairs are monotonic, locally small) and to chunk_ids, as a new encoding id (4-255 reserved) selectable per-section in the manifest, scored off mmap with zero-copy varint decode in nest-runtime. Order-preserving bytes also reinforce nest's deterministic build: a canonical sort + delta layout is inherently reproducible and content-hash-stable.
repos.compression_relevance: High for non-embedding sections. Delta+varint is the classic way to compress monotonic/locally-clustered integer streams (spans, ids, future adjacency) and stacks under zstd for further gains, advancing 'compress more than everyone'. It does NOT touch embeddings (kept raw for SIMD hot-path scoring per nest's contract), so it complements the tiny/compressed presets rather than conflicting. The delta-to-owner trick specifically unlocks compact graph-search payloads later.
repos.perf_notes: Varint decode is branchy but cache-friendly and zero-copy off mmap; delta decode is a single running-sum (prefix-sum) pass, trivially fast and SIMD-able for bulk neighbor-id reconstruction (NEON/AVX2 prefix sum). Order-preserving layout means traversal/range queries are memcmp-ordered scans, no separate index load. Main cost is encode-time sorting and id assignment, a build-time (python) concern, not runtime.
repos.license: Apache License 2.0 (permissive; safe to learn from and reimplement the encoding ideas in nest's own Rust codecs).

repos.one_liner: In-memory C++ property-graph engine using lock-free concurrent skip lists for vertices/edges, delta-chain MVCC (Hekaton-style snapshot isolation), full-snapshot + WAL durability with a section-offset binary file format, and a USearch/HNSW vector index using a single-store reference pattern.
repos.core_innovation: The PropertyStore "single-store reference + variable-length packed-metadata-byte" encoding: each property is prefixed by one metadata byte that bit-packs the value type tag, the byte-width of the property-key ID, and the byte-width-indicator of the payload, so integers/strings consume the smallest of 1/2/4/8 bytes and large values (like embedding vectors) are never duplicated in the row store but replaced by a small index-ID reference. A self-describing, additive, per-record variable-width codec that gives size wins without a separate schema and without a global dictionary pass.
key_techniques: Packed metadata byte: bit-fields for {type tag, property-ID width, payload-size-width-indicator} in 1 byte before each value
Variable-length integer storage: ints in the minimum of 1/2/4/8 bytes that hold the value (LEB128-like family)
Name-to-ID mapper: intern property keys/labels to small integer IDs once, store IDs not strings per record
Single-store reference pattern: store a fat value (vector) only in its index backend; property store keeps just a u32/u64 index-ID reference
Snapshot/WAL layout: magic+version header, a section-offset table, then encoded-edges / encoded-vertices / indices / name-mapper / metadata / batch-info sections for seek-and-parse recovery
Batched + parallel snapshot writer/reader recorded in a batch-info section so write and recovery parallelize
Delta-chain MVCC: per-object delta linked list, visibility resolved at read time by transaction timestamp (snapshot isolation)
USearch HNSW with per-node fine-grained locking instead of one global mutex
repos.nest_application: Steal the packed-metadata-byte + name-to-ID interning into nest-format. (1) In crates/nest-format/src/encoding add a 'varpack' codec for chunks/provenance/json-like sections: each scalar gets a 1-byte tag {type, len-width, int-width} so small ints and short strings shrink to 1-2 bytes vs fixed f32/u64 fields; additive (new encoding id in reserved 4-255), deterministic. (2) Add a name-to-ID mapper section (new reserved section id 0x09+) interning repeated provenance keys, model fingerprints, metadata field names to u16 IDs, dictionary stored once, IDs per record; deterministic via alphabetical key order. (3) In nest-runtime apply the single-store reference pattern: bm25/hnsw sidecars reference chunk_ids by small interned IDs not re-embedded strings. (4) Adopt the section-offset table + batch-info idea for the nest-format manifest/reader so large sections seek (and later mmap-parse in parallel) without scanning. All four respect single-file/offline/deterministic/additive and fit the <=300-line codec-per-file rule.
repos.compression_relevance: On-mission for "compress more than everyone" on NON-embedding sections (text/json/yaml/provenance/metadata) which nest currently treats as zstd-only. Packed-metadata-byte + varint + name interning is how to shrink small-integer-heavy and repeated-key-heavy structured payloads (provenance, spans, json/parquet datasets nest wants to ingest) before zstd, often beating generic zstd on structured data by removing per-record type overhead and key-string repetition. mmap-friendly, decode-cheap, does not touch the hot scoring path (embeddings stay raw/f16/int8). Single-store references also stop duplicating large blobs across index + payload, shrinking hybrid/tiny presets.
repos.perf_notes: In-memory engine targets sub-millisecond traversals; skip lists give O(log n) lock-free reads, coordinated writes. Per-object RAM cost is high (Edge >=88B incl 56B Delta, Vertex >=136B) which is the opposite of nest's goal, so steal the on-disk encoding ideas NOT the in-RAM skip-list/delta layout. Snapshot write/recovery are batched and parallelized via a batch-info section. PropertyStore zlib compresses whole per-vertex property blobs (nest should keep zstd, applied AFTER varpack). USearch HNSW uses per-node fine-grained locks; nest's HNSW is single-threaded deterministic build, so reference-only.
repos.license: Business Source License 1.1 (BSL 1.1; converts to Apache 2.0 after a time window). Core is source-available, not OSI-open: treat as LEARN-FROM-ONLY, do not vendor/copy source into nest. The ideas (varint metadata byte, name interning, section-offset layout) are standard techniques and safe to reimplement cleanly.

repos.one_liner: NebulaGraph is a distributed C++ property-graph database that translates graph operations into RocksDB key-value scans using a custom prefix-locality key encoding where a vertex and its out-edges share a sorted key prefix, plus bidirectional (out/in) edge materialization and fixed-offset schema-versioned property values.
repos.core_innovation: see core_innovation field
key_techniques: prefix-locality key encoding
repos.nest_application: Add an optional graph adjacency section to nest-format (reserve a v1 section id 0x09, additive-only) holding HNSW/k-NN edges as a CSR-style structure: a sorted offsets array indexed by chunk ordinal plus a flat neighbor-id array, mirroring Nebula's prefix-locality so one node's neighbors are a single contiguous mmap slice (no per-node random reads). nest-runtime/ann already builds the HNSW graph (build.rs, select_neighbors.rs) holding neighbor lists in memory; serialize those lists in this contiguous layout via nest-format/sections so the runtime mmaps adjacency straight off disk and walks it with zero allocation, matching the existing 'score directly from mmap' discipline. Borrow the Rank-as-sort-key trick to store the float16/int8 edge distance INLINE next to each neighbor id (delta-sortable), letting hnsw expansion skip a separate distance lookup. Borrow the sign-encoded-direction byte to fold bidirectional/typed edges (e.g. bm25 term-postings vs hnsw vector edges) into one section without a second container, keeping single-file. Compression angle: neighbor-id arrays are monotone-ish within a node, so delta + varint/zigzag encode them in nest-format/encoding (new codec id 4-255, reserved-range, never on the embedding hot path) -- adjacency is a NON-embedding section so zstd over delta-coded ids is fair game and shrinks the graph index materially, advancing the 'compress more than everyone' north star while keeping graph traversal as cheap sequential mmap reads. Schema-version-byte idea maps to nest's manifest: a per-section format byte lets the adjacency codec evolve additively without a true v2 bump.
repos.compression_relevance: Direct: graph adjacency (HNSW edges, future graph-search index) is a non-embedding section, so delta+zigzag+varint over monotone neighbor ids then zstd compresses it hard while CSR prefix-locality keeps traversal as O(1) contiguous mmap reads. Co-locating fixed-offset distances inline avoids a parallel array. This is the cheapest path to add 'graph search' to nest's mission without inflating the .nest file or breaking the offline/single-file/mmap guarantees.
repos.perf_notes: Nebula's design makes 'get neighbors' a single RocksDB prefix range scan rather than N point lookups -- the same asymptotic win nest gets from a CSR adjacency slice over mmap (sequential, cache-friendly, prefetchable, zero alloc). Bidirectional dual-write trades ~2x edge storage for O(scan) reverse traversal; nest can choose single-direction for vector graphs (HNSW is undirected-symmetric anyway, so store once) and reserve dual-write only for typed/directed graph-search edges. Fixed-offset property decode = O(1) field access, the analog of nest reading f32/f16/int8 lanes at known strides off mmap.

repos.one_liner: Kuzu is an embedded, single-file columnar graph DBMS (Cypher, ACID, archived Oct 2025) that stores nodes as Parquet-style compressed node groups and relationships/HNSW topology as bit-packed disk-resident CSR adjacency lists, with a native NaviX HNSW vector index that runs SIMD distance kernels directly on buffer-manager pages.
repos.core_innovation: Lossless floating-point compression (ALP - Adaptive Lossless floating-Point) makes it viable to compress embedding-grade float arrays WITHOUT giving up exact, in-place SIMD scoring: ALP maps doubles/floats that originated as decimals to integers via two multiplications then bit-packs to the minimum bit width (ALPRD splits the bit pattern into a dictionary-coded left part + bit-packed right part), all in 1024-value vectors using auto-vectorizing scalar code. This breaks nest's current hard assumption that "embeddings can never be compressed because they are scored straight from mmap."
key_techniques: ALP / ALPRD lossless float compression: doubles->int via 2 multiplications + bitpack to min bits, or split bitwise into dict-coded left part + bitpacked right part, in 1024-value vectors (FastLanes-style auto-vectorized scalar kernels)
Per-column-chunk adaptive codec selection driven by node-group min/max zone maps (constant, RLE, integer bitpacking with chosen bit width, string dictionary, ALP for floats)
Integer bitpacking with per-chunk bit-width chosen from observed value range (INT8/16/32/64), incl. bitpacked InternalIDs and var-list offsets
Disk-based CSR adjacency lists with automatic bit compression, packing multiple adjacency lists into a single 4KB page for cache efficiency
NaviX two-level HNSW: small upper layer (GU) pinned in memory, large lower layer (GL) stored as on-disk CSR relationship table, vectors stored separately via buffer manager
Zero-copy in-buffer-manager distance computation: SIMD (SimSIMD) kernels run directly on page bytes with no copy, ~1.6x latency win
Predicate-agnostic filtered ANN via node semimasks + adaptive-local heuristic picking onehop-s/directed/blind per candidate using local selectivity sigma_l
In-memory metadata file mapping (node-group id, column name) -> compressed column-chunk location
repos.nest_application: Three concrete steals. (1) nest-format encoding codec: add ALP/ALPRD as a new RESERVED encoding id (4-255 space, additive within v1) for the embeddings section, plus per-section adaptive codec choice driven by min/max stats. This is the big unlock: lossless f32 embedding compression that still decodes to exact bits, so the search contract's exact-cosine-rerank stays byte-true while shrinking the largest section. Decode must be a tiny auto-vectorizing scalar kernel to stay single-file/offline/deterministic. (2) nest-format hnsw_index(0x07): store HNSW neighbor lists as bit-packed CSR (offsets + min-bit-width neighbor ids) instead of fixed-width arrays, and bitpack the var-length offset array - cuts the index section size, directly improving the 'tiny' preset's 0.283 ratio. (3) nest-runtime simd dispatcher + search: formalize the zero-copy 'distance on mmap bytes, never copy' discipline nest already relies on, and if ALP lands, fuse on-the-fly ALP decode + AVX2/NEON dot-product per 1024-lane block so embeddings decompress in-register on the hot path instead of being materialized. The adaptive-local semimask heuristic is a reference design for a future filtered/graph search path.
repos.compression_relevance: Directly central. ALP is the single most relevant external idea found: it is the state-of-the-art lossless float codec (beats Gorilla/Chimp/Patas/Elf and matches/beats Zstd while being far faster) and it specifically targets FLOAT/DOUBLE arrays - nest's embeddings, the section nest currently refuses to compress and the dominant byte cost of every container. Landing ALP-decode-then-SIMD-score lets nest compress its biggest section losslessly without breaking exact in-place scoring, advancing the 'compress more than everyone' north star past today's int8/f16 (which are LOSSY) by adding a LOSSLESS float path. Bit-packed CSR further shrinks the hnsw_index section the 'tiny' preset already ships.
repos.perf_notes: ALP decodes via scalar code that auto-vectorizes (FastLanes blocks of 1024) - fast enough for a query hot path, unlike Gorilla/Chimp. NaviX zero-copy in-buffer distance compute gave ~1.6x latency improvement vs copying; uses SimSIMD for SIMD distance kernels. HNSW lower layer GL ~7.8GB vs upper GU ~200MB on Wikipedia dataset (upper stays resident). Disk-based ANN costs ~2 buffer-manager lookups per adjacency access (vs DiskANN co-locating vector+neighbors in one page) - a tradeoff nest could avoid by co-locating. Vectors up to 1024 dims; efs tunes recall (~95% target). Multiple bit-packed adjacency lists per 4KB page improve cache locality.

repos.one_liner: A C++ high-performance property-graph database (Ant Group, LDBC SNB #1) that builds a graph storage layer on top of LMDB's memory-mapped B+tree, packing CSR-like adjacency topology and compact-encoded properties into single key-value pairs with an adaptive mixed/split mapping scheme.
repos.core_innovation: Adaptive mapping: a vertex's entire neighborhood (vertex props + out-edges + in-edges + edge props) is packed CSR-style into ONE key-value blob when small (mixed mapping), but auto-splits into separate VERTEX/OUTEDGE/INEDGE key-value records once the blob exceeds a size threshold (merge under ~2KB, split over ~4KB). The split records all share the same VertexUid key prefix, so the KV store keeps them physically adjacent and a single prefix scan plus two binary searches still serves sequential traversal at full speed, while bounding the per-write repack cost. The threshold is deliberately tuned to fit hot blobs in L1 cache and to amortize SSD ~150us page latency.
key_techniques: Adaptive mixed/split mapping: single packed KV blob below ~2KB, auto-split into VERTEX/OUTEDGE/INEDGE records above ~4KB threshold, sharing a common VertexUid key prefix for locality
CSR-like topology packing: VertexUid header followed by inline sorted OutEdgeUid[] and InEdgeUid[] arrays in one contiguous value, giving pure-sequential adjacency scans
Composite EdgeUid key = (SrcVid, LabelId, TemporalId, DstVid, Eid) ordered so same-label edges cluster; enables vertex-centric range scans by label and time window
Length-based varint compression of EdgeUid: LabelId/DstVid/Eid are small auto-incrementing integers from 0, stored in minimal byte length; optional TemporalId omitted entirely when absent
Compact property packing: [Nullable bitmap | FixedData | VariableOffset table | VariableData] so fixed fields are O(1) indexed and variable fields located via offset table, zero pointer overhead
External-sort bulk import: assign monotonically increasing VertexUid, hold only the vertex primary-key->VertexUid map in memory, sort edges externally (sorted insert ~10x faster than random)
Threshold sizing tuned to hardware: value size bounded to fit L1 cache and amortize SSD page-fault latency
Optimistic query-level concurrent writer plus WAL durability layered over LMDB's single-writer B+tree
repos.nest_application: Two distinct steals. (1) For a future graph_index section (reserved 0x09+, additive within v1): adopt the CSR-like adjacency layout verbatim in nest-format -- one contiguous, mmap-friendly array of sorted neighbor ids per source node with an offset table, which is exactly the SIMD-scannable, zero-pointer, deterministic shape nest already uses for embeddings. nest-runtime would traverse it straight off mmap with no deserialization, matching the existing hot-path discipline. (2) The bigger, immediately-relevant steal for compression is the length-based varint encoding of small monotonic integers: nest's chunk_ids section and any id/offset arrays (chunks_original_spans offsets, future graph neighbor ids) are dense ascending integers ideal for delta+varint or frame-of-reference encoding. Add this as a new encoding id (4-255 reserved space) in nest-format/encoding alongside raw/zstd/float16/int8, applied to NON-embedding id/offset sections only -- preserving the rule that embeddings stay raw for mmap dot-products. The adaptive mixed/split threshold idea also maps onto nest's section sizing: keep tiny sections inline, split only when a size threshold is crossed, tuned to mmap page (4KB) boundaries.
repos.compression_relevance: Directly relevant on the id/offset axis, not the embedding axis. The length-based varint trick (exploiting that ids are small auto-incrementing integers from 0) plus delta encoding can shrink nest's chunk_ids and span-offset arrays substantially with zero accuracy loss and full determinism -- a cheap, lossless win that compounds the tiny preset's 0.283 ratio. The CSR layout is a compactness win specifically for the eventual graph-search capability in nest's north star (graph search over whole repos/databases), giving the smallest possible on-disk adjacency representation. Neither touches the embedding hot path, so both respect the never-compress-embeddings rule.
repos.perf_notes: LMDB is copy-on-write mmap'd B+tree: zero-copy reads straight from the page cache, exactly nest's mmap model. TuGraph targets a 20:1 read:write ratio and chooses B+tree over LSM precisely to avoid LSM background-merge latency jitter -- validation for nest's static single-file read-mostly stance. Threshold tuned so hot blobs land in L1 and writes amortize ~150us SSD page latency. Sorted bulk import is ~10x faster than random insert. Single-writer LMDB is the bottleneck they patched with optimistic concurrency plus WAL; nest sidesteps this entirely by being build-once/serve-many.
