repos.one_liner: A property-graph database built on Redis modules that represents every relationship type as a GraphBLAS sparse adjacency matrix and executes openCypher traversals as sparse linear algebra (matrix multiply / masked semirings) rather than pointer-chasing adjacency lists.
repos.core_innovation: Model a graph as a set of sparse boolean adjacency matrices and let an adaptive storage layer (SuiteSparse:GraphBLAS) pick the most compact of four formats per matrix at runtime -- hypersparse (DCSC) / sparse (CSC) / bitmap / full -- plus an "iso" mode that stores a single scalar instead of a value array when all stored entries are identical (e.g. unweighted edges = all-true). Adjacency is thus compressed by structure (sparsity-tier selection) AND by value (iso de-duplication), and the entire k-hop traversal collapses to A^k matrix products, so the relationship topology is both the index and the query plan.
key_techniques: Adaptive 4-tier sparse format auto-selection per matrix: hypersparse DCSC (only nonempty columns get a pointer), sparse CSC, bitmap (1 bit/cell), full -- chosen by density so storage tracks actual occupancy
Iso / uniform-valued matrices: when every stored value is identical, store ONE scalar instead of an N-length value array (ideal for boolean adjacency / unweighted graphs)
Doubly-compressed sparse column (DCSC/hypersparse): a second index level over column pointers so empty columns cost zero, scaling to billions of dimensions with few nonzeros

Delta-Matrix write buffering: M (committed) + delta-plus (pending adds) + delta-minus (pending deletes); reads merge the three, writes batch until DELTA_MAX_PENDING_CHANGES then a single GrB_wait flush, avoiding per-write resort
Traversal-as-linear-algebra: friends-of-friends = F^2, pattern (A)->(B)->(C)<-(A) = A*B*transpose(A); masked matrix-multiply with semirings prunes the result during the multiply
One matrix per relation type + one type-agnostic adjacency matrix + symmetric diagonal label matrices, so labels/edge-types are selected by matrix choice not by per-row filtering
Transpose matrices maintained alongside forward matrices so reverse traversal is also a multiply, never a scan
repos.nest_application: Add an optional graph/relations section to nest-format (reserved section id 0x09+, additive within v1) that stores adjacency as a DCSC/hypersparse triple (column-pointer array, row-index array, optional iso-scalar value) with all integers little-endian unsigned per the repr(C) rule -- this lets a .nest container carry the edge structure of a corpus (citation links, chunk-to-chunk references, knowledge-graph edges) at near-zero extra bytes when iso/boolean. The biggest steal is the FORMAT-SELECTION HEURISTIC for nest-format's encoding layer: today encodings (raw/zstd/f16/int8) are chosen per-preset, but FalkorDB's per-matrix density-tiered pick (bitmap when dense, hypersparse when ultra-sparse, iso when constant) is exactly the discipline nest needs to choose the smallest codec PER SECTION based on measured statistics, deterministically. In nest-runtime, a small CSC/DCSC reader behind the existing mmap+SIMD dispatcher enables graph-search (1-2 hop neighbor expansion as sparse mat-vec straight off mmap, scalar-portable, no GraphBLAS dependency) which is a named north-star gap. The delta-plus/delta-minus buffer pattern is the clean blueprint for nest's planned real-time edit: keep the frozen mmap'd section immutable and merge a tiny pending-add/pending-delete overlay at read time, flushing to a new deterministic container on commit -- preserving the single-file/deterministic guarantees.
repos.compression_relevance: High and direct. Iso (single-scalar) storage plus density-tiered sparse formats is a textbook way to compress structured/relational data far below generic zstd: a boolean adjacency with N nonzeros costs ~N row-indices + column pointers and ONE value byte, versus a dense or text edge list. This is precisely the 'compress whole databases/repos and graphs' part of nest's north star, and the per-section format-selection heuristic raises the compression ceiling for every section, not just graphs.
repos.perf_notes: GraphBLAS uses OpenMP-parallel saxpy-vs-dot meta-algorithm for masked matmul and exploits AVX where available; the 256-variant masked C<M>=A*B kernel dispatch is overkill for nest. For nest, the relevant takeaway is the access pattern, not the parallelism: DCSC/CSC are pure flat arrays (col-ptr, row-idx, vals) that mmap and scan linearly, so a sparse mat-vec for k-hop neighbor expansion is cache-friendly and SIMD-amenable with nest's existing scalar/AVX2/NEON dispatcher -- no need to vendor SuiteSparse (heavyweight C, would blow the small-core and offline constraints). Iso matrices also make integrity hashing cheaper since the value array is a single scalar.
repos.license: FalkorDB core is Server Side Public License (SSPL) / source-available (not OSI-permissive); SuiteSparse:GraphBLAS itself is Apache-2.0. Do NOT vendor FalkorDB code; reimplement the DCSC/iso/delta ideas from scratch (they are public algorithms, CSC/DCSC predate FalkorDB) to keep nest's licensing clean.

repos.one_liner: A Rust-rewritten (3.0) typed-hypergraph database that flattens an n-ary entity/relation/attribute model with inheritance onto RocksDB's LSM key-value engine using fixed-prefix, type-grouped, sort-order-preserving key encodings.
repos.core_innovation: The attribute-value IID encoding: a value is packed into a fixed-width, sort-stable key where small values inline directly and large/variable-length values (strings) switch to an [8-byte prefix][8-byte hash][1-byte tag] form. The high bit of the final tag byte flags inline-vs-hashed, the low 7 bits double as either a length (inline) or a collision disambiguator counter (hashed, up to 128 colliding values per prefix+hash before overflow). This gives a content-addressed, bounded-width handle for arbitrarily long values while keeping the first 8 bytes as a sort-meaningful prefix so range scans and prefix iteration still work.
key_techniques: Fixed 1-byte prefix kind tag (e.g. 0x1e entity, 0x1f relation) + TypeID + counter forming a self-describing IID that encodes the instance's direct type
Type-and-connection-grouped key layout so edges/vertices of the same type/relation sort adjacently in the LSM, giving locality and prefix-iterable traversal without pointer chasing
Inline-vs-hash attribute encoding: strings <=16 bytes stored raw with a [0b0|7-bit length] tag byte (17 bytes total); longer strings as [8B prefix][8B u64 hash][0b1|7-bit disambiguator]
Caller-provided &[u8]->u64 hash with snapshot-checked collision disambiguation via a 7-bit counter (128 variants per prefix+hash)
Struct values always hashed: 1-byte value-type-category + 7-byte hash-with-disambiguator (8 bytes total)
Fixed-width-per-type value encoding (bool/int/double/decimal/date/datetime/duration all 8 bytes) so keys are memcmp-comparable and sortable
Centralized value comparators in one encoding module so traversal predicates (>, <) and sort share one byte-order definition (no comparator drift)
Disabling vertex/edge caching on read paths so multi-million-element scans stay O(1) memory; only written vertices get cached
repos.nest_application: Steal the inline-vs-hash bounded-width value encoding for nest-format. Today nest stores chunks_canonical text and chunk_ids as separate sections; adopt TypeDB's [prefix][hash][tag] scheme as a new optional codec/representation for chunk_ids and any future fixed-width id/key section, so a chunk_id or content-key is a bounded 17-byte (or 16-byte) handle whose first 8 bytes stay sort-meaningful and whose tag-byte high bit distinguishes inline-short vs hashed-long. This is content-addressed by construction, aligning with nest's existing content_hash/SHA-256 surfaces; reusing a truncated content_hash as the 8-byte hash field would let nest://content_hash/chunk_id citations resolve via a memcmp prefix scan over a sorted id section instead of a hashmap, and keeps the format additive (new encoding id in the reserved 4-255 range, deterministic since hashing is seedless). The fixed-width-per-type, memcmp-sortable value packing is also directly applicable if nest adds a structured/json/parquet column section: pack scalar columns as 8-byte sort-stable keys so range filters run as ordered scans straight off mmap. Lower relevance to raw embedding compression (those stay raw f32/f16/int8 for SIMD), but high relevance to compressing/serving id/key/metadata sections and to the graph-search and structured-data items on the north star.
repos.compression_relevance: Medium-high for nest's metadata/id sections, low for embeddings. The bounded 17-byte handle replaces storing full variable-length keys inline, compressing id/key columns and any high-cardinality string column to fixed width while preserving range-scan ability. The transferable extreme-compression idea is that the SAME bytes serve as both a sort key and a content-addressed handle (prefix stays meaningful, hash gives uniqueness, 1 tag byte multiplexes mode+length+collision-counter) at zero extra bytes for the discriminator. Does not help the embedding hot path (kept raw for SIMD dot products), so it complements rather than competes with nest's zstd/f16/int8 codecs.
repos.perf_notes: RocksDB LSM gives graceful degradation past RAM (TypeDB ~25% throughput drop 100->400 warehouses vs Neo4j ~51%), the payoff of memcmp-sortable type-grouped keys over pointer-chasing property graphs. Tradeoff: ~24GB vs Neo4j 17GB on disk because TypeDB auto-builds bidirectional/ad-hoc indices. Read paths deliberately skip caching vertices/edges to scan millions without OOM. Query pipeline is synchronous (non-async) Rust, coupled to RocksDB. No SIMD in the encoding path; the win is branch-light fixed-width comparisons, not vectorization.
repos.license: Mozilla Public License 2.0 (MPL-2.0) for the typedb engine; TypeQL grammar Apache-2.0. MPL-2.0 is file-level copyleft, so vendoring TypeDB source files into nest would carry MPL obligations on those files. Safe path: reimplement the encoding scheme (ideas are not copyrightable) rather than copy source.

repos.one_liner: SurrealDB is a Rust multi-model (document/graph/vector/full-text) database that layers SurrealQL over pluggable sorted KV backends (RocksDB/SurrealKV/TiKV/FDB), built on two reusable in-house encoding crates: `revision` (revision-tolerant binary serialization for schema evolution) and `storekey` (order-preserving lexicographic key encoding).
repos.core_innovation: The `revision` crate: a `#[revisioned(revision = N)]` derive macro that prefixes every serialized struct/enum with a varint revision number, then uses per-field attributes (`start = N`, `end = N`, `convert_fn`, `default_fn`) so bytes written by an older schema deserialize losslessly into the newest in-memory type via declared migration/default functions. This makes binary records forward/backward compatible WITHOUT a format-version bump and without a self-describing schema in each record -- the version tag is one varint, fields stay positional. It separates a cheap additive field-add (default_fn) from a true breaking change (convert_fn), which is exactly nest's v1-additive vs v2-breaking distinction, but expressed at per-field granularity instead of per-file.
key_techniques: revisioned macro: leading varint u16 revision tag per record + positional (non-self-describing) field layout, so the schema lives in code not in bytes
per-field lifecycle attributes start=N / end=N with convert_fn (old->new migration) and default_fn (fill new fields) -- additive vs breaking encoded per field
optimised envelope: u16 revision varint | u32_le payload_length | optional field offsets | fields, enabling O(1) skip of whole records
SkipRevisioned / WalkRevisioned traits: consume-without-allocate skip and per-element walk to seek one field/blob without decoding the rest (lazy partial decode off a buffer)
specialised-vectors bulk encoding for Vec<primitive>/Vec<Uuid>/Vec<Decimal> (contiguous, no per-element framing) vs per-element framing for sets/heaps
storekey: order-preserving binary key codec where lexicographic byte order == logical order (sign-flip signed ints, IEEE754 float bit-twiddle, null-escaped strings), aiming for fewest bytes
hierarchical key construction (ns -> db -> tb -> id) so every logical scope is a contiguous byte-range prefix scan; prefix()/suffix() range mappers per item type
HNSW/DiskANN low-precision storage TYPE clause (F32/F16/I8/U8) -- quantization is a per-index storage-type choice decoupled from the distance metric
repos.nest_application: Adopt the `revision` pattern in nest-format for the manifest and future binary sub-records, augmenting today's JCS canonical-JSON manifest (crates/nest-format/src/manifest/canonical.rs). Concretely: give each reserved section (ids 0x09+) and each future manifest field a `start = N` revision tag so a v1 reader can skip-or-default unknown additive fields deterministically -- turning nest's prose rule ('additive-only within v1; bump NEST_FORMAT_VERSION only on meaning change') into machine-checked per-field metadata, and crucially distinguishing a default_fn add (stays v1) from a convert_fn change (forces a true v2). The SkipRevisioned/WalkRevisioned traits map onto nest-runtime's mmap hot path: lazily walk a section to one chunk's span without decoding neighbors, complementing reader/parse.rs. Separately, steal `storekey` order-preserving encoding for nest-format/src/sections/chunk_ids.rs and any future sorted index (e.g. a chunk_id->offset table or a graph-edge section): sign-flipped/escaped lexicographic keys enable prefix range-scans and let monotonic ids be delta+varint compressed far tighter than raw u64 arrays, directly serving 'compress more than everyone'. Both are pure codecs: deterministic (positional layout + canonical order) and offline (no socket), respecting nest's hard constraints; keep each new rust file <=300 lines.
repos.compression_relevance: Real but layered. `revision`'s positional non-self-describing layout plus a one-varint version tag is far more byte-frugal than nest's JSON manifest and gives compatibility for free, removing per-record schema overhead. `storekey`'s order-preserving + minimal-byte key encoding is the directly compression-relevant piece: sorted, sign-flipped, escaped keys make chunk_ids and any index section delta-encodable and varint/zstd-friendly (monotone ids compress near-entropy), and the prefix-scan hierarchy avoids storing redundant high-order key bytes. DiskANN's per-index F16/I8/U8 storage type confirms nest's tiny-preset int8 quantization is mainstream.
repos.license: SurrealDB core: BSL 1.1 (converts to Apache-2.0 after ~4 years). The reusable sub-crates `revision` and `storekey` are permissive (Apache-2.0 / MIT) -- safe to vendor or depend on for nest-format. Verify exact SPDX before vendoring.
repos.perf_notes: revision uses bincode under the hood; specialised-vectors gives contiguous bulk encode/decode for Vec<primitive> (fast, cache-friendly) but its walk path rejects each element before reading length (must use DeserializeRevisioned/SkipRevisioned there). The u32_le payload_length + optional offset table enables O(1) record skip and selective field decode -- good for mmap partial reads. storekey targets minimal byte count, keeping key sections small and zstd-friendly. SurrealDB 3.0 added a streaming/batched execution engine and concurrent HNSW writes; DiskANN (DEGREE 64, L_BUILD 100, ALPHA 1.2) targets larger-than-memory graphs -- not needed by nest's single-file in-memory model but validates int8 quantization.

repos.one_liner: A distributed property-graph compute stack (GAE/GIE/GLE on the vineyard zero-copy in-memory store) whose most transferable artifact is GraphAr: a chunked, columnar, CSR/CSC-semantic on-disk graph format that delta-encodes adjacency to reach ~27% of naive plain+offset storage.
repos.core_innovation: Store graph topology as sorted CSR split into a per-vertex offset table plus a destination adjacency column, then delta-encode the monotone internal vertex ids and offsets so columnar payload reaches ~27.3% of a plain id+offset baseline; dense contiguous internal ids are the enabler for both delta coding and zero-copy mmap.
key_techniques: sorted CSR/CSC: edges ordered_by_source (CSR) or ordered_by_dest (CSC), with an offset table whose first entry is 0 recording each vertex's edge run start
delta encoding of monotone columns (continuous internal vertex ids + offset arrays) before columnar compression -> 27.3% of plain+offset size
vineyard compact_edges = variant (varint) + delta encoding of the CSR adjacency
dense contiguous internal vertex ids (= row index within a label) enabling a single zero-copy mmapped id space and O(1) offset lookup
chunking: vertex chunk 2^18, edge chunk 2^22, each physical chunk = one file, enabling selective/partial reads of one vertex or one chunk without reading the whole graph
self-descriptive YAML metadata that fully determines how to resolve the binary so CSR is stored directly with no serialize/deserialize round-trip
separation of topology (2-column adjList) from properties (separate columnar property groups) so a traversal reads only the adjacency, never property bytes
multiple coexisting adjacency orderings (CSR + CSC copies) selected per access pattern
repos.nest_application: Add a reserved section to nest-format (section id 0x09, graph_adjacency) plus a delta+varint codec in crates/nest-format/src/encoding/ (a new delta_varint.rs sitting beside int8.rs/float16.rs/zstd_codec.rs, registered as a new encoding id in the reserved 4-255 range, additive so NEST_FORMAT_VERSION stays 1). Layout: store a per-chunk offset array (u32/u64 LE, monotone) zig-zag delta-varint encoded, and a destination-id adjacency column where dst ids are delta-coded within each source's run; vertex ids are nest's existing dense chunk_ids row index, so no extra id map is needed. In nest-runtime, add ann::graph (a graph_search path next to ann::HnswIndex) that mmaps the offset+adjacency arrays and walks neighbors with O(1) offset lookups -- decoding varints lazily per row, never materializing the whole graph -- and feeds candidates into the existing mandatory exact-cosine rerank so graph traversal stays a candidate generator, not a score source (mirrors the hnsw contract). This unlocks the mission's stated 'graph search' goal while keeping single-file, offline, deterministic (sorted CSR + alphabetical/seeded order = byte-identical builds), and content_hash stable because the decoded adjacency is canonical regardless of varint packing.
repos.compression_relevance: Directly on-mission. Delta+varint CSR is the canonical way to compress graph adjacency and is proven here at 27.3% of plain+offset. It is the missing codec for nest's 'graph search' north-star item and generalizes: the same monotone-column delta-varint codec also shrinks nest's own chunk_ids and chunks_original_spans (offset/span arrays are monotone), so it pays off even before any graph section ships. Unlike zstd it is decode-cheap and seekable straight off mmap, fitting the 'score/traverse directly from disk, never inflate' hot-path rule.
repos.perf_notes: Columnar topology/property split means a traversal touches only the 2-column adjList, not property bytes (the dominant data). Offset table gives O(1) per-vertex neighbor-run lookup; varint decode is sequential and branch-light. Recommended chunk sizes (vertex 2^18, edge 2^22) balance file-count overhead vs parallelism; for nest's single-file model use one logical chunk per section so there is one mmap region, not thousands of files. Delta+varint is far cheaper to decode than general entropy coders, so it suits scoring-from-mmap; vineyard demonstrates the CSR can be mapped and shared zero-copy with no deserialize step.
repos.license: Apache-2.0 (GraphScope and the spun-out Apache GraphAr are both Apache-2.0); format spec and encoding ideas are freely adoptable, clean-room reimplementation in Rust is trivial since the technique is just delta+varint over sorted CSR.

repos.one_liner: Apache TinkerPop is a vendor-neutral graph computing framework whose core transferable assets are the Gremlin traversal language compiled to language-agnostic bytecode optimized by rewrite strategies, and GraphBinary, a compact self-describing length-prefixed type-coded binary serialization for graph elements (vertices, edges, paths, properties) that round-trips deterministically without an external schema.
repos.core_innovation: Two separable ideas. (1) GraphBinary's wire model: every value is `{type_code:1 byte}{type_info}{value_flag:1 byte}{value}`, integers are fixed-width big-endian, and strings/lists/maps/composites are length-prefixed (4-byte length, so each value is capped at 2^32-1) so a reader can skip or materialize any value with zero schema lookup. GraphBinary4 adds "TinkerPop Defined Types" carrying explicit per-field numbers so new fields are additive and old readers skip unknown fields, plus a single canonical null replacing per-field null flags. (2) Gremlin's bytecode-as-IR: a query is lowered to a language-agnostic serializable instruction list, then a pipeline of pure rewrite strategies (FilterRankingStrategy reorders filters cheapest-first, IncidentToAdjacentStrategy fuses outE+inV into one adjacency step, IdentityRemovalStrategy deletes no-ops) transforms the IR before it compiles to executable steps -- optimization happens on a serializable IR, not on live objects.
key_techniques: GraphBinary fully-qualified value layout {type_code}{type_info}{value_flag}{value} for schema-free self-describing decode
4-byte length-prefixing of strings/lists/maps/composites (value capped at 2^32-1, full object must be in memory to compute length)
GraphBinary4 'TinkerPop Defined Types' with explicit per-field numbers: additive evolution, old readers skip unknown fields, single canonical null
Graph elements (Vertex/Edge/Path/VertexProperty) as nested composite typed values, references-only (parent serialized as null) to avoid cycles
IO test-suite-as-spec: golden byte files every serializer must round-trip read+write to prove conformance
Gremlin bytecode: query lowered to a language-agnostic serializable instruction-list IR
Traversal strategy rewrite pipeline on the IR: FilterRankingStrategy, IncidentToAdjacentStrategy (outE+inV fusion), IdentityRemovalStrategy
Vertex-centric index pattern: outE().has(label).inV compiled to one VertexQuery against a log(m) per-vertex edge index
repos.nest_application: Graph search is a stated nest north-star gap; TinkerPop gives two ready blueprints. (1) Add a frozen graph section to nest-format (reserved section id 0x09+, additive within v1) using GraphBinary4's per-field-number Defined-Type scheme as the encoding so adjacency/node-attribute records evolve additively and old readers skip unknown fields -- nest's additive-only rule expressed as a wire format. It pairs with content_hash because GraphBinary's deterministic byte layout (fixed-width ints, sortable map keys) gives reproducible byte-identical output. CRITICAL adaptation: mandate little-endian unsigned (GraphBinary is big-endian, so adapt do not copy). Adjacency lists as length-prefixed neighbor blocks are mmap-skippable and zstd-friendly (topology is a non-embedding section so zstd is allowed), advancing compression of whole databases/repos. (2) In nest-runtime add a small graph::plan module (under the 300-line cap): represent a graph query as a tiny instruction list and run deterministic rewrite strategies (filter-cheapest-first; fuse edge-then-vertex hops into one adjacency scan) before executing against the mmapped adjacency section. The IncidentToAdjacentStrategy fusion is the highest-value steal: it turns two index hops into one sequential mmap scan, stays offline/deterministic/never-panics. nest-cli gains a graph-search subcommand mirroring search-ann. Skip Gremlin-the-language, Gremlin Server, and OLAP/Spark -- they violate the no-socket, small-core, offline constraints.
repos.compression_relevance: Indirect but real. GraphBinary's length-prefixed fixed-width schema-free layout is a denser graph-topology encoding than JSON/GraphSON (TinkerPop docs note a significantly smaller wire footprint), and because it carries no inline schema and orders fields by number it is highly zstd-compressible -- directly serving the goal to compress json/datasets/whole-databases more than everyone. The per-field-number additive scheme also lets a graph section shrink over versions without a format bump. It never touches embeddings (the hot SIMD path), so no conflict with the never-compress-embeddings rule.
repos.license: Apache License 2.0
repos.perf_notes: GraphBinary trades streaming for size determinism: length must be known upfront so the full object is serialized in memory to compute its 4-byte length, raising peak serialization memory and capping any single value at 2^32-1 bytes (fine for nest's Python-build/Rust-serve split since the heavy build side is Python). Decode is allocation-friendly: length prefixes let the reader pre-size buffers and validate bounds, and unknown field numbers are skipped by length without parsing -- ideal for mmap. On traversal, TinkerPop benchmarks show strategy application (the optimizer) costs ~5-6x bytecode construction, so the rewrite pass is the expensive phase; keep nest's strategy set tiny and run it once at plan time, not per-traverser, to respect the boot-overhead budget.

repos.one_liner: Blazegraph (formerly bigdata) is a Java RDF/SPARQL graph database built on a key-range-partitioned B+Tree over a single-file journal (RWStore), where every triple/quad is materialized into multiple sorted "covering" statement indexes (SPO/POS/OSP) whose unsigned-byte[] keys are compressed at the page level with front-coding and order-preserving canonical Huffman raba coders.
repos.core_innovation: The "raba coder" page model: B+Tree leaves store keys as a logical sorted byte[][] and compress it with FrontCodedRabaCoder using a ratio parameter -- every `ratio` keys one full key is emitted, the rest store only (shared-prefix-length, suffix) -- AND the codec is searchable in place (binary search over the periodic full keys, then linear scan inside the bucket), so you decompress nothing to look up. A sibling CanonicalHuffmanRabaCoder compresses while strictly preserving lexicographic order, so even Huffman-coded keys remain range-scannable. This is order-preserving, search-on-compressed, tunable-ratio prefix compression for sorted byte strings.
key_techniques: Front coding with tunable ratio: every Nth sorted key stored in full, intervening keys as (shared_prefix_len, suffix); binary-search the full keys then linear-scan the front-coded bucket -- no full decompression to search
Order-preserving canonical Huffman coder for byte[][] (CanonicalHuffmanRabaCoder) that keeps lexicographic order of coded values, so range scans work on compressed keys
Covering/clustered indexes: same triples materialized in multiple key orderings (SPO,POS,OSP triples; 6 for quads, YARS-style) so every access pattern is a prefix range-scan with locality
Value inlining: small RDF values encoded directly INTO the statement-index key with order-preserving encoding to skip dictionary indirection
Two-way dictionary (TERM2ID forward, ID2TERM reverse) mapping terms to compact numeric term-ids so statement keys are fixed-width integer tuples
BLOBS index: large literals pulled into a separate hash-keyed index so dictionary index stride stays small and cache-friendly
RWStore fixed-size slot allocators + free-lists with small-slot optimization (~1024B), page split when a leaf exceeds 8k after compression
Unsigned big-endian byte[] keys so numeric/temporal order == lexicographic byte order, which makes prefix range-scans and front coding correct
repos.nest_application: Adopt front-coded, search-on-compressed encoding for nest's sorted-string sections in nest-format. (1) chunk_ids section: encode as a FrontCodedRabaCoder-style block -- sort the ids, store every Nth id in full plus (prefix_len:varint, suffix) for the rest, plus a small offset table to binary-search the full keys. New encoding id in the RESERVED 4-255 space (additive, no NEST_FORMAT_VERSION bump), applied to chunk_ids only, never to embeddings (which stay raw/f16/int8 for mmap SIMD scoring). (2) bm25_index(0x08): its term dictionary is already required to be alphabetical for determinism -- ideal front-coding input, so the vocabulary shrinks with zero loss and stays binary-searchable on compressed bytes (no decompress on the search path, preserving offline-mmap discipline). The codec lives in crates/nest-format/.../encoding as a deterministic pure function (sorted input => byte-identical output), respecting the <=300-line single-responsibility rule and typed thiserror (never panic). Order-preserving canonical Huffman is a phase-2 entropy upgrade for the same dictionaries. The covering-index idea informs nest-runtime: if nest adds graph search, materialize edge tuples in multiple sorted orderings so traversals become prefix range-scans, not full scans.
repos.compression_relevance: Directly on the north star ("compress data more than everyone"). Front coding plus order-preserving entropy coding gives large lossless reduction of sorted string columns (chunk_ids, bm25 term dictionary) while keeping them searchable on the compressed bytes -- nest compresses these harder than a generic zstd pass without paying decompression on the hot search path. Textbook technique for the sorted-identifier and sorted-vocabulary data nest carries, and it composes with existing zstd (front-code first, then zstd the residual).
repos.license: GPLv2 (SYSTAP historically offered a separate commercial license); Java codebase, Amazon acquired SYSTAP in 2018 and the OSS project is effectively abandoned -- treat as reference/learn, not vendor (GPL + Java rule out direct linking into nest's Rust core).
repos.perf_notes: Single-file journal mmap-friendly model parallels nest's mmap design. Front coding's key property for nest is search-on-compressed: O(log) binary search over periodic full keys + O(ratio) linear scan in a bucket touches a few hundred bytes, not a decompressed buffer -- keeps the search path allocation-light and cache-resident. The `ratio` knob is a direct compression-vs-lookup-latency dial. B+Tree pages split past an 8k boundary after compression; RWStore small-slot ~1024B, branching factor 256 -- evidence ~1-8k compressed blocks are the cache/IO sweet spot, a useful block-size hint for nest's encoded sections. No SIMD in the Java codec, so a Rust prefix-compare kernel can beat it.

synthesis.summary: Across 13 graph engines the single convergent idea is: compress structured integer/ID streams (adjacency lists, ID columns, postings) with sort -> delta -> minimum-bit-width packing, and keep them searchable/traversable WITHOUT decoding by mmapping a flat CSR layout. Every serious engine (Neo4j, GDS, Kuzu, GraphScope/GraphAr, JanusGraph, Nebula, TuGraph) lands on the same Pareto winner over varint+zstd for monotone columns; Dgraph's sroar pushes it further (the compressed bytes ARE the in-memory layout, zero decode tax — exactly nest's hot-path rule); Kuzu's ALP is the lone idea that legitimately challenges nest's "never compress embeddings" axiom with a LOSSLESS float codec that still decodes to exact bits for SIMD scoring. FalkorDB contributes per-section density-tiered codec auto-selection (iso/bitmap/sparse), Blazegraph contributes front-coding that is binary-searchable on compressed bytes (ideal for nest's alphabetical bm25 vocabulary and sha256 chunk_ids), and VPack/Memgraph/TypeDB contribute packed-metadata-byte + key-interning for the structured/json payloads nest wants to ingest next. nest currently stores all of these as raw or zstd: HNSW neighbor lists as fixed u32 (ann/codec.rs:30), bm25 postings as raw u32 doc/tf pairs (bm25/codec.rs:33-36), spans as raw u64 pairs. Grounding correction to the extracts: nest's chunk_ids are sha256:<hex> STRINGS not dense ints, so the dense-ordinal delta trick applies to the implicit 0..N row index (HNSW/graph/bm25 doc ids) and to span offsets, not to chunk_ids values directly; front-coding is the right codec for the sha256 strings. The mission-critical sequence: (1) ship one delta+bitpack integer-stream codec in encoding/ (reserved id 0x04..0xFF), (2) re-encode hnsw_index and bm25_index postings with it, (3) add a CSR graph_adjacency section (0x09) reusing it for the north-star graph-search gap, all additive within format v1, all deterministic, none touching the embedding hot path. Then evaluate ALP as the high-risk/high-reward lossless embedding path.
synthesis.state_of_the_art: The field has converged on a single canonical recipe for graph/ID storage: sort target IDs ascending, delta-encode into small monotone gaps, then bit-pack per fixed-size block to the minimum bit width the local maximum needs ("integer packing" / PForDelta family), laid out as flat CSR (offsets array + degrees + packed-targets blob). This beats both global encodings and per-value continuation-bit varints on the speed/ratio Pareto front because block unpack is branchless, cache-local and SIMD-friendly, and crucially it is mmap-pure: no dictionary/window state, decodes a single block in place off disk (Neo4j, GDS report ~6x over uncompressed at memcpy decode speed; GraphAr reports 27% of plain+offset; GDS ~1.4 bytes/edge). The frontier idea is making the compressed representation directly operable: Dgraph's sroar serialized roaring bitmaps run set-intersection (graph join = bitmap AND) with zero unmarshal (~7x faster, ~15x less memory than reference roaring); FalkorDB auto-selects the most compact of four sparse tiers per matrix plus an iso single-scalar mode for boolean adjacency; Blazegraph front-codes sorted keys so they stay binary-searchable on the compressed bytes (search-on-compressed, no inflate). For the float problem specifically, Kuzu's ALP/ALPRD is state-of-the-art lossless float compression (beats Gorilla/Chimp/Patas/Elf, matches/beats zstd, far faster, auto-vectorizing 1024-value blocks) and is the only credible path to compress embedding-grade arrays while keeping exact in-place SIMD scoring. For structured/document payloads the consensus is self-describing trailing-offset tables with smallest-width offset selection plus a per-file key dictionary (VPack ~2-3x on repeated-schema json; Memgraph/TypeDB packed-metadata-byte + name interning). Licensing reality: the algorithms (delta, varint, bit-packing, CSR, front-coding, roaring) are decades-old public-domain; the GPL/BSL/SSPL engines (Neo4j, GDS, memgraph, FalkorDB, blazegraph) are learn-from-only, while Kuzu (MIT), GraphScope/GraphAr, JanusGraph, Nebula, TuGraph, sroar/badger (Apache-2.0) and SurrealDB's revision/storekey sub-crates (MIT/Apache) are clean-room or vendorable references.
top_innovations: Delta + per-block minimum-bit-width integer packing (PForDelta family) over sorted ID streams: the universal codec that beats zstd on monotone integers at memcpy decode speed and is mmap-seekable per-block. Drawn from Neo4j integer packing, GDS PackedAdjacencyList, GraphAr delta CSR, TuGraph length-varint. This is the single highest-value steal: nest stores HNSW neighbor lists, bm25 postings and span offsets uncompressed/zstd today, and all three are textbook inputs.

Flat CSR adjacency (u64 offsets array + packed neighbor-id blob) as a frozen, mmap-traversable graph section: one node's neighbors are a single contiguous slice walked with zero allocation, identical discipline to nest's embedding rows. Drawn from Neo4j/GDS CSR, Nebula prefix-locality, Kuzu disk-CSR, GraphAr, TuGraph. This is the concrete delivery vehicle for nest's named graph-search north-star gap.

ALP / ALPRD lossless float compression decoded in-register before SIMD dot-product: the only idea that challenges nest's 'embeddings can never be compressed' axiom while keeping exact-cosine rerank byte-true. Drawn from Kuzu (MIT, vendorable). Highest payoff (embeddings are the dominant byte cost and the largest section) but highest risk to the hot path.

Serialized roaring bitmaps where the compressed bytes ARE the in-memory layout, enabling set-intersection with zero decode: matches nest's no-decode-on-hot-path rule exactly. Drawn from Dgraph sroar (Apache-2.0). Best fit for bm25 postings (term -> sorted doc-id set) and a boolean chunk-to-chunk graph.

Per-section density-tiered codec auto-selection driven by measured min/max/cardinality stats (raw vs delta-pack vs roaring vs iso-single-scalar), chosen deterministically at build time. Drawn from FalkorDB 4-tier sparse + iso, Kuzu per-chunk adaptive codec, GraphAr. Raises nest's compression ceiling for EVERY section, not just graphs, replacing today's per-preset hardcoding.

Front-coding (every Nth sorted key full, rest as shared-prefix-len + suffix) that stays binary-searchable on the compressed bytes: search-on-compressed with no inflate. Drawn from Blazegraph raba coders (learn-only, GPL). Ideal for nest's sha256:<hex> chunk_ids and the alphabetically-ordered bm25 term dictionary.

VPack trailing-offset-table + smallest-width offset selection + object-key dictionary for structured/json payloads: zero-parse random sub-document access off mmap plus 2-3x shrink on repeated-schema corpora. Drawn from ArangoDB VelocyPack (Apache-2.0), reinforced by Memgraph packed-metadata-byte and TypeDB inline-vs-hash. The codec for nest's json/yaml/parquet ingest roadmap.

SurrealDB revision pattern (leading varint version tag + positional non-self-describing fields with per-field start=N/default_fn vs convert_fn): turns nest's prose 'additive-within-v1 vs true-v2' rule into machine-checked per-field metadata, far more byte-frugal than the current JSON manifest. revision/storekey sub-crates are MIT/Apache, vendorable.

Inline distance co-location: store the f16/int8 edge distance inline next to each neighbor id in the CSR adjacency so graph expansion skips a separate distance array lookup. Drawn from Nebula rank-as-sort-key, Kuzu. Cache-locality win for the future graph traversal kernel.

Order-preserving / sort-as-index byte layouts (lexicographic byte order == logical order) so range scans need no separate index. Drawn from JanusGraph edge-as-cell, TypeDB memcmp keys, storekey. Reinforces nest's determinism: canonical sort + delta layout is inherently content_hash-stable.
