compression_wins: chunks_original_spans byte_start/byte_end: u64 pairs that are locally monotone (byte offsets into source docs). Delta+zigzag+bitpack collapses these from 16 bytes/span toward 1-3 bytes/span losslessly, decode at memcpy speed off mmap (vs raw today). First and cheapest intpack target — pays off before any graph work.

hnsw_index(0x07) neighbor lists: currently fixed u32 per neighbor (ann/codec.rs:30-31). Sort+delta+bitpack each list to ceil(log2(max_gap)) bits — GDS reports ~6x on adjacency; directly improves the tiny preset's 0.283 ratio with zero recall change (the neighbor SET is identical, only its encoding shrinks).

bm25_index(0x08) postings: raw u32 doc + u32 tf pairs (bm25/codec.rs:33-36) with doc ids already implicitly ascending. Delta-code the doc column and bitpack tf; for high-df terms switch to a serialized roaring bitmap (sroar-style, bytes==memory layout) so fusion runs posting AND with no decode. Shrinks the hybrid preset and speeds fusion.

chunk_ids sha256:<hex> strings: after sorting, the hex strings share long common prefixes — front-coding (every Nth full, rest as shared-prefix-len+suffix) is lossless, stays binary-searchable on compressed bytes, and shrinks a section that currently stores 70+ bytes per id raw. Correction to the extracts: chunk_ids are strings not dense ints, so front-coding (not delta) is the right codec here.

Future graph_adjacency(0x09) section: delta+varint CSR is proven at 27% of plain+offset (GraphAr); with FalkorDB iso mode an unweighted/boolean chunk graph costs ~N row-indices + offsets + ONE value scalar. Adds graph search to the mission at near-zero extra bytes, keeping the .nest container compact.

Structured json/yaml/parquet ingest (roadmap): VPack key-dictionary + smallest-width offsets gives 2-3x on repeated-schema data like the PT-BR datasets while preserving zero-decode random field access — the compress-AND-serve combination, beating naive zstd-of-json on access cost. Composes with zstd on the cold parts.

provenance(0x05) JSON blob + repeated metadata keys: name-to-id interning (Memgraph/VPack) replaces repeated long keys/model-fingerprints with u16 ids, deterministic via alphabetical key order; shrinks the structured metadata before zstd.

Embeddings(0x04), the dominant byte cost and the section nest currently refuses to compress: ALP/ALPRD is the only LOSSLESS path that keeps exact in-place SIMD scoring (decodes to exact bits per 1024-block in-register before the dot product), advancing compress-more-than-everyone past today's LOSSY float16/int8 — gated on a no-latency-regression benchmark.
watch_outs: Do NOT vendor source from GPL/BSL/SSPL engines: Neo4j + GDS (GPLv3), memgraph (BSL 1.1), FalkorDB core (SSPL), blazegraph (GPLv2). These are learn-from-only. The underlying algorithms (delta, varint, bit-packing, CSR, front-coding, roaring) are decades-old public-domain and must be clean-room reimplemented from spec. Safe to port/vendor: Kuzu (MIT), sroar/badger + GraphScope/GraphAr + JanusGraph + Nebula + TuGraph (Apache-2.0), SurrealDB revision/storekey sub-crates (MIT/Apache — verify SPDX first). VPack is Apache-2.0 (the ArangoDB server moved to BSL but the format lib/spec did not).

NEVER apply the integer codec, roaring, or zstd to the embeddings section on the current hot path — they require decode/window state and would break the score-directly-from-mmap rule. The ONLY embedding-compression candidate is ALP because it decodes to EXACT bits in-register per block; even then it must be benchmarked against the search-latency budget before landing, and the search contract's mandatory exact-cosine rerank must remain byte-true.

Block/page co-location and alignment (Neo4j Block format, Kuzu 4KB pages) can use MORE disk than tightly-packed layouts due to padding/headers — directly against nest's size-first goal. Take the integer codec and CSR layout, NOT the page-padding. Likewise reject the in-RAM structures (memgraph skip-lists, Edge>=88B / Vertex>=136B; TypeDB auto-built bidirectional indices ~24GB vs 17GB) — those optimize RAM/write, the opposite of nest's compact read-only file.

Skip every server/LSM/multi-file storage engine wholesale: Badger (Dgraph), RocksDB (TypeDB/Nebula/SurrealDB backends/ArangoDB), LMDB (TuGraph), Redis modules (FalkorDB), Cassandra/HBase (JanusGraph), Gremlin Server/OLAP/Spark (TinkerPop). They violate single-file/offline/no-socket. Only the on-disk byte-layout discipline transfers.

Determinism must hold for every new codec: bit-packing block size must be FIXED, sort order canonical (ascending ids / alphabetical terms — already nest's rule), roaring container choice is a pure function of cardinality, no entropy-coder dictionary state. content_hash must stay STABLE across encodings — so decode-then-hash must yield identical canonical bytes regardless of whether intpack/roaring/front-code was used (mirror the existing 'content_hash hashes decoded bytes' rule in encoding/mod.rs lines 15-18).

Endianness: GraphBinary (TinkerPop) is big-endian and many graph engines use big-endian keys for lexicographic ordering — nest mandates little-endian unsigned everywhere. Adapt the layout, do not copy byte order. For order-preserving keys, replicate storekey's sign-flip/IEEE754-twiddle in LE rather than relying on raw BE byte order.

File-hygiene: each new codec (intpack, frontcode, vpack, alp) must be a single-responsibility file <=300 lines (333 hard cap), repr(C), all integers LE-unsigned, typed thiserror errors, never panic in library code. The graph module must split mod.rs/csr.rs/overlay to respect the cap.

Two-pass build-time costs (VPack key dictionary, sort+id-assignment, FalkorDB stat-driven codec selection, front-code offset tables) are acceptable in the Python BUILD stage but must NEVER appear on the Rust serve path. Keep the runtime to mmap + branchless unpack + dot product. Beware the search-text ~300-500ms python boot overhead is already a known gap — do not add per-query planning cost (TinkerPop notes strategy application costs ~5-6x bytecode construction; run any graph query rewrite ONCE at plan time, not per-traverser).

Roaring/sroar zero-decode benefit only materializes if the on-disk container layout EQUALS the in-memory layout with correct LE alignment; a naive roaring port that requires an unmarshal step loses the entire hot-path advantage and is then just worse zstd. Mirror sroar's single-buffer contract exactly or use plain delta+bitpack instead.

categories.name: semantic-rdf
categories.focus: RDF triple stores, semantic web, graph query languages

repos.one_liner: Apache Jena is a Java RDF/SPARQL framework whose TDB2 store persists triples as three permuted B+tree indexes (SPO/POS/OSP, six for quads) over 8-byte NodeIds resolved through a dictionary node table, with scalar values inlined directly into the NodeId to skip the dictionary entirely.
repos.core_innovation: NodeId tagged-union inlining: an 8-byte (64-bit) identifier uses bit 63 as a discriminator — 0 means the low 63 bits are a pointer (file offset) into the dictionary node table; 1 means the value is self-contained in the id. A second tag bit then selects an encoding: doubles (62-bit double with exponent range reduced 2 bits), or a 6-bit XSD-type field + 56-bit value carrying signed integers, decimals (8-bit scale + 48-bit signed mantissa), dates/datetimes at ms precision, and booleans. The win: common scalar literals carry their full value in the index key itself, so they never allocate a dictionary entry, never trigger a hash lookup, and sort/compare correctly inline. The dictionary is only paid for strings/URIs/IRIs that genuinely need it.
key_techniques: NodeId tagged-union: bit63 ptr-vs-value, bit62 sub-encoding select, 6-bit xsd type + 56-bit payload
Inline scalar encodings: 56-bit signed int, 8-bit-scale+48-bit decimal, ms-precision date/datetime, boolean, range-reduced 62-bit double
Dictionary node table: bidirectional Node<->NodeId via 128-bit MD5 hash key plus sequential value file for reverse lookup
Permuted multi-index storage: 3 B+trees SPO/POS/OSP (6 for quads) each holding full tuple, enabling index-only scans for any bound prefix
Fixed-length-key/fixed-length-value custom B+tree (keys are packed NodeId tuples, no variable-length records)
Rule-based cardinality estimation (stats.opt) reordering patterns by selectivity tokens VAR/TERM/URI/LITERAL
xloader bulk build: emit binary tuples, external merge-sort via unix sort(1), compress intermediate sort runs to shrink peak temp space, build each index as a separate streamed phase
Copy-on-write MVCC B+tree blocks for single-writer/multi-reader without blocking readers
repos.nest_application: Two concrete steals. (1) Tagged-NodeId inlining maps onto nest-format as a typed-scalar codec for structured payloads (json/yaml/parquet columns, dataset cells): instead of a flat chunks_canonical text section, add a future column/value section where each cell is an 8-byte tagged word — bit63 = inline-vs-span, lower bits = a 4-bit encoding tag + payload (i56 int, 8-bit-scale i48 decimal, ms-epoch date, bool, f16/range-reduced double). Numbers/dates/bools cost zero dictionary bytes and zero chunk-span indirection; only strings keep a chunks_original_spans pointer. This is a new RESERVED section id (0x09+) and a new encoding id (4-255) — fully additive within v1, no NEST_FORMAT_VERSION bump. Directly advances compress-more-than-everyone for tabular/json corpora where today every integer round-trips through text+zstd. (2) The xloader pattern — stream tuples, external-merge-sort, compress intermediate runs — is the blueprint for nest-python's deterministic builder when corpora exceed RAM: sort chunk_ids/terms with a stable alphabetical external sort (matching the bm25 deterministic-term-order constraint), zstd the spill files, build hnsw_index(0x07)/bm25_index(0x08) as separate streamed passes; keeps builds deterministic/reproducible while removing the in-RAM ceiling. (3) Reference-only: SPO/POS/OSP permuted-index idea informs a future graph-search section — store an edge tuple in multiple sort orders so any bound prefix is an index-only range scan, the on-disk substrate for the north-star graph search.
repos.compression_relevance: High for structured/tabular data. The inline-NodeId trick is a domain-specific entropy win orthogonal to zstd: it removes dictionary entries and span-pointer indirection for the most common literal types (ints, dates, bools, decimals), packing each into <=8 self-describing bytes that also sort correctly. For json/yaml/parquet/dataset payloads (explicitly in nest north-star scope) this beats text+zstd because zstd still pays for the textual representation and a per-value span offset. The embedding hot path and mandatory exact-cosine rerank are untouched — this is a non-embedding section, so it can even be zstd-wrapped on top.
repos.perf_notes: NodeIds are fixed 8 bytes, so B+tree keys are fixed-length tuples — comparisons are word-aligned integer compares, ideal for branchless/SIMD-friendly scanning and mmap-resident range scans (matches nest mmap + scalar/AVX2/NEON dispatch). Inline values avoid a random dictionary read (MD5-keyed hash lookup) per scalar, a large latency saving on selective queries. xloader compresses intermediate sort runs to cut peak temp disk substantially. MVCC copy-on-write blocks give lock-free readers; for nest (read-mostly, mmap, offline) the takeaway is fixed-width keys + permuted sort orders, not the transaction machinery.
repos.license: Apache License 2.0 (permissive; safe to vendor/learn from, no copyleft concern)

repos.one_liner: A Java RDF quad store whose embedded backends (NativeStore B-tree, LMDB store) split storage into a value dictionary mapping every RDF term to a compact integer ID plus B-tree/B+tree permutation indexes (spoc, posc, ospc) that store only those IDs, with the LMDB store adding an order-preserving variable-length integer (Varint) codec for the IDs.
repos.core_innovation: Dictionary-encode every repeated term to a small integer ID once, then store and index ONLY the IDs (never the bytes), and encode those IDs with an order-preserving variable-length integer whose length is recoverable from the first byte alone, so sorted key storage stays correct while small/common IDs cost 1-2 bytes instead of a fixed 4-8.
key_techniques: order-preserving varint: smaller values use fewer bytes, total length decodable from the first byte, and byte-wise lexicographic order equals numeric order so it doubles as a sort key
value-type tag (URI/BNode/Literal) packed into the low 2 bits of the integer ID, avoiding a separate type column
two-level dictionary: ValueStore maps each distinct term to a sequential integer ID; indexes store 4 IDs (s,p,o,c) not the terms; ID 0 reserved as null/default-graph context
IRI factoring: split each IRI into namespace + local-name, give the namespace its own ID, store only [type 1B][namespaceID 4B][localname UTF-8] so shared prefixes are paid once
literal layout [type 1B][datatypeID 4B][langLen 1B][langTag<=255B][label UTF-8], referencing datatype by ID not inline

fixed-slot B-tree page: 16B header (magic btf, version, blockSize, valueSize, rootID), nodes one block each, slotSize=4+valueSize, branchFactor=1+(blockSize-8)/slotSize, direct offset math with no per-node scan
configurable index permutations (spoc/posc/ospc/psoc) chosen per query shape so the most selective access pattern is a sorted range scan
dictionary-scoped WAL for crash recovery leaving primary .dat files authoritative; mmap + OS page cache makes the store behave in-memory when RAM suffices
repos.nest_application: nest-format: add a dictionary-encoded section family plus an order-preserving Varint codec (new RESERVED encoding id 4-255, additive within v1) for any section that is a column of monotone or repeated integers, principally chunk_ids and future graph/edge sections. The biggest concrete win is provenance and repeated metadata: factor repeated source strings/URIs into one per-file string/namespace table and store only small IDs (mirroring RDF4J ValueStore), which beats zstd-on-raw because redundancy becomes integer locality. nest-runtime: when nest adds the promised graph search, store edges as (src_id, rel_id, dst_id) Varint triples in spo/ops permutation orders so adjacency is a sorted range scan straight off mmap; RDF4J permutation indexes are the proven blueprint, and nest's mandated deterministic alphabetical/seeded ordering maps cleanly onto preserve-lexicographic-order so the index stays byte-identical and reproducible. nest-cli: the cite path can reuse the namespace/localname split so nest://content_hash/chunk_id URIs are stored factored.
repos.compression_relevance: Directly central. Dictionary encoding + order-preserving Varint is the textbook way to push the non-embedding sections nest already zstd-encodes (chunk_ids, provenance, future graph edges) BELOW what a generic entropy coder reaches on raw bytes, by removing structural redundancy (repeated terms, monotone IDs, shared IRI prefixes) before the entropy stage rather than relying on the coder to rediscover it. It never touches embeddings (correctly, since those are scored from mmap on the hot path), so it stays fully inside nest's never-compress-embeddings rule while lowering the size ratio on everything else.
repos.perf_notes: mmap + OS page cache lets it behave like an in-memory store when RAM suffices (matches nest mmap model). Fixed-slot B-tree pages give O(1) in-node offset addressing, no scan. Varint decode is branch-light (first byte gives length), good for a tight Rust loop; order preservation means you can binary-search encoded keys WITHOUT decoding. Reported LMDB footprint ~120-130 bytes/quad with 3 permutation indexes, so the cost of graph search is redundant permutations: nest should keep permutation count minimal (e.g. spo plus one inverse) to stay compact.
repos.license: Dual Eclipse Distribution License 1.0 (BSD-3-Clause style) and Eclipse Public License 2.0; permissive enough to study and reimplement. nest should clean-room the Varint/dictionary ideas in Rust rather than vendor Java.

repos.one_liner: A Rust embedded RDF triple/quad store and SPARQL engine that encodes every term as a 17-byte fixed-width (type-byte + 16-byte value) record, inlining small strings and all XSD numeric/date literals as native bytes while hashing only large strings via SipHash-2-4-128 into an id2str side table, so the six SPOG-permuted RocksDB indexes never store raw strings.
repos.core_innovation: Hash-or-inline content-addressed typed-value encoding: a 1-byte kind tag plus a <=16-byte value that inlines small strings and native numerics/dates and replaces only large strings with their content hash, eliminating the forward string->id dictionary index and making identical values produce identical deterministic ids.
key_techniques: Type-byte + <=16-byte value fixed-width term encoding (17 bytes total, big-endian for range scans)
Inline-small-string rule: UTF-8 strings <16 bytes stored verbatim, no dictionary entry
Native typed-literal encoding: i64 integers, i128 fixed-point decimals (x10^18), dateTime as decimal timestamp + i16 offset, 1-byte booleans, raw f32/f64 bits
SipHash-2-4 128-bit content hashing for large strings -> id2str side table, no forward string->id index
Six SPOG permutations (SPOG/POSG/OSPG/GSPO/GPOS/GOSP) so any triple pattern maps to a prefix range scan
Big-endian key layout so lexicographic key order = numeric/range order for range queries
MVCC memory backend: single quad hashset + per-quad 'last inserted matching S/P/O/G' pointers + selectivity counters for greedy join ordering
Volcano iterator evaluation with greedy join reordering by triple-pattern selectivity (sparopt: filter pushdown, join reorder)
repos.nest_application: Steal the hash-or-inline typed-value encoding for nest-format as a new optional section codec on chunk metadata / provenance / structured-payload sections (NOT embeddings, which stay raw f32 on the mmap hot path). Concretely: in crates/nest-format/src/encoding add a 'typed-dict' encoding (claim a reserved encoding id 4-255) where each metadata field value is emitted as a 1-byte kind tag + <=16-byte value; integers/timestamps/booleans/decimals go native (i64/i128-fixed-point/i16-offset) instead of as JSON text, small UTF-8 strings inline, and any string >=16 bytes is replaced by its SHA-256-prefix id (nest already computes SHA-256 everywhere, so reuse content_hash machinery instead of SipHash to stay within nest's four-integrity-surface story) pointing into a per-file id2str dictionary section. This is directly content-addressed and deterministic -- identical metadata yields byte-identical encoding, preserving nest's reproducible-build guarantee. It unlocks (a) large compression wins on repetitive structured metadata (datasets, parquet schemas, json/yaml provenance) where the same IRIs/keys/timestamps repeat across millions of chunks, deduped to one dictionary entry; (b) a future graph-search section (the mission's 'graph search' north-star) -- adopt the six-permutation SPOG index layout in nest-runtime/src as a new section (reserved 0x09+) so relationship triples over chunks become prefix-range scans on the mmap with no separate forward index; (c) native typed columns for the 'compress whole databases/repos' goal. The i128 fixed-point decimal trick (value x 10^18) and dateTime-as-decimal+offset give nest exact, range-scannable numeric columns without floats.
repos.compression_relevance: High and direct. The encoding is a compression scheme in disguise: it turns variable-length text literals into fixed 17-byte content-addressed ids and inlines anything under 16 bytes so it never costs a dictionary slot, then dedupes everything larger into a single id2str table. For nest's repetitive structured payloads (per-chunk provenance, dataset schemas, json/yaml/parquet keys, timestamps), encoding values natively instead of as text plus deduping long strings to a content hash can beat zstd on highly repetitive structured metadata because dedup happens at the semantic-value level before the byte entropy coder ever runs -- and it stacks with zstd (nest can zstd the resulting dictionary section since it is non-embedding). The native i64/i128/i16 numeric encoding also removes JSON text bloat for numbers/dates entirely. This squarely serves 'compress data more than everyone' for the structured/dataset/database payload classes nest wants to swallow.
repos.perf_notes: Fixed 17-byte records mean term comparison and index scans are branch-light and cache-friendly; big-endian keys make range queries pure prefix scans (no comparator). Inlining sub-16-byte strings and native numerics removes a pointer-chase to id2str on the common path -- only large strings pay a lookup. SipHash-2-4-128 is fast and collision-free on a full 2019 Wikidata dump per their docs (nest would substitute its existing SHA-256 to keep one hash family; SHA-256 is slower but nest already pays it at build time, not on the search hot path, so no runtime cost). RocksDB LSM gives write throughput but nest does not want RocksDB -- nest must reimplement the layout as flat mmap'd sorted sections, which is actually simpler and faster to read than an LSM and matches nest's zero-server, mmap-and-scan model. Six permutations cost ~6x index storage; nest should make graph/triple indexing an OPTIONAL section so default builds stay tiny.
repos.license: Dual-licensed Apache-2.0 OR MIT (permissive; safe to read and reimplement the encoding scheme; do not vendor RocksDB which is GPLv2/Apache-2.0 and brings a C++ LSM dependency that violates nest's small single-file offline core).

repos.one_liner: A pure-Python RDF toolkit whose in-memory Store indexes triples in three redundant permutation dictionaries (SPO/POS/OSP) plus context maps, and evaluates SPARQL 1.1 via an algebra of lazy nested-loop joins with dynamic most-bound-first triple-pattern reordering.
repos.core_innovation: The "triple of permutations" index: store every edge three times under SPO, POS, and OSP nested-dict orderings so that any of the eight subject/predicate/object binding patterns resolves to a direct prefix walk (O(1) descent then iterate), giving symmetric fast lookup no matter which graph terms are known. This is the canonical compact way to make a graph adjacency structure queryable from any direction without a query planner.
key_techniques: Three permuted nested-dict indices SPO/POS/OSP, each leaf=presence bit, so any bound-prefix (s, sp, p, po, o, os, spo, none) maps to one permutation's descent

Term-as-interned-string: all terms subclass Python str (URIRef/BNode/Literal) so identity reuses CPython string interning; Literal hash = str_hash XOR hash(lang.lower()) XOR hash(datatype) to fold the 3-tuple into one dict key
Context/quad layering: triple->{context:quoted_bool} map plus inverse context->set(triple) map sit on top of the shared triple indices so named graphs share one physical edge (dedup across graphs)
SPARQL BGP evaluation as recursive algebra with dynamic triple-pattern reordering by count of already-bound variables (most-selective-first heuristic), no cost statistics needed
Lazy nested-loop join (evalLazyJoin) with push-down of bound variables into the next pattern and FrozenBindings immutable solution mappings instead of materializing intermediate relations
Pluggable Store API (add/remove/triples(pattern)/contexts) decoupling the graph algebra from physical storage (memory, BerkeleyDB, remote SPARQL)
repos.nest_application: Adopt the three-permutation triple index as a new OPTIONAL nest-format section (next reserved id 0x09) to deliver the north-star "graph search" capability over chunk relationships. Concretely: in nest-format add a graph_index section storing edges as three sorted little-endian u32 arrays (SPO, POS, OSP) over integer-densified term ids, plus a term dictionary section mapping term-id->canonical string (reuse the existing chunk_ids interning pattern). Because each permutation is monotonically sorted, store it delta+varint or just sort and let zstd(non-embedding section) crush it -- graph edges are highly compressible, which directly serves "compress more than everyone." In nest-runtime add a graph::TripleIndex that mmaps the three arrays and does binary-search prefix walks (no dict, no allocation) to answer any bound-pattern, then port RDFLib's most-bound-first BGP reordering as a deterministic seeded join order (alphabetical/id-order tiebreak) so multi-hop graph queries stay reproducible and never panic (typed thiserror). nest-cli gains a search-graph subcommand; nest-python exposes pattern queries. The XOR-folded term hashing and str-interning idea informs how to dedup term strings in the dictionary section. Files stay <=300 loc by splitting graph/term_dict.rs, graph/index.rs, graph/join.rs.
repos.compression_relevance: High for the graph modality: the three-permutation layout looks 3x redundant but each permutation is a sorted integer sequence, so delta-coding + zstd makes the redundancy near-free while unlocking direction-agnostic queries; term-id densification + a string dictionary turns long repeated URIs/strings into small ints (dictionary compression), and cross-graph edge sharing (one physical edge, many contexts) is exactly the dedup nest wants when compressing whole databases/repos into one .nest container.
repos.license: BSD-3-Clause
repos.perf_notes: Pure Python, dict-of-dict-of-dict: fast for interactive use but memory-heavy (every edge stored 3x as Python objects, ~hundreds of bytes/triple) and not mmap-able; scales to ~low millions of triples in RAM, not billions. The lazy nested-loop join has no hash-join, so large joins are O(n*m) in the worst case. nest should keep the algorithmic shape (3 permutations, most-bound-first reorder) but replace Python dicts with sorted mmap'd u32 arrays + binary search to get zero-allocation, SIMD-free but cache-friendly prefix scans straight off disk.

repos.one_liner: A Git-for-data document/graph database whose Rust storage core (terminus-store) stores RDF triples as immutable, content-addressed delta layers built from HDT-derived succinct data structures (front-coded string dictionaries, bit-packed integer arrays, and rank/select bit vectors over adjacency lists), reaching ~13 bytes per triple.
repos.core_innovation: Decompose data into integer-ID triples and store the whole thing as a stack of immutable, content-addressed "delta layers", where each layer is built entirely from query-time-no-decompression succinct structures: a Plain-Front-Coded (PFC) string dictionary that assigns implicit integer IDs by sorted position, bit-packed fixed-width LogArrays for the ID columns, and a two-level block/superblock rank-select bit index over adjacency-list bit sequences. Compression and the queryable index are the SAME bytes, so you search directly on the compressed form, and new data is just another append-only layer addressed by the hash of its content.
key_techniques: Plain Front Coding (PFC) string dictionary: lexicographically sort strings, fixed-size buckets, store shared-prefix-length + suffix per entry; ID = implicit sorted position; bidirectional id<->string via bucket binary search (Martinez-Prieto INFOSYS 2016)
LogArray: bit-packed array of fixed-width integers using ceil(log2(max+1)) bits per slot instead of fixed u32/u64, with explicit on-disk width header for portability

Two-level rank/select BitIndex: 64-bit blocks grouped into superblocks (SBLOCK_SIZE=52), precomputed block+superblock popcount tables stored as LogArrays; rank = sblock_rank + block_rank + masked popcount; select via binary search over superblocks then a 64-bit scan
Adjacency-list triple encoding: SP and SPO orderings expressed as bit sequences + LogArrays (HDT bitmap-triples model) so subject->predicate->object navigation is rank/select with no pointers

Content-addressed immutable delta layers: every commit is a new layer named by a 20-byte hash; additions+removals stored separately; queries resolve current state by traversing the layer stack newest-wins
Delta rollup compaction: periodically squash the layer stack into a fresh base layer to bound read amplification and in-memory footprint
Single-archive on-disk format (v0.20+): all primitive structure files for a layer bundled into one mmap-friendly archive blob, ~13 bytes/triple on billion-triple sets
Buffer-oriented zero-copy structures: every structure is parsed as a view over an existing (mmappable) byte buffer rather than heap-constructed, so reads operate straight off disk
repos.nest_application: Two concrete steals into nest-format. (1) Add a PFC codec (encoding id in the reserved 4-255 range) for the non-embedding string sections, primarily chunk_ids and provenance, and for nest's future json/yaml/dataset payloads: front-coding crushes URI/path/repeated-prefix data far below generic zstd while staying queryable. Implement as crates/nest-format/src/encoding/pfc.rs plus a bucketed FrontCodedDict reader in nest-runtime so id<->string lookups run zero-copy off mmap. (2) Add a LogArray + two-level rank/select BitIndex primitive (crates/nest-runtime/src/succinct/ logarray.rs + bitindex.rs, each <300 lines) and use it to shrink the HNSW index section (0x07): replace u32 neighbor-id arrays with ceil(log2(N))-bit LogArrays and represent level/neighbor occupancy bitsets with rank/select. This directly attacks the 'tiny' preset size ratio (0.283) by removing wasted high bits in every adjacency list while keeping deterministic, seekable layout. The content-addressed delta-layer idea maps onto nest's existing content_hash + nest://content_hash/chunk_id citation model: it is the blueprint for nest's real-time-edit goal, append an immutable additive layer-section (reserved id 0x09+) carrying added/removed chunk_ids + embeddings, resolved newest-wins at query time, with periodic rollup to a fresh base file, all without breaking the FROZEN v1 single-file determinism.
repos.compression_relevance: Directly central to nest's north star of compress-more-than-everyone. PFC is a domain-specific entropy win on exactly the structured/prefix-heavy data nest wants to ingest (paths, URIs, JSON keys, dataset columns) that generic zstd misses, and it stays query-without-decompress. LogArray + rank/select removes the largest source of slack in nest's ANN index (fixed-width 32-bit IDs over small N), shrinking the index section that dominates the 'tiny' preset footprint. The ~13 bytes/triple result is the proof that succinct-but-queryable beats compress-then-decompress for the search hot path, the same principle nest already applies by never zstd-compressing embeddings.
repos.perf_notes: Succinct structures are queried with no decompression: rank/select are O(1) (block+superblock table lookup plus one 64-bit popcount); select is O(log superblocks) binary search then a single-word scan. All structures are buffer-views (Bytes) over a single mmappable archive, so reads happen straight off disk with zero heap copy, architecturally identical to nest's mmap+SIMD hot path. Reported ~13 bytes/triple in-memory on billion-triple datasets. Two-level index overhead is small (blocks every 64 bits, superblocks every 52 blocks, a few percent). Cost: read amplification grows with layer-stack depth, mitigated by periodic delta rollup, a tradeoff nest must budget if it adopts append-only edit layers.
repos.license: Apache-2.0 (both terminusdb and terminusdb-store)

repos.one_liner: A tokio-backed immutable triple store whose entire on-disk format is built from succinct data structures (front-coded dictionaries, minimum-bit-width packed integer arrays, and two-level rank/select bit indexes) queried directly from mmapped bytes with no decompression step, reaching ~13.6 bytes/triple on 17B-triple graphs.
repos.core_innovation: Store integer columns and string dictionaries in succinct, query-in-place encodings so the file IS the index: data stays compressed on disk and in the page cache yet supports O(1) random access (LogArray.entry) and O(1) rank/select navigation (BitIndex) without ever materializing a decompressed copy. This is the missing middle for nest between "raw f32 (fast, big)" and "zstd block (small, but must decompress to read one element)".
key_techniques: LogArray: pack N unsigned ints at W = ceil(log2(max+1)) bits each into 64-bit words plus a trailing control word holding N (u32) and W (u8); entry(i) reads at most two words and shifts/masks W bits

BitIndex two-level rank/select: per-64-bit-block popcount counts in a LogArray plus per-superblock (52 blocks) cumulative counts in a second LogArray; rank1 = sblock_rank - block_rank + count_ones(masked word); select1 = binary search over superblocks then linear block scan
use_linear_bitscan cache-line shortcut: if start and end share a 512-byte cache line, popcount-scan directly instead of consulting the index

Plain Front Coding (PFC) dictionary: sort strings, group in blocks of 8, store block head verbatim, each successor as vbyte(common-prefix-len)+nul-terminated suffix; prefix compression plus binary-searchable string<->id both ways
AdjacencyList = LogArray (right-hand values) + BitIndex (1-bit marks last pair of each left id); traverse a subject's predicates via rank/select with zero stored pointers
vbyte (HDT-style, msb=last-byte flag) for prefix-length and gap encoding inside dictionary blocks
WaveletTree over a u64 sequence (log2(alphabet) bitarray layers) for positional/range/reverse-traversal queries
TFC typed dictionary: order-preserving per-XSD-datatype byte encodings (sign-magnitude varint integers, decimals, datetimes) so numeric values stay sorted and front-codable in one dictionary
repos.nest_application: Add a succinct integer/string codec family to nest-format under crates/nest-format/src/encoding using reserved v1 encoding ids 4-255 (additive, no version bump). (1) Encode chunk_ids and monotone offset arrays (chunks_original_spans, per-section length tables) as a LogArray: ~64k chunks need ~17 bits not 32/64, cutting those sections ~2x with O(1) mmap random access and zero decode on cite/materialize. (2) Add a PFC front-coded dictionary codec for repetitive string metadata (provenance fields, source URIs, tags, BM25 vocabulary in bm25_index 0x08); prefix sharing beats per-field zstd for sorted short strings and stays binary-searchable from mmap. (3) Port BitIndex rank/select into nest-runtime for sparse presence/tombstone bitmaps (optional-field presence, deleted chunks for real-time edit) at ~1.05 bits/bit with O(1) navigation. (4) The two-level rank/select plus cache-line bitscan upgrades BM25 posting lists and any future graph-search adjacency without pointer overhead. Keep deterministic (sorted/seeded), but flip terminusdb's big-endian words to little-endian per nest's constraint; each module fits the <=300-line single-responsibility rule.
repos.compression_relevance: Directly central to "compress more than everyone": succinct structures give near-entropy size while keeping random access, which is exactly nest's bind since embeddings must be scored from mmap and block compressors are banned on the hot path. LogArray/BitIndex/PFC compress every surrounding integer/string/offset/index section without the full-block decode that zstd forces, complementing zstd (cold sections only) and the f16/int8 quantizers. They do not shrink the dense embedding matrix itself.
repos.perf_notes: Block=64 bits (one register), superblock=52 blocks. rank1 is O(1): two LogArray lookups + one word read + hardware popcount; select1 is O(log #superblocks) binary search then linear block scan; use_linear_bitscan skips the index when a range fits a 512-byte cache line. LogArray.entry(i) touches at most 2 contiguous words (cache-friendly). PFC blocks of 8 bound the suffix walk to 7 strings. All structures are immutable/read-only: lock-free, trivially parallel, matching nest's mmap-and-serve model. Reported density ~13.57 bytes/triple at 17B triples with a full 6-way index.
repos.license: Apache-2.0

repos.compression_relevance: Essentially none. openCypher is a language specification (grammar + formal semantics + conformance tests). It contains no entropy coder, quantization, columnar layout, delta encoding, or any storage/compression machinery. The only tangential link is that a Cypher-subset query AST could one day be the textual surface for nest's aspirational graph-search feature, but that touches query ergonomics, not byte-level compaction. For the north-star goal of compressing data more than everyone, this repo offers nothing directly.
repos.core_innovation: The TCK's canonical, encoding-independent result model: every query outcome (primitives, lists, maps, nodes, relationships, paths) has a single deterministic string serialization plus an explicit ordered-vs-unordered-set comparison semantics, so two conforming engines are declared equivalent by comparing normalized outputs rather than internal representations.
key_techniques: TCK canonical result-table serialization: one normalized string form per value (single-quoted strings, [v0,v1] lists, {k:v} maps, (:Label {p:v}) nodes, [:Type] rels)
Explicit unordered-multiset vs ordered-sequence result comparison (ORDER BY + 'in order' asserts sequence; otherwise set equality)
Side-effect accounting as observable deltas only (nodes/rels/properties/labels added/removed), transient state ignored
Typed errors tagged with compile-vs-runtime phase (SyntaxError/SemanticError/TypeError raised at parse|runtime)
Single-source XML grammar deterministically generating ANTLR4 .g4 + ISO-14977 EBNF + railroad diagrams via Java/XSLT, with --INCLUDE_LEGACY gating
Reusable named deterministic fixture graphs (binary-tree-1/2) shared across conformance scenarios
repos.nest_application: See detailed field; two adaptations -- a golden-file search-conformance harness (nest-cli/tests) that machine-checks the search_contract (ann results rerank to identical real-cosine top-k across exact/tiny/hybrid presets, proving query-layer determinism the way content_hash proves storage-layer determinism), and a single-source format-spec codegen pattern in nest-format so the FROZEN .nest layout and its diataxis docs cannot drift. Both are test/codegen scaffolding only; the additive v1 format is untouched.
repos.one_liner: openCypher is the open specification of the Cypher property-graph query language -- an XML-sourced grammar that generates ANTLR4/EBNF/railroad artifacts, plus a Cucumber-based Technology Compatibility Kit that defines engine conformance via canonically-serialized, order-aware query result tables.
repos.perf_notes: No runtime performance characteristics relevant to nest: this is a build-time specification and test corpus (Maven, Scala 2.12/2.13 cross-compile, Java/XSLT grammar generation, Cucumber execution). No SIMD, no memory-mapped data, no hot-path concerns. Value is entirely in determinism/conformance methodology, not throughput.
repos.license: Apache License 2.0 (with an additional grant-of-rights / no-derivative-grammar-name clause per the openCypher project terms). Permissive enough to learn from and adapt the methodology; nest would only borrow ideas/conventions, not code or grammar.

synthesis.summary: The semantic-rdf category (Jena, RDF4J, Oxigraph, RDFLib, terminusdb-store/tdb-succinct, openCypher) converges on one architecture nest can mine hard: store data as integer-ID triples, dictionary-encode every repeated term once, and index those IDs in multiple sorted permutations so any query shape is a prefix range scan. The frontier splits into two storage philosophies. (A) Dictionary + B-tree/LSM (Jena TDB2, RDF4J, Oxigraph): map terms to compact IDs, inline small scalars/strings into the ID itself to skip the dictionary, and keep multiple permutation indexes. The standout trick is value inlining: Jena packs i56/decimal/date/bool/range-reduced-double into the 8-byte NodeId, Oxigraph inlines <16-byte strings + native i64/i128/dateTime into a fixed 17-byte record, RDF4J uses an order-preserving varint whose length is recoverable from byte 1 so encoded keys binary-search WITHOUT decoding. (B) Succinct query-in-place (terminusdb-store, tdb-succinct): the file IS the index, no decompress step, reaching ~13 bytes/triple on billions of triples via Plain Front Coding string dictionaries, bit-packed LogArrays (ceil(log2(max+1)) bits/int instead of fixed 32/64), and two-level rank/select BitIndex over adjacency lists. This succinct family is the single most important steal for nest: it is the missing middle between "raw f32 (fast, big)" and "zstd block (small, must decompress to read one element)", and it is architecturally identical to nest's mmap-and-scan-off-disk model. Grounding the analysis in the codebase: nest's HNSW codec (crates/nest-runtime/src/ann/codec.rs) stores neighbor IDs as fixed u32 regardless of N, and the BM25 codec (crates/nest-runtime/src/bm25/codec.rs) stores raw term strings and u32 doc/tf postings with no front-coding or delta/varint, so both optional sections carry exactly the high-bit slack and structural redundancy LogArray/PFC/varint remove. The encoding dispatch (crates/nest-format/src/encoding/mod.rs::decode_payload) and reserved encoding IDs 4-255 plus reserved section IDs 0x09+ (crates/nest-format/src/layout/mod.rs) give clean additive extension points, so every recommendation lands inside v1 with no NEST_FORMAT_VERSION bump. openCypher is a non-storage spec (low value): it contributes only a conformance-harness methodology for proving search determinism, not compression.
synthesis.state_of_the_art: Two coexisting storage philosophies. (1) Dictionary + permutation indexes: every distinct RDF term is mapped to a small integer ID; indexes store only IDs (4-17 bytes/term) in multiple sorted permutations (SPO/POS/OSP for triples, +context for quads) so any bound-prefix pattern is a sorted range scan with no query planner needed. Three increasingly aggressive inlining variants eliminate the dictionary for common values: Jena TDB2 inlines scalars into a tagged 8-byte NodeId (bit63 ptr-vs-value, then i56/decimal/date/bool/range-reduced-double); RDF4J packs a 2-bit type tag into the ID and uses an order-preserving varint (length recoverable from byte 1, byte-order == numeric-order so you binary-search encoded keys without decoding); Oxigraph uses a fixed 17-byte type-byte+16-byte record that inlines <16-byte UTF-8 strings and native i64/i128-fixed-point-decimal/dateTime, hashing only large strings into an id2str side table (content-addressed: identical value -> identical id, no forward index). (2) Succinct query-in-place (terminusdb-store, tdb-succinct): the compressed bytes ARE the queryable index, no decompression step. Plain Front Coding (sort strings, bucket by 8, store shared-prefix-len + suffix, implicit ID = sorted position, bidirectional via bucket binary search); LogArray (pack N ints at ceil(log2(max+1)) bits with an on-disk width header, entry(i) touches at most 2 words); two-level rank/select BitIndex (64-bit blocks, 52-block superblocks, precomputed popcount tables, O(1) rank / O(log superblocks) select, plus a cache-line linear-bitscan shortcut); adjacency lists as LogArray-of-values + BitIndex-marks so navigation needs zero stored pointers. This reaches ~13.6 bytes/triple at 17B triples with a full 6-way index. Cross-cutting: big-endian keys so lexicographic order == numeric order for range scans (nest must use little-endian per constraint, so it pays an explicit comparator or stores keys sorted and binary-searches by decoded value); content-addressed immutable delta layers (terminusdb) for git-for-data append-only edits with newest-wins resolution + periodic rollup. openCypher contributes only conformance methodology (canonical result serialization, ordered-vs-set comparison, side-effect-as-delta accounting), no storage or compression machinery.
top_innovations: Succinct LogArray (bit-pack ints at ceil(log2(max+1)) bits/slot, not fixed 32/64, with on-disk width header) - query-in-place, O(1) random access off mmap, the highest-leverage steal because it directly shrinks nest's existing fixed-u32 HNSW neighbor IDs and span/offset arrays with zero decode (tdb-succinct, terminusdb-store)

Plain Front Coding string dictionary (sort, bucket by 8, store shared-prefix-len + suffix, implicit ID = sorted position, bidirectional binary search) - crushes URI/path/repeated-prefix data below generic zstd while staying binary-searchable from mmap; directly attacks BM25 vocabulary, chunk_ids, provenance, and future json/yaml/dataset keys (tdb-succinct, terminusdb-store)

Dictionary-encode-then-store-only-IDs with order-preserving varint (length recoverable from byte 1, byte-order == numeric-order so encoded keys binary-search without decoding) - removes structural redundancy before the entropy stage so it stacks under zstd (RDF4J, terminusdb TFC)

Hash-or-inline typed-value encoding (inline <16-byte strings + native i64/i128-fixed-point/dateTime/bool; replace only large strings with a content hash into id2str) - turns repetitive structured metadata into fixed content-addressed records, deterministic and dedup-at-value-level before bytes (Oxigraph, Jena NodeId)

Two-level rank/select BitIndex (64-bit blocks, 52-block superblocks, precomputed popcount LogArrays, O(1) rank, cache-line linear-bitscan shortcut) - pointer-free navigation primitive for sparse presence/tombstone bitmaps, BM25 posting lists, and graph adjacency (tdb-succinct)

Multi-permutation sorted-ID indexes (SPO/POS/OSP) so any bound-prefix graph pattern is an index-only range scan with no query planner - the on-disk substrate for nest's north-star graph search (Jena, RDF4J, Oxigraph, RDFLib)

Adjacency-list-as-LogArray+BitIndex (HDT bitmap-triples): store edges with zero pointers, navigate src->rel->dst via rank/select - ~13 bytes/triple, makes graph edges highly compressible (terminusdb-store)

Content-addressed immutable delta layers (each commit = a hash-named layer of adds/removes, newest-wins, periodic rollup) - blueprint for nest's real-time-edit goal without breaking single-file determinism (terminusdb-store)

Most-bound-first BGP triple-pattern reordering by count of bound variables (no cost statistics needed) - a deterministic, seeded multi-hop graph join order that stays reproducible (RDFLib, Jena stats.opt)

xloader external-merge-sort bulk build (stream tuples, sort via external sort, compress intermediate spill runs, build each index as a separate streamed pass) - removes the in-RAM ceiling from nest's deterministic builder for corpora exceeding memory (Jena)

Register a new reserved encoding id (4-255) in decode_payload's match arm.

compression_wins: LogArray on HNSW neighbor IDs: the tiny preset's index section currently stores every edge as a fixed u32; packing at ceil(log2(N)) bits removes 10-20 wasted high bits per neighbor across the densest part of the smallest preset, directly lowering the 0.283 size ratio with zero query-time decode.

LogArray on offset/length arrays (chunks_original_spans, per-section length tables, chunk index): ~64k chunks need ~17 bits not 32/64, roughly halving those sections while keeping O(1) mmap random access for cite/materialize.

Plain Front Coding on sorted string sections (BM25 vocabulary, chunk_ids, provenance, future json/yaml/dataset keys): prefix sharing beats per-field zstd on sorted short strings/URIs/paths and stays binary-searchable, a domain-specific entropy win orthogonal to and stackable with zstd.

Delta+varint BM25 posting lists: monotone doc IDs become small gaps, and order-preserving varint shrinks both doc gaps and tf to 1-2 bytes vs fixed 8 bytes/posting on the largest part of the bm25 section.

Dictionary-encode repeated provenance/metadata into one per-file string/namespace table storing only small IDs: redundancy becomes integer locality, beating zstd-on-raw because dedup happens at the semantic-value level before the entropy coder runs.

Native typed-column encoding for structured payloads (json/yaml/parquet/datasets): integers/dates/bools/decimals stored as i56/i64/i128-fixed-point/ms-epoch instead of text+span, eliminating JSON text bloat and per-value span offsets that zstd still pays for, then optionally zstd-wrapped on top.

Graph-edge permutations compress near-free: each SPO/OSP permutation is a sorted integer sequence, so delta-coding + zstd makes the multi-permutation redundancy cheap while unlocking direction-agnostic queries; cross-context edge sharing dedups when swallowing whole databases/repos.

Succinct query-in-place is the strategic win: LogArray/PFC/BitIndex give near-entropy size WITH random access, the missing middle between raw-f32 and zstd-block, letting nest compress every non-embedding integer/string/offset/index section without the full-block decode zstd forces, while leaving the embedding hot path untouched.
watch_outs: Big-endian assumption: RDF stores use big-endian keys so lexicographic byte order equals numeric order, enabling comparator-free range scans. nest mandates little-endian, so naive LE packing breaks byte-order==value-order. Either store keys pre-sorted and binary-search by decoded value, or use an explicit order-preserving codec; do not silently inherit the big-endian range-scan trick.

Permutation index storage multiplies: 6 SPOG permutations cost ~6x index storage (RDF4J ~120-130 bytes/quad at 3 permutations). Graph/triple indexing MUST be an optional section (0x09+) gated by a capability flag, and nest should ship the minimum permutation set (e.g. SPO + one inverse), or default builds stop being tiny.

Do NOT vendor RocksDB (Oxigraph), LMDB (RDF4J), tokio (terminusdb-store), or any Java (Jena/RDF4J/RDFLib): these bring C++ LSM, server/async, or JVM dependencies that violate nest's small single-file offline-by-construction core. Clean-room the encoding ideas in Rust; reimplement layouts as flat mmap'd sorted sections, which is simpler and faster to read than an LSM and matches nest's zero-server model.

Keep the never-compress-embeddings rule intact: every steal here targets non-embedding sections (IDs, strings, offsets, indexes, metadata, graph edges). The dense embedding matrix stays raw f32/f16/int8 scored from mmap on the hot path; succinct structures do NOT shrink it and must not be placed in its path.

Substitute nest's SHA-256 for Oxigraph's SipHash and terminusdb's MD5/20-byte content hashes to preserve the single four-integrity-surface hash family; SHA-256 is slower but is paid at build time, not on the search hot path, so there is no runtime cost.

Content-addressed delta layers add read amplification that grows with stack depth; adopting append-only edit layers requires periodic rollup and an explicit depth budget, and must preserve content_hash/citation byte-exactness so nest://content_hash/chunk_id never breaks.

Determinism: HNSW must stay seeded and BM25 alphabetical; PFC bucketing, LogArray width selection, varint encoding, and any graph term-id densification must be a pure deterministic function of sorted input so same chunks + same model fingerprint still yields a byte-identical file. Most-bound-first BGP reordering needs an explicit id-order tiebreak to stay reproducible.

Additive-only discipline: use reserved encoding ids 4-255 and section ids 0x09+; bump only the in-section payload version (HNSW_PAYLOAD_VERSION, BM25_PAYLOAD_VERSION) for codec changes, never NEST_FORMAT_VERSION, and never let new optional sections enter content_hash (which is the canonical six only) or citations across corpora break.

Library code must never panic: all new codecs (LogArray width overflow, PFC bucket bounds, varint EOF, graph term-id range) must return typed thiserror NestError/RuntimeError, matching the existing ByteCursor EOF-as-error pattern in ann/codec.rs and bm25/codec.rs, not unwrap/index-panic.

File hygiene: every new module must stay <=300 lines (333 hard cap) and single-responsibility. Split graph into term_dict.rs/index.rs/join.rs and succinct into logarray.rs/bitindex.rs/pfc.rs rather than one large file.
openCypher is near-zero compression value: do not invest in Cypher grammar/TCK as a compression source. Borrow only the conformance-test methodology for proving search determinism, and only if cheap.

repos.one_liner: A durable, immutable Datalog database that ports DataScript onto a content-addressed Hitchhiker tree (a fractal B+ tree with buffered write-logs) over the konserve pluggable KV store, giving append-only temporal facts, snapshot/time-travel, and structural-sharing dedup.
repos.core_innovation: Content-addressed persistent index nodes: every tree node is stored under an ID that is a cryptographic hash (hasch, SHA-512) of the node's own contents, so identical sub-structures across versions/snapshots automatically collapse to the same physical block (structural sharing + dedup for free), and a whole database version is named by a single root hash. This is the same idea nest already uses for content_hash, but pushed down to per-block granularity so that incremental edits only write the changed nodes while unchanged nodes are shared by reference.
key_techniques: Hitchhiker (fractal) tree: B+ tree whose internal index nodes carry a bounded append-log of pending insert/retract ops, flushed downward in batches only when the buffer overflows, amortizing write amplification across many mutations
Content-addressed nodes: node UUID = hash(node contents) via hasch SHA-512, yielding deterministic IDs, automatic dedup, and verifiable integrity (analogous to nest per-section SHA-256)
Datom = [entity, attribute, value, tx] fact tuples stored in three sorted covering indexes EAVT / AEVT / AVET, giving column-store-like locality without a separate columnar layout
Append-only fact log: retractions are new datoms with an assertion flag, so history is never overwritten; time-travel (as-of / history) is a filter over tx ids, with snapshots sharing structure
Block granularity in KV: leaf data nodes hold a sorted vector of many datoms (a block), not one-datom-per-key, cutting KV overhead and improving scan locality
konserve KV abstraction decoupling logical index from physical store (File/LMDB/S3/JDBC), with only the root-id map mutated in place
GDPR 'excision': because facts are addressable, specific historical values can be purged while keeping the rest of the immutable log intact
repos.nest_application: Two concrete steals into nest-format and nest-runtime. (1) In nest-format hashing.rs: extend nest's content_hash model to PER-BLOCK content-addressed chunk nodes so that when nest gains real-time edit, an edit rewrites only the touched blocks and shares unchanged ones by their SHA-256 id inside the single .nest file -- this is exactly the structural-sharing dedup that lets a v2 'append region' grow without rewriting the whole file, while keeping byte-determinism. (2) In nest-runtime, model edits/retractions as an append-only fact log (a reserved section 0x09+, additive within v1) carrying [chunk_id, op, tx] tuples plus a small fractal-style buffered-flush index, so temporal 'as-of' queries and undo become a filter over tx ids without mutating frozen sections -- gives nest the 'real-time edit' and 'temporal' pillars of the north star while preserving the frozen-format/offline/deterministic guarantees. The EAVT/AEVT/AVET sorted-covering-index trick informs how to lay out a future graph-search section (chunk-relations) as sorted tuple blocks scored directly off mmap.
repos.compression_relevance: Medium-high for compression specifically: the per-block content-addressed structural sharing IS a compression mechanism -- duplicate chunks/embeddings/index-nodes across versions or across similar corpora deduplicate to a single physical block, so a multi-version or multi-corpus .nest pays once. This directly serves 'compress more than everyone' when nest stores whole evolving databases/repos with overlapping content, and the fractal write-buffer keeps that dedup cheap under real-time edit instead of forcing full re-encode.
repos.perf_notes: Hitchhiker tree trades a small read cost (must merge a node's pending log on read) for large write-amplification savings: O(buffered) flushes instead of per-insert rebalances, ideal for high-ingest append workloads. Block-granular leaves give sequential scan locality similar to a column store. Content-addressing makes reads cache-friendly and integrity-checkable but adds a hash computation per node write (SHA-512 there; nest would reuse its existing SHA-256 surfaces, no new dependency). All structures are persistent/immutable so reads are lock-free -- aligns with nest's mmap read path.

repos.compression_relevance: Indirect but real. The structural-sharing copy-on-write B+ tree is the cheapest known way to make an append-only single-file container support edits without rewriting (or duplicating) the whole file: an edit costs ~3 dirty nodes, so versioned/edited corpora compress dramatically vs naive re-serialization. Node arenas of packed sorted keys are also delta/front-coding friendly (shared prefixes between adjacent keys), and the index itself is a non-embedding section so it is eligible for nest's zstd codec. It does NOT compress embeddings, but it directly unlocks the 'real-time edit' north-star while preserving single-file size discipline.
repos.perf_notes: In-memory range scans ~3x faster than Clojure's built-in sorted-set due to contiguous-array nodes and cache-friendly binary search within a node. Bulk insert via transients is 2-3x faster than persistent conj. Per-edit persistence touches only ~log_b(N) nodes (~3 for millions of elements at depth 3). Lazy restore means read working set ~ query reach, not total size — ideal pairing with mmap demand paging. No SIMD; the win is allocation/IO economy, not raw scan throughput, so it complements rather than competes with nest's SIMD dot-product hot path (which must stay on raw mmap embeddings).
